MY BAIRNIES. My bairnies!—they are round me. They whisper at the door; . Their little feet climb up the stair, And patter on the floor: They come and nestle by me, . I hear their laughing words; They come, they go, I hear them pass, Like a flight of reckless birds! My bairnies they are bonny,' With curls of golden hue, The roses in their blooming cheeks, Their laughing eyes of blue: I raise the winsome faces And kiss them o'er ando'er ; I think that time has sent them back Across its boundless shore. My bairnies! I am dreaming The years have come and gone, And empty is my little nest, • My birds are fledged and flown! The bairnies come no longer, The days are sadly still; I pace the empty homeless rooms, And come and go at will. _ My bairnies shall I know them In the home beyond the skies, With golden crowns upon their brows, And glory in their eyes? Shalld claim you, 0 my bairnies, With a sweet subdued surprise, Th 3 loved old faces found again In earth's new Paradise? —Tinsley's Majazine for March

That was a wise prayer of the aged saint, when the close of his_ pilgrimage drew nigh: "pow, Lord, for grace to end

Well." Being less annoyed at the defects of others is one of the best proofs that we are approaching freedom from defects ourselves. ' Some lives are like footprints on the hard rock, enduring for ever; and some are like a footprint in the sand, to be erased by the coming tide. The infinity of God is not mysterious, it is only unfathom- able—not concealed, but incomprehensible. It is a clear infinity—the darkness of the pure, unsearchable sea.— Buskin. "'What kind of a picture would you prefer, miss?" in- quired the photographer of a young lady customer. "Well," was the reply, "take me with an expression as if I were writing a poem on love." Mark Twain is credited with a smart epigram on Science —it gives you such wholesale returns of conjecture for such trifling investments of fact. Science smiles, but replies that what is not fact is not Science. " .04.*A1M Little Arthur had been to church. "flow did you like the sermon?" asked his sister. "Pretty well," responded the youthful eritic. "The beginning was -very good, and so AU the end; but—it had too much middle." A clergyman, whose peculiarities of preaching were pro- verbial, and who was blessed with a temper of great value, was one day told by a parishioner that he did not like his sermons. "Well," said the old man, "I do not wonder at it; I don't like them much myself." Thinking to stock his depleted larder, an editor advertised "Poultry taken in exchange for advertising." The villain- ous compositor, seeing his opportunity to put up a long- standing grudge, set it up, "Poetry taken, &c.," and since that time the office boy has been clearing -five shillings a day from the waste paper man. There are men who are living practical Christian lives, who pray, who love God and believe in Christ, but who have so habituated themselves to think they are not Chris- tians, that they keep in the old ruts, when a very slight change of the switch would put them on the right track. It is a change that they need to make, and then the cause would gain much from them.—Golden Rule. A lady engaged a raw new servant, who, of course, pro- feeeed to be worthy of fabulous wages, and had only left her last place because the locality or the society did not suit her. The new Phillis was instructed to prepare a hare for dinner, and an hour afterwards came up in great trouble. "Sure, ma'am, was it to prepare the cratur for dinner ye axed me? It's my two arrums is aching wid picking the baste, an sorra a bit cane is it now." She had been trying to pick the hare like a fowl! Marshal Turenne happening one hot day to be looking out at the window of his antechamber, a servant entered the room. and, deceived by his dress,' mistook him for tone of the under cooks. He came softly behind him, and with a hand which wai not one of the lightest gave him a vio- lent slap on the rear part of his person. The Marshal in- stantly turned about; and the fellow, frightened out of his wits, beheld the face of his master. Down he dropped on his knees. "Oh ! my lord! I thought it was George." "And suppose it had been George," replied the Marshal, "you need not have struck so hard." - PHYSICAL EXERCISES IN BOARD SCHOOLS.—We are glad to learn that the authorities of Board schools in some large 1 towns are now giving their attention to the physical, as well as the mental, training of the children under their charge. Systematic instruction, by special teachers, in the simpler gymnastic exercises, is being given in some schools twice, or oftener, weekly, being officially recognised as an integral portion of the education to be afforded to boys and girls alike; and proficiency in physical performances is being stimulated and rewarded by occasional public dis- plays and by suitable prizes and distinctions. This is as it should be, and we hope the good practice to which we refer may soon' become general throughout the schools of the country. Those who have the care of young persons in schools may do much in aiding the physical development of their pupils; and, as a consequence, in making their lives longer and happier, by the judicious use of the gymnasium. —British iledical Journal. ,a HOTTENTOT HABITS.—When food can begot the Hotten- tots are enormous eaters. Suppose an elephant or any other large animal is killed, the kraal, as soon as the news reaches it, strike the tents, and remove to the vicinity of the car- case, finding it easier to remove their houses to the game than to bring thegameto their houses. Then ensues a scene of gorg- ing. The meat is roughly boiled, and men,women,andehildren —supposing there is enough and to spare for all—commence to gorge themselves, full to repletion, they throw them- selves back and sleep for a few hours in a :torpid condition, only to wake up and again attack the provender until the picked bones attest the trencher powers of the assembled village. In a hot climate meat must be soon eaten, but semi-putrefaction is no barrier to a Hottentot; if anything, he rather likes his game "high." We have hinted that sleep is one of the blessings of life which the Hottentot makes use of in no stinted measure. He can sleep at any time. If he has taken a full meal, he takes his sleep; if he is gorged after an eating bout, he is forced to sleep; and if he is hungry, he simply tightens his belt and drops off to sleep as a relief to his hungry thoughts and the pain of gnawing hunger. • Like Sancho Panza he says, if not in words at least in sentiment, "God bless the man that first invented sleep. It covers a man all over, longings and all, as with a garment; it is food for the hungry and drink for the thirsty; heat for the cold and cold for the hot; God bless the man that first invented sleep."—" The Peoples of Me World."

KING JAMES I. OF SCOTLAND AS A POBT.—Bing James I. of Scotland, born in 1394, was intercepted at sea, and made prisoner by Henry IV., in 1405. He was educated in England during the reign of Henry V. Every attempt was made to train him in English habits of thought, and by marriage with Jane Beaufort he was attached to the Royal Family of England. His love for Lady Jane Beaufort was expressed in a poem of some length, called "The King's Quair," which means the King's little book, written before his release. King James returned to Scotland soon after the death of Henry V., was crowned at Scone in 1424, and was for twelve years a vigorous Scottish king, endeavouring to establish law and order among turbulent nobles, and to assure the rights and just liberties of his people. His firm upholding of justice led to his assassination in 1430. A famous old poem, that dwells heartily upon the humours of a festival day in a Scottish town "Peblis to the Play," is agcribed to King James I. by John Mair, who was born 33 years after the King's death. Though James Vs authorship b4lB been questioned, no evidence in favour of anotherauthor is as good as this. The first words forming the old title to " Peblis the Play" are "At Beltane ;" the subject of the poem is the Beltane festival at Peebles, and, as Mair says, others, when the original could not be got at, gave imita- tions of it, when the scene was laid elsewhere. We have such an imitation extant in the poem of "Christ's Kirk on the Green," which describes, after the manner of "Peebles to the Play," a rustic festival, of which the scene seems to be laid at Leslie, in Aberdeenshire, where the ruins of an 014 Christ's Kirk still stands on a green, and a fair used to be held. The other imitations of King James's playful *ketch of life among his people have been lost. In choice of the theme of "Peebles to the Play" there was a poet's feeling. Beltane Day was an ancient festival, originating in the days of Celtic paganism,held on old-May Day by the Bcots, and in Ireland on the 21st of June, at the time of the solstice. The word Beii-tine meant Eel's fire; Bel being one of the old Celtic names of the sun. Advance of the can's beneficent power over the earth fixed the time of this ancient festival for joyous worship of one of the great forces of nature. The celebration was first and last a rustic one, aid it was kept at last especially by cowherds, who gathered in the fields and dressed themselves a dinner of boiledmilk ed and eggs, with cakes of mystical form, design, doubtless, by heathen priests of old, for they were studded with lumps in the shape of nipples. Peebles kept Beltane Day with so much holiday fun that strangers were &awn even from Edinburgh. The author oft" Peebles to the Play" begins his sketch of the humours of this Beltane festival with a description of the gathering in the fields. Then he proceeds to the dinner, the dance, the fun of an incidental fight, and so forth; his song being alive throughout with homely in- cident. It may be noticed that a "Beltane Fair" is still held at Peebles on the second Wednesday of May.--Cassell's Library of English Literature. LAYING DOWN LAND TO PERMANENT PASTURE.—Before selecting the proper grasses for permanent pasture farmers would derive the greatest advantage by adopting the fol- lowing simple experiment :—" Select the previous year a small plot of ground, as nearly as possible the condition of the field when being laid down; then sow separately plots of the most approved grasses and clovers, and carefully note results. Then make a mixture from what Nature proves the most-suited to the soil—besides it proves a good test of the genuineness and vigour of the seeds." It is also very advisable and instructive, when laying down, to put in a separate plot of each seed—both as a test on tbe seed, and also to prove which are permanently the most suited to the soil. THE LAWN AND WALKS.—Before the operation of mow- ing commences, all sticks should be removed carefully, either by sweeping, raking, or hand-picking. In these days of economy in labour mau prefer not to sweep, but simply distribute the worm-eastrover the surface and thoroughly roll the grass. Wherever moss shows itself, a top-dressing of guano, superphosphate, lawn-sand, or any similar in- vigorating manure should be applied: also a dressing of lawn seeds mixed with a portion of finely-sifted soil should be sprinkled Over the ground in mild weather and the roller ' run over it. Where plantain or other coarse weeds are pre- sent, they should be destroyed. For this purpose the best remedy is carbolic acid. A small quantity should bepoured into a jug or other glazed vessel, then dip a short-pointed stick into the acid, and place it on the centre of each plant; this is a much quicker and more effectual method than dilating the acid and pouring it on the plant from a lipped vessel. Great care should be taken not to let the acid drop on any part of the person, and to guard against accident it is desirable to have a can of water or oil always close at hand, so as to.saturate instantly any part which may acci- dentally receive any of the acid.—Gardeners' Chronicle. HARVEST SAVING.—Mr. Pidgeon, in a recent paper, at the Society of Arts, reiterates the assertion of the Reading judges, to the effect that we must continue to lose our har- vests in bad seasons. As this is calculated t 9 perpetuate a great national misfortune, and as it has already been com- pletely disproved by at least twenty large landow.ners and farmers in various parts of the kingdom, will you allow me to state the latest commentary on that curious and dismal dictum? It is simply this :—At Reading the machine stig- matised (after half a day's mock trial) "as useless" saved 180 tons of hay from irrigated grasses, and for Reading a new (350) machine of the same size and form is now being constructed by order of the Board of Works Council. Whilst Mr. Taylor, of Compton, Abdale, who borrowed the harvest- saver, after the trials, at 11 gs. per diem, and saved 150 tons of barley with it, is also in negotiation for the purchase of another. I trust that you will allow that facts and expe- rience ought to outweigh opinions and assertions, however often, and however pertinaciously these latter are reiterated. With ensilage as a new resource for our dairy farms, stack fans for small holdings, and for those who find them suffi- cient, and harvest-savers !or the great landowners and large farmers, our harvests can and must be saved in all weathers, despite Fa the Dog,berrys and Verges' "dismal jemmies" and croakers of the kingdom.— Wm. A. Gibbs. . INSTITUTE OF AGRICULTURE.—The first series of evening lectures on agricultural science was delivered in the lecture theatrd, at the South Kensington Museum, last week, by Mr. W. Carruthers, F.R.S., F.L.S., the subject beink "Farm Seeds and their Adulterations." Sir John Lubbock, M.P., presided. These lectures form part of the scheme of agri- cultural instruction now being carried out by the Institute of Agriculture, which seeks to furnish an education on agri- cultural science suitable for -the sons and daughters of tenant farmers, and to give assistance to persons engaged in giving instruction on the principles of agriculture in science classes and elementary schools. Sir John Lubbock said that they knew that, during the last few years, agriculture in this country had been in a condition of almost unprece- dented depression; and it would be agreed, therefore, that the Institute of Agriculture had been started at a time when it was necessary to leave no stone unturned, if pos- sible, to replace agriculture once more in a prosperous con- dition. The old moralists said that the evils that heaven sent might be avoided, but not those that we brought on ourselves. He was not sure he was able to agree as to the first portion of the saying, but the latter part could not be denied; and although we had done nothing to bring on our- selves the bad weather of the past few years, on the other hand it must be admitted that we had hardly taken all the steps that might have been taken in order to place ourselves in a position to meet the bad seasons. Considering the im- portance of agriculture, it was a very remarkable fact how much the subject was neglected in all schools and colleges in this country, from the most elementary up to the great universities. No agriculture was taught in any of the ele- mentary schools, and there was no professor of agriculture in any of the great universities, and in this respect this country was very much behindhand as compared with other countries. There were in this country two colleges of agri- culture, with 130 students. Germany had more colleges of agriculture than there were students in the two English colleges; and the other great European States, although not, perhaps, to the same extent, also contrasted most favourably with England. There was another great de- partment connected with the land which was perhaps being even more neglected—namely, forestry, foi there was no school of forestry at all here, and Englishmen going to superintend forests in India and the colonies were obliged to go to France or Germany to obtain instruction. The Institute of Agriculture had been commenced for the pur- pose, as far as possible, of giving technical instruction on various sections of agricultural practice. Professor Car- ruthers then proceeded with his lecture, pointing out that it was important that seed used should be fully ripe, and from the previous harvest. Speaking of wheat, he said that of fresh seed about 98 per cent, would germinate, while seed two years old would only germinate about 84 per cent., and seed- six years old only 5 per cent. Grass seeds were re- ceived in this] country in a state of great impurity, and, without reflection, often distributed amongst farmers in the same condition.

CATTLE AT THE PORT OF NEw YORK.—It appears from recent statistics that the number of beeves at New York port during the year 1882 was 636,317 head, against 679,423 in 1881 ; 4,994 cows against 5,989 in 1881; 190,089 calves against 177,483 in 1881; 1,982,181 sheep, against 1,747,445 in 1881; and 1,385,752 swine, against 1,551,452 in 1881. The reports thus show a reduction on the year for all receipts, as compared with 1881, of 43,106 beef cattle, 995 mulch cows, and 155,700 hogs, and an increase of 12,606 calves and 234,730 sheep. The total number of head of beef cattle exported from New York to Europe in 1882 was 18,226, and of beef quarters 219,939; of sheep per head 18,183; of mutton carcases 46,303; and of dressed hogs 1,395. The shipment of live hogs was completely discon- tinued, although in 1880 the trade reached 4,751. The whole statement shows a decrease of 21,845 cattle, 69,697

quarters, 25,584 carcases of mutton, and 14,736 dressed hogs, and an increase Of 3,906 live sheep. But taking into consideration the export statistics from the United States and Canada, the figures show a decrease, as compared with 1881, of 66,760 live cattle, 171,641 quarters of beef, 26,604 carcases of mutton, and 15,234 dressed hogs, and an increase of 30,391 live sheep. LUCERNE is one of the most useful of our forage plants for soils of a dry, sandy, or chalky nature, sheep downs and hill sides; it will also succeed on good lovas, but* should not be sown on clay soils unless they are well chalked. It is a certain green crop at all seasons of the year, and we do not hesitate to say that no farm (unless the land is very heavy) should be without Lucerne. It grows very quickly, produces several cuttings during the year, lasts a long time, resists drought (in consequence of its long taperinc, root) better than any other green crop, and is much liked by horses and all kinds of stock, whether as hay or cut green. Its value for dairy stock is unquestionable; it increases the quantity as well as the quality of the milk, while it is ex- cellent for ewes and lambs, as they are not liable to get blown upon it. Lucerne is suitable for and prospers ex- ceedingly on soils of a light and friable character, particu- larly when containing a proportion of chalk and lime. It also does well on good deep barns. The previous crop should be corn turnips, potatoes, cabbage, or mangel. The land should he well ploughed, manured in the autumn, ridged up rough during the winter, cross-ploughed and har- rowed in the spring, harrowed finely down, anda light roller passed over previous to sowing. Sow from the end of March to the end of April. Until recently Lucerne has been al- most universally sown in England in drills 12 inches apart, to admit of constant hoeing and cleaning, and this was a necessity, because of the custom of keeping the Lucerne plant down for ten or twelve years. But this is a mistaken practice, and the Continental plan of sowing thickly broad- cast, and breaking up and re-sowing in three or four years, as soon as the plant begins to get foul, is no doubt the proper method, for nothing so much interferes with the growth of Lucerne as meddling with its roots and loosening the soil by hoeing. Twenty to 28 lbs. should be sown per acre, and care should be taken to sow clean seed. If any artificial manure is necessary, 3 cwt. of superphosphate sown at the same time as the seed will be found the beat. As soon as the plant is six inches high, which will, in a favour- able season, be in August, it should be mown (always pre- vious to flowering), and may be sit at intervals of a month or six weeks up to the end of October or beginning of November. During the winter a top-dressing of farmyard manure will be well repaid, and the next year cutting will be ready about the end of April. Between that time and November at least four cuttings may be taken every year, which, with good cultivation, will average from three to five, and occasionally up to eight, tons per acre. If required for sheep, they should be turned in either early in the spring or in September. Lucerne generally attains its full vigour the third year.—Sutton's Farmers' Year Book.

THE RANGE OF THE NIGHTINGALE.—From the bushes by the stile on the left hand, which I have just passed, fol- lows the long whistle of a nightingale. His nest is near; he sings night and day. Had I waited on the stile, in a few minutes becoming used to my presence, he would have made the hawthorn vibrate, so powerful is his voice when heard dose at hand. There is not another nightingale along this path for at least a mile, though it crosses mea- dows and runs by hedges to all appearances equally suitable; but nightingales will not pass their limits; they seem to have a marked-out range as strictly defined as the lines of a geological map. They will not go over to the next hedge— hardly into the field on one side of a favourite spot, nor a yard farther along the mound.—Richard Jellies, in "Good Words."

PIGEONS.—FEEDING THE SQuEAKEns..--Sometimes the supply ef " pap " or soft food which the birds are able to give to their young ones is insufficient, and even when feeders are specially provided they are often from one cause or another unable to give enough. This may be caused by the parents or feeders not having a sufficient supply of proper food, and hence the necessity of seeing that the hopper is always kept replenished with a mixture of sound wheat, dari, and grey peas; or it may be that after the birds have been hatched a week or ten days, the supply of soft food fails. If there is a common feeder handy, well and good, but if not, then some other means must be adopted. Many pigeon fanciers adopt the simplest, easiest, and quickest way, namely, to chew small mouthfuls of some plain milk biscuit into a smooth pap, and holding the little squeaker in the hand, feed it from the lips, into which its beak is inserted. Those who object to this method may get a small glass syringe with a large aperture, such as can be bought of most chemists. The biscuit is mashed up with hot milk, and the bird fed by inserting the point of the syringe into its mouth. It is always useful to have one of these syringes at hand, so that if any of the young birds are noticed not to be feeding well they can be examined, and if their crops are found to be empty and insufficiently filled they can be fed in this manner. When older, and the pap in the old birds has gone off, the latter feed the squeakers with peas or grain softened in their crops, and it is very im- portant that these should be watched at this period. If it is thought that the young ones are not getting enough, then soak some peas in cold water all night, and just before feed- ing have some hot water poured on to them, sufficient to make them lukewarm. Open the mandibles of the squeaker between the thumb and finger of the left hand, with the second or third finger behind the neck, and pass the soaked peas down the throat with the right hand until the crop is very closely filled. There is no danger in this plan, and very great benefit accrues from it. THE AQUARIUM—SELECTION or ',NlL—When the plants have become fairly established, and the beetles, kt. Tc., have settled down in their new home, it will be time to consider what kinds of fish shall be chosen to complete the furnish- ing of the aquarium. For the sake of appearance prece- dence must be given to the golden carp; two of these, not exceeding four inches lohg, will be sufficient for a circular glass. The most interesting of the fish which may be kept in confinement is, however the minnow ; and these little creatures will live for a considerable time—sometimes for years—in a healthy condition, and become so tame that ' they will take food from the fingers at the surface of the water, and follow the hand that feeds them round the glass. From 6 to 12 of these will not be too many for a small aquarium. The roach is also to be recommended as an inhabitant of the aquarium. It agrees well with other fish, soon becomes tame, and invariably thrives; its movements are somewhat curious, for instead of gliding about like the rest, it lies at the bottom, turns over the pebbles in seauh of food, and jerks itself round the glass with a spasmodic motion. It is also useful in a sanitary point of view, for it picks up the stray morsels that may have fallen to the bottom, and thus prevents the water from becoming foul by decayed frag- ments of food that have been unobserved by its more lively neighbours. To the ones just named may be added the com- mon carp, the roach, the tench, and the gudgeon; but amongst those to be avoided is the stickleback, which, though an amusing little creature, is too pugnacious, and , the same may be said of the perch. In the management of an aquarium care must be taken that the water does not get too warm or too cold, and also that no more food be given than can be consumed. The best food is a little biscuit powder kneaded into pills about the size of pinheads, and shreds of raw beef cut with a pair of scissors. These should be dropped in alternately, when the fish will catch the bits • before they sink to the bottom. Feeding should only take place once a day. Water in the tanks, if properly stocked • with plants, needs to be very seldom changed, and when it has to be done it should be very carefully performed. The best way is to insert an indiarubber tube into the tank, and • by allowing it to form a syphon, drain off a portion from the bottom of the tank. Then fill up with fresh water and repeat the process until it is quite clear. I CAGE BIRDS.—THE SONG THRUSH.—This well-known

bird is one of the greatest charms of our woods. It is much smaller than the Missel Thrush, and in length is generally about eight and a half inches, three and a half of which be- long to the tail. The beak is three-quarters of an inch long, is horn brown in colour, excepting the underpart, which is yellowish at the base and yellow within. The iris is nut brown, the shanks a dingy lead colour, and about an inch high. All the upper part of the body is olive brown; the throat is yellowish white with a black line on each side. The sides of the neck and breast are of a pale reddish white, variegated with dark brown spots, slaved like a heart re- versed, and the belly is white, and covered with more oval spots. In the female the two black lines on the throat are narrower, the breast is lighter, and of a plain yellowish white; the spots on it are larger, whilst those on the wing coverts are somewhat smaller. It is necessary to take these birds when very young, as old birds that have been accus- tomed to their liberty seldom sing when kept in confine- ment, and often pine away and die. The food which should be given is oatmeal moistened with milk, or the prepared food we have often recommended. Water must be given freely, as these birds use it both for bathing and drinking. When properly attended to, thrushes have been known to live in captivity five or six years, and their beautiful song is very pleasing indeed. A good sized cage is required if kept in one, or they may be placed with other birds in the aviary,. MICE.—BREEDING.—In breeding ordinary white mice, one buck and six does may run together, and these should, of course, be the finest ones to be had, so that the produce may be good and of a nice size. Small mice neither look nor sell well. Pairs or any number of does up to six, can run with the buck, and should a promiscuous stock of coloured mice be required, let the does be of different colours and the buck of a different colour to the does, by which means a large variety of mixed colours can be had with a small stock. The young animals should not be paired until they are about three months, or perhaps a little older, as this allows them to develop fully, and the progeny will con- sequently be much finer than if mated at an early age. If allowed they will breed at six weeks old, but the result of this is that the young ones are weak and small. When the doe takes to the nest she should not be disturbed for a fort- night, by which time the young ones are able to take care of themseves. When they appear outside the nests a few crushed groats should be given them, and continued for ten days or so, when they will go on with oats. The period a doe goes with young is about twelve days. As soon as the young ones get to a good size, some must be removed, as on no account should more than six or seven be kept in one cage. Cleanliness must also be strictly nhsarved.

FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

Damage amounting to £45,000 was caused by fire in the English factory and warehouses at Lisbon, on Saturday, A shock, supposed to have been caused by an earthquake, has been experienced in Amsterdam. No serious conse- quences are reported. The report that Prince Gortschakoff was poisoned gains credence in Russia, and excites great curiosity, but people are at a loss to find a motive. Three French anarchists Guesde, Lafargue and Chapouilly—have been condemned at Moulins to two years' imprisonment for speeches delivered at Moutlucon in which they incited their hearers to mur&r, pillage, and revolution. A desperate attempt has been made to blow up the house of a banker at Taganrog, in Russia. An explosion of dyna- mite shattered the entrance hall, but a case containing the destructive agent, which had been placed in the cellars, failed to explode. The new Egyptian loan will be for the amount of £5,000,000, bearing interest at the rate of 5 per cent. Out of the prpceeds of the loan it is proposed to appropriate £1,500,006 for the cost of the army of occupation and £3,000,690 in payment of the indemnity claims. It is reported that the Bechuana chiefs have leagued themselves together to resist Boer aggressions. A Durban telegram to the Standard states that the country near the I Transvaal border is in a state of anarchy, and that the natives are everywhere taking up arms against the oppres- sion of the Boers. Prince Dolgoroukoff, Governor-General of Moscow, has received a letter declaring that, as the Emperor will not grant a constitution to Russia, at the approaching coronation ceremony an attempt will be made to prevent its taking place, even if it were necessary to blew up the Kremlin Palace with all the assembled guests. A new Cabinet has been constituted in Bulgaria, with General Soboleff as President of the Council, Minister of the Interior, and, ad interim, of Finance. It is understood that the programme of the new Ministry provides for the main- tenance of the existing order of things in the Principality, and for the execution of the laws passed by the Chamber of Deputies. Two serious conflagrations are reported. Forest city, in California, has been destroyed by fire. Hundreds of the in- habitants have been left homeless, and great suffering has been caused by the destruction of almost the entire stock of provisions. Considerable damage has been done by a fire at the English factory and warehouses on the banks of the Tsgus, opposite Lisbon. CETEWAYo.—According to a private despatch from Maritz- burg, messengers from Cetewayo complain that he is threatened with starvation owing to the retention of the Royal cattle by the lately-appointed chiefs. Grave accounts are also to hand of Mr. John Shepstone's action in the Zulu reserve. Besides imposing fines right and left, he is said to have personally assaulted one chief and caused others to be severely beaten for not renouncing Cetewayo. Tesa SuEz CANAL.—A return of the shipping and tonnage which has passed through the Suez Canal from its opening in 1869 to the end of last year has been issued as a Parlia- mentary paper. This showed that the amount for 1882 far exceeded that of any previous year. Of the total of 3,108 ships (as against 2,827 in 1881) which passed through the canal in 1882,2,565 were English, their gross tonnage being 5,795,584, as against 1,326,541, the gross tonnage of the foreign vessels. Loss OF EIOFITy-THREE FISHERMEN.—Business letters received in Dundee mention that on the night of the sth inst. a fear ml storm raged on the Dutch Coast. A fleet of 18 boats, belonging to a fishing village on the North Coast of Friesland, near Dokkum, was lost, and 83 fishermen were drowned. The loss of property is estimated at £B,OOO. Fifty-three widows and families were left in poverty, and appeals were being made for public subscriptions to assist them. It is stated in a telegram from Paris that within the past few weeks the anarchical party have been trying all sorts of rnanceuvres to currupt the army. Seditious appeals have found their way into the barracks, and offers of bribes have been made in some quarters. Althought the attempt has failed, the Goverment have nevertheless thought it prudent to take precautions to prevent the insurrection propaganda among the military, and henceforth a stricter surveillance will be kept over all civilians who visit their friends in the garrisons. ROBBERY OF DYNAMITR—A Paris correspondent says a robbery of dynamite has just taken place on the railway from Lyons to Geneva. A train containing one sealed van, marked "Dynamite," left Lyons station for Bellegarde. On the journey the guard noticed that the seals had been broken, and that the dynamite had disappeared. The explosive., weighing 25 kilogrammes, was made up into cartridges. The police commenced an inquiry, but up to the present time no clue has been found either to the dynamite or to the robbers. TUB PARIS COMICUNE CELEBRATION. The banquets which were held in Paris and other cities in celebration of the Paris Commune passed off very quietly. Several patriots who were members of the Commune in 1871 were present at one of these banquets, and eulogised the proceed- ings of the Government which so long opposed itself to the forces of Marshal MacMahon. Louise Michel was heartily applauded, in absentid. The Communists of New York met together on Sunday, and listened to an address from Herr Most, late editor of the Freiheit. This worthy de- clared that the Commune was "too humane," and he pre- dicted that in future Communists "would act regardless of humanitarian considerations," a warning which will not cause the efforts for the suppression of Communists to be relaxed. MaesnEn OF A EUROPEAN AT CAPE COAST.—lietweee: I the night of the 2nd and morning of the 3rd January a [ murder was committed under circumstances of great brutality I at Aboosu, in Warsaw. Mr. John Barrow, the victim, who r held the position of European accountant to the African I Gold Coast Mining Company, lived in a small house L situated pretty close to another. The murderers made good I their entrance through the side of the bedchamber, anel [ I struck Mr. Barrow while sleeping in his bed. He appears to I have made an attempt to ward off the blows, as one of his • hands was badly cut. An axe and knife were used, and r with the former the deceased's head was nearly severed from r the body. The murderers opened the safe with the deceased's key, and took from it £9O in specie with which they de- • camped. Four men have been arrested, three of them in the employ of the company, and the fourth had recently been r dismissed, and had been heard to utter threats against the life of the deceased. The four prisoners are natives of El mina. THE MURDER OF A LETTER CARRIER It( BERLIN.—A great sensation has been caused at Berlin by the cruel and daring murder which has been already reported, of which the perpetrator has not been captured. It is the custom for • Post-office orders to be cashed at the residence of the peyees, by special money-order messengers, instead of at the offices, , as in England. Taking advantage of this practice, the murderer drew upon himself a small sum, which he knew would be handed to him on Monday morning, when the carriers have generally a double freight of coin, and then hired a room close to a branch office, so as to be first on the messenger's list, and to ensure entrapping him before he had parted with any of his cash. The carrier entered, and was at once killed by blows on the head from a heavy hammer. • First robbing his victim and then leaving him in his blood upon the floor, the murderer turned the key in the door and decamped without exciting any attention—nor was the deed discovered until the day after. His name is Ernst Robert Sander; he is aged 39, and is a man of great bodily strength. He formerly served in a Cuirassier Regiment. In conse- quence of the murder the Postmaster-General has directed that in future money orders shall be paid in the presence of third persons.

THE RECHNT TEMPERA-NCH MISSION AT EARLESTOWN.— As a result of the special temperance mission at EarlesLown last week, about 50 persons signed the pledge for the first time. In addition to these, a goodly number of others, already members of some temperance society, donned the blue ribbon, the number of ribbons disposed of being 48. This is looked upon as encouraging by the promoters of the mission.

MISSION TFiSIT ANNIVERSARY B}inlto24B.—Tha anniversary services in connection with the Mission Tent, Legh-street, Ear!Mown, were held on Sunday last. Special sermons were preached in the afternoon and evening by Mr. G. S. Langley, of Manchester, and there was a good attendance on each occasion. The choir sang a selection of hymns suitable for the occasion, with orchestral accompaniments, and several anthems were rendered by the Earlestown reed and string band. Collections were made in aid of the ex- penses incurred, and the sum of .L 2 61. was realised. GOOD TEMPLAIIS MRETING.—The members of the Hope of Earlstown Lodge of Good Temptars held their usual weekly meeting on Monday evening last. Bro. George E. Warburton, W.C.T., occupied the chair. After the formal business several new members were proposed, after which Bro. John Taylor read an essay, entitled ' Our obligation," written by Bro. the Rev. F. Wagstaff. The essa ywas a very interesting and instructive one, and the members much appreciated it. References to points in the paper were made by some of the members, the evening being spent in a profitable manner.

AN UNCLEANLY MILK SELLER AT Sr. HELENS.—On Friday, at St. Helens Police Court, James Owen, a milk. seller, living at Marshall's Cross, was charged with neglect- ing to have the room in which milk was sold cleaned and washed before 12 noon; and was further charged with failing to have the words "registered for the sale of milk" painted over the entrance door, according to the regulations of the Local Authority.—lnspector Wood said that on the afternoon of the 6th inst. he visited the house of the defendant, who was a registered cow-keeper, at Marshall's Cross. He examined the milk-shop and found a mug con- taining two or three quarts of milk on a counter. It was covered over with a dirty black board, and the top of the milk was nearly black with dust. There were other vessels emtaining milk standing on the floor near to a mug con- taining pigs' bellies, and there was also seine horse harness scattered about, besides about a birrowful of turnips. The sides of the room were papered and covered with dust, and the floor was so dirty that it did not seem to have been washed for several weeks. He asked defendant's wife how often she washed the floor and she said once a week. Altogether, the place was in a very offensive state, and there was a very bad smell. The words "registered for the sale of milk " were not painted over the entrance door.—ln defence, defendant said that he had only one cow and did not sell any milk, but a constable spoke to having seen de- fendant going about selling milk, and said also that his wife had purchased some from him Whi.lll NVI.S so dirty that he told her not to get any more from him.—The Bench decided to fine defendant .€1 and costs for having his house in a filthy' state, but dismissed the other charge. THE STATE OF IRELAND. ANOTHER MURDER CONSPIRACY. The case of the 13 men from Crossmaglen, county Armagh, charged with conspiracy to murder and with treason-felony, came on at the Antrim Assizes, at Belfast, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Lawson. Six of tbe prisoners were first put on trial, and they were indicted for conspiracy to mur- der. It was alleged that in March, 1881, a man named Burns took premises at Crossmaglen, from which he displayed the United States flag, and that he sat there to enrol members of a secret society which had for its object the assassination of p-rsons opposed to "the public wish of the country." The society was called the Patriotic Brotherhood, and its members were sworn to take up arms to free their country, and to obey if it fell to them to murder or assist at murder. In process of time meetings were held, at which assassinations were discussed, and one of the results was the decision to murder two landlords,' named M‘Geough and Brookes. Books recording the proceedings of the society had been found, and counsel said it was a significant fact that upwards of 40 persons whose names were recorded had left the country since these secrets were disclosed. There was also an entry of £lO "to aid in blowing up Dublin Castle." An "informer," who was examintd on Wednesday, said the object of the society was to free Ireland from British rule, and to murder any persons who made themselves obnoxious to the members. He de- posed that he and others were sworn on the Prayer-book to shoot Mr. Brookes at the first opportunity, and that at one meeting advice was read from O'Donovan Rossa urging them to extirpate all landlords, and "money would be forthcoming from America."

The trial was continued on Thursday. Constabulary officers depos2d to seeing the prisoners at meetings late at night in suspected quarters, and to the discovery of books purporting to be records of the Patriotic Brotherhood. Mr. Brooke and Mr. M`Geough deposed to receiving threatening letters, and an "expert" gave it as his opinion that the writing of most of the threatening letters corresponded with that of the paisoner Watters, and also with the writing in one of the books found by the police. The prosecution was closed and the defence proceeded with, and the court adjourned.

Mr. John Walsh, the organiser of the Invincibles in the North of England, who was arrested at Havre, has, like Mr. Byrne, been set at liberty. Thus neither in France nor in America have the extradition proceedings which resulted from Carey's revelations led to any result. Mr. Mayne, Nationalist, was on Tuesday returned as member of Parliament for Tipperary, in room of Mr. John Dillon. Two other candidates were proposed, but the no- minations were declared invalid on the ground that the as- senting electors were the same in each case. A private investigation into the charge against Richard Hodnet, for posting at Ballydehob, a parcel of dynamite addressed to Earl Spencer, was concluded at Bantry on Tuesday, the prisoner being committed for trial at the next Cork Assizes.

It is stated that James Carey has received several threat- ening letters from all parts of the United Kingdom, warning him of his fate, and telling him not to imagine that he is safe, as there are plenty of men to take the places of those who have been arrested.

Henry Rowles, one of the men in Kilmainham prison awaiting trial in connection with the Dublin murder con- spiracy, died on Sunday night, in consequence of an attack of epilepsy which disclosed itself on the previous Wednes- day. He was 47 years of age. The Archbishop of Cashel, in sending £5O for the Parnell Testimonial Fund, says that, when closed and given to the public in its complete form, the subscription list will supply an admirable test as to who really belongs just now or does not belong to the Irish party. Additional contributions were announced on Monday amounting to about 250. On Tuesday Dr. Wade (Liberal) was elected town coun- cillor for Trinity Ward, which James Carey, the informer, lately represented. Dr. Wade received 154 votes, while his Conservative opponent obtained 117. A movement is on foot to establish a number of Conservative Associations in Dublin and its vicinity.

According to a private telegram from Rome, Cardinal M‘Cabe will, on his recovery, proceed there, it is the in- tention of the Pope to call also the Archbishop of Cashel to Rome The object of Leo XIII., it is said, is to make far- ther efforts to bring the influence of the Catholic clergy to bear for the pacification of Ireland.

A murderous attack was made on Sunday night upon a bailiff by a party of men at Corbally, near Limerick, who beat him with sticks, &c., inflicting very serious wounds on his head and body. On Monday morning his employer, Mr. Place, appeared before the magistrates with tke injured man, whose depositions were taken. He accused three men, whom he named, and against whom warrants have been issued.

AR UNPOPULAR PRIM. Lord Oranmore and Browne, only recently returned to Ireland after an absence dating from the early days of the Land League agitation, has again left the country. A few nights ago the magnificent gate at the entrance to the grounds of Castle Macgarrett, the residence of his lordship, was much damaged, and the adjoining ornamental railings were torn down. Some young trees in the avenue were also damaged. Arrests are expected. Addressing the Grand Jury at the Belfast Assizes, on Monday, Mr. Justice Lawson cited recent outrages in Eng- land as evidence that " the ssake tho' scotched was not killed; " but be took hope from the fact that we now knew with whom we had to deal. The yenemous reptile said his lordship, endeavoured in the last throes. of its death-like struggle to cast out as much venom as it could, but this could not last long, and he trusted that before long the reign. f order !Mild be re-estabilehed• GUARDING TIM JUDGES ON CIRCUIT, Judge O'Brien and Lord Justice Fitzgibbon arrived at Cork on Tuesday. Extraordinary and elaborate precautions were taken to en- sure their lordships' safety. They were met at the railway station by a large force unier arms, and were escorted to their lodgings by a troop of Scots Greys and mounted police with drawn swords. At their lodgings temporary and mili- tary and police huts have been established, and the premises are surrounded by sentries. This display attracted a large crowd, but there was nothing like a hostile feeling ex- hibited.

TRAGIC SUICIDE IN Dunux.—The Dublin coroner held an inquest on Monday afternoon on the body of an accom- plished young man named Mackenzie, who poisoned himself in the presence of an actress with whom he was intimate and a friend. The deceased had been a tutor, and had graduated at Trinity College, and was only a few;weeks back appointed editor of the Dublin comic journal the Irish Diamond. On Saturday he had a quarrel with the actress in the presence of a friend, and in a moment of desperation, and, despite the efforts of the other two, he drank a bottle of laudanum, and died soon after. ACCIDENT AT A DISTILLERY: Two LIVES LOST.—A fatal explosion occurred on Saturday evening at Candy's distillery, Monasterevin, county Kildare. The accident is supposed to have originated in the collapse of one of the stills, canaed by the rapid condensation of the vapours within while the still was being charged with spirit. he spirit having reached the fire below ignited and exoloded the vapour within the still. The 113111e5 quickly enveloped the building, but were by the prompt efforts of the engineer confined to the stillhouses. Two men, named Michael Doolin and James Ready, were burnt to death, and three others, Patrick M'Evoy, Michael Dunne, and Michael O'Dohertv, severely injured.

div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
Professor Nordenskjold is to proceed shortly to Greenland, to explore that region and to make astronomical observa- tions. _ .... _ . . ~.

"What did the ancient Chinese know of Greece ana Rome?" is the question asked and answered by Dr. Edkins in communication to the North China Branch of the Asiatic Society. This subject he illustrates from the records of the journey of a traveller who visited Bactria about 140 8.C., and from various incidental passages in Chinese literature. There were two embassies from Rome in the second century of the present era, and information would also be spread by the Buddhist missionaries. __ _

_ Another interesting, and probably important, communica- tion on the phenomena of "inhibition" was made to the Academie des Sciences on Monday last by M. Brown Sequard. He gave an acount of methods of suddenly arrest- ing epileptic and similar attacks by irritating various parts of the nervous system, by means of _currents of carbonic acid and other applications and operations, in some instances at remote points. In a report on Paraguay just published in a blue-book, Mr. Vansittart, of the British Legation in Buenos Ayres, quotes a report drawn up, at his request, by Dr. Stewart, who has been resident in the country 26 years. Dr. Stewart comments on the marked absence of the principal zymotic diseases, Paraguay contrasting in this respect very strongly with Brazil and the River Plate countries. He adds that vaccination is obligatory in Paraguay and that there is now not a single case of small-pox in the country, although the disease made great ravages there before vaccination was made obligatory. The Panama Star and Herald says that Lake Titicaca, the highest navigable sheet of water in the world, and its almost unknown neighbour Lake Poopoo, are reported to be drying up in a remarkable and unprecedented manner. The Indian inhabitants of the surrounding regions are much alarmed, and believe the waters are finding a subterranean outlet to sea, thus reviving an old Inca tradition. The true cause of the phenomena, however,'is the exceptional dryness of the past season. The streams running from the Cordil- leras are not furnishing their customary supplies. AN ELECTRICAL TRAMCAR.—A number of scientific and commercial gentlemen met at Kew-bridge on Saturday to witness the running of a tramcar propelled by electricity. The car ran well at the rate of six miles an hour, and the experiment was held to be quite successful. General Hut- chinson, who had closely observed the working of the car, and was satisfied with what he had seen, expressed himself confident that the Board of Trade will grant the necessary license, and when this official sanction is obtained, the first , electrical cars will run on Acton-road. NON-ALCOHOLIC TREATMENT OF DlsaAsE.—The Rev. Dawson Burns, D.D., hon. secretary of the London Temper- ' ance Hospital, writes to the Daily News :—As the subject of the non-alcoholic treatment of disease has been raised is your columns permit me to state that in this hospital up- wards of 1,600 in-patients have been treated without alco- hol, the results being of a highly satisfactory kind. Many of the cases have been of a severe type, and have included surgical operations of the utmost gravity. The visiting I medical staff are permitted to prescribe alcohol if they con- sider its administration necessary, but this permission has been acted upon in but a single case, and without good effect. The cases of out-patients have numbered upward of 12,000. ART AND SURGERY.—Mr. Seymour Haden, whose artistic accomplishments are equalled by his skill as a surgeon, was, in the course of his ,stay- at New York, the guest of the Academy of Medicine, and ia responding to the welcome then given him explained the reasons which had led him to devote his energies to art as well as to surgery. A dissecting wound received in his youth prevented him from pursuing his medical work for two years, and he spent that time in Italy and studied art most industriously. After regaining his health and begin- ning the'practice of medicine, he continued to practice art, and he is convinced that the training thus given to his eye and hand has been of great value to him in surgical work. He has also worked in art to encourage independence in the medical profession, and to oppose the idea sometimes held in England, that a medical practitioner should be a man of only one idea. STUDY AND STIMULANTS.

Mr. A. A. Reade having made an appeal to a number of eminent men of letters for their testimony as to "the use of intoxicants and narcotics in relation to intellectual life," has published their replies in book form. No work which contained expressions of opinion on any conceivable subject from so many eminent men and authors, English and French, American and German, and especially upon any matter of personal experience, as here testify concisely and pointedly, could fail to be both entertaining and instructive. Nor could the differences of opinion of such men be wanting in amusement. These differences begin even with the scope and method of inquiry. Professor George Rawlinson doubts "that the method of the inquiry can lead to any important results." The first line of the very next testimony, that of Mr. Charles Reade, runs, "Your subject is important, and your method of inquiry sound." But this is nothing to the amusing variety of opinions and testimonies on the "drink" and the "weed." There are enthusiasts for tobacco like Mr. Wilkie Collins, who finds in it so "good a friend to his irritable nerves," that when he reads learned attacks on the habit of smoking, he feels indebted to the writer for "add- ing largely to the relish of his cigar ;" or Mark Twain, who has "smoked immoderately" during thirty-eight years out of his life of forty-six years, beginning with a hundred
_ . ... _ cigars a month, an a going on to three hundred ! This lat- ter allowance he thinks sufficient to "keep his constitution

on a firm basis," though in holiday times he exceeds it. He might be supposed to be "romancing," but for the soberness of his testimony respecting alcoholic stimulants. So far as his experience goes, he says, "wine is a clog to the pen, not an inspiration," and he has "never seen the time when he could write to his satisfaction after drinking even one glass of wine." Moreover, his allowance of tobacco is plainly exceeded in Germany, one learned man in Bavaria being cited as smoking five hundred cigars a month! On the other hand, eminent French authors, whilst not condemning tobacco altogether, give warning notes from the ill effects upon some of their confreres of its use in excess. The Abbe Moigno testifies from experience Through snuffing and smoking together he became" con- scious of a decay of memory ; ' by discarding both he at- tained to "a complete resurrection, not only of the memory, but of general health and well-being." But, somewhat re- versing Mark Twain's experience, this excellent Abbe, who, in spite of his eighty years, claims to be the" greatest hard-working man of his century" (sic), says' "I find it well to take at breakfast a small half-cup of coffee without milk, to which, when only two or three teaspoonsful re- main at the bottom of the cup, I add a small spoonful of brandy or other alcoholic liquor." He continues, with the delicious self-complacency that breaks out all over his re- ply, "That is my whole allowance of stimulants. How happy would those be who should adopt my regime !" The toughest of French literary men and statesmen, such as Dnfaure, Thiers, Guizot, and Victor Hugo, have been or are non-smokers. Of twenty men of science quoted in this book, only two smoke; and Professor Huxley, who is one of them, did not begin till he was forty years of age. The effects of smoking, as of almost every habit, differ with differing constitutions. Mr. Reade himself says," No_eyi- _ _

deuce lias yet been adduced proving that modeiate smoking is injurious," i.e., to men of full years. But the testimony to its ill effects upon young men, in stunting their growth, both physical and mental, is so strong that at Annapolis and West Point, the Naval and Military Schools of the United States, it is forbidden. "At Harvard College," Dr. Dio Lewis says "no young man addicted to the use of to- bacco has graduated at the head of his class ;" and the testimony from the Iz/cies of Douai, St. Quentin, and Chain- Wry is that "smokers are inferior to non-smokers." As to alcoholic stimulants, it is at least noteworthy that it finds no enthusiasts. On the contrary, the reader must be struck with the large proportion of eminent men of Eng- land. France, and the United States who abstain from it altogether, in every form. The Germans are the most im- pervious to reasons for total abstinence; Bavarian beer seems to them to be the ultimate goal of temperance. Several of the French writers reprehend the use of "alco- hol," but own to taking "wine"—of course, the light wines of their country—at meals, M. Paul Bert's interesting, though rather academie, testimony conclude with these words—" I very seldom drink alcoholic liquors, but I take wine to all my meals, because I like it!" Other stimulants, such as tea and coffee, are also brought into the contro- versy, some witnesses strongly inclining to them, aa Pro- fessor Haeckel, of Jena, who says he finds "strong coffee very useful in mental work ;" while others, as the vener- able William Cullen Bryant, have found it as needful to abstain from both tea and coffee as from alcohol or tobacco. Victor Hugo's stimulation is charmingly characteristic. Mr. Philip Gilbert Hamerton, after remarking wisely that "when a writer feels dull, the best stimulant is fresh air," says, "Victor Hugo makes a good fire bef6re writing, and then opens the window." They are happy who need not write by night. If authors' studies and editors' rooms could be made warm, and yet be kept fresh through proper lighting and ventilation, there would be less of resort to alcoholic stimulation than there is said to be, especially in Lendon. Mr. Reade's own conclusions, adverse to both tobacco and alcohol, are very clearly and moderately stated. Of all the testimonies in his volume, that of the Rev. James Martineau stands out pre-eminent for its felicity. At 77 years of age he persists in an almost total abstinence from alcoholic beverages (of tobacco he cannot bear even the smell), and still has the "Annual delight of reaching the chief summits of the Cairn Gorm mountains" during his summer residence in Inverness. He adds, "Few things, I believe, do more at a minimum of cost to lighten the spirits and sweeten the temper of families and of society than the repudiation of artificial indulgences."

div.p: A lady recently took her son of some five years to church. After the minister had been preaching about half an hour, the little fellow grew sleepy and began to nod. The mother -roused him into attention several times by pinching; but, as it seemed a hopeless case, she concluded to let him sleep undisturbed. After the little fellow had had his nap out, he awoke, and saw the minister still holding forth. He looked up in his mother's face and innocently asked, "Mother, Is it this Sunday night, or is it next Sunday night?" At a school examination recently the inspector put the following question :—" On what side of a jug is the handle placed?' The boy " dux " said it was on the right side; but, on being asked to prove it, it was found that he could not. Thesecond boy thought it was on the left side, but he likewise could not prove it. The inspector passed round the class without getting another answer until he came to a bright little fellow at-the foot, who exclaimed, "'Why, it's on the outside." He go i the certificate.

div.head: BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL AT ST, HELENS,
div.p: THE BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL AT ST, HELENS,

The Right Rev. Bishop Ryle preached on Sunday molt- ing is St. Helens Parish Church, when he pleaded on behalf of the Church Pastoral Aid Society. There were very large congregations. His lordship at the morning service, took his text from Acts xvii., 10th and 17th verses: —"Now while Paul waited for them at Athens his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry. Therefore disputed he in the synagogues with the Jews; and with the devout persons, and in the market daily with them that met him." The Bishop said he had to speak shout a very remarkable man and about a very remarkable city. It was eeecileee tO tell that congregation that Paul was the man after Christ who had made a greater mark upon the history of the world through his preaching and teaching than any other man. Athens was in the days of Paul the most famous city in the world, being unequalled for its learning, its statesmen, its philosophers, and was in fact to the world then what Oxford and Cambridge are to England now—the seats of learning. Paul saw in Athens the most perfect buildings that had ever been erected, the statliest palaces, its extensive shipping, and the results of great commercial enterprise; but what struck him most forcibly was its being "wholly given to idolatry." Dividing the subject into three sections, viz., what Paul saw, what he felt, and what he did, the Bishop said what a proof was afforded that all the learning this world san give, all the knowledge and all the philosophy that men can possibly compass, did not prevent them from bowing down to idols if they had not the Word of God—the inspired Bible. But there were other forms of idolatry, and they existed even in Christian cpuntries. Men might make idols of wealth, in accumulating money, of eating and drink- ing, of pleasure, and of everything worldly, just as much as the Athenians were idolaters of the wretched gods to which they bowed down. In the second place they were told that Paul's heart was stirred within him—stirred with compas- sion—when he saw the city "wholly given to idolatry," and he disputed with them, i.e., argued, about Jesus and the resurrection. Those intellectual peple sneered at Paul, but as they could not answer or refute his arguments they post- poned their decision, saying they would hear him again some other time. His lordship forcibly appealed to his hearers to promptly decide those questions concerning their soul's eternal salvation, and concluded by urging the claims of the Church Pastoral Aid Society, which for 45 years had oonferred such great blessings noon the Church of England by lightening the labours of hundreds of curates and pro- viding lay helpers. The Church of England, the Bishop said, needed educating in this respect. The people did sot know what it was to give like the Presbyterians of Scot- land, like the Wesleyans, like the Independents, and like other Dissenting bodies. Churchmen did not give in the proportion those other bodies did for the spread of the Gospel, and it was time their people came forward and gave of their substance more gladly and liberally. The collection was then made.

We understand that a new weekly journal, devoted to the popular exposition of sanitary matters and to the education of the people in the laws of health, will be shortly issued by Messrs. Wyman and Sons, London. The new journal will ba entitled Health. The Morning Post says :—Signatures continue to be attached to the national declaration against the proposal of the Government to abolish the Parliamentary oath. A great many come from the Dissenting bodies, and notably the Presbyterians, Wesleyans, and Baptists. Lord Carlingford has been appointed Lord President of the Council. The duties of Minister of Agriculture will in future be assMiated with the office. Lord Rasebery is mentioned as likely to succeed Lord Carlingford in the office of Lord Privy Seal. Mr. Biggar has resolved not to carry to the House of Lords the appeal in the case of Hyland v. Biggar. If it were otherwise such action would not stay execution of the order of the caurt for the payment of damages and costs. The latter are now being taxed. When this process is com- plete, payment will, it is said, forthwith be made. PROBATE AND LEGACY DUTIES.—A parliamentary return has been published, which states that the total number of estates of deceased persons in respect of which affidavits under the provisions of "the Customs and Inland Revenue Act, 1881," were delivered during the year 1882 in England and Wales was 44,350, and the number that were, as regards personal estates exempt from legacy duty was 32,915, "A CAULD PREACHER."—WhiIe the Rev. Dr. Sprott was giving out the text for the afternoon discourse in the Estab- lished Church, North Berwick, on Sanday' a gentleman residing in the outskirts of the town rose to his feet and in- terrupted him with the remark, "You're a cauld preacher, Dr. Sprott; but excuse me for saying so." Some further remarks were added, when the church officer got him quietly removed, and the service was continued. THREATNING LORD EUSTACE CECIL.—At the Central Criminal Court, on Tuesday, George Broadbent Calvert, 18, clera, was charged be'ore Mr. Justice Day with feloniously sending a threatening letter to Lord Eustace Cecil, M.P., demanding money with menaces. Lord Bustace proved the receipt of the letter, and evidence of identification was then given. The prisoner admitted sending the letter, but said another man parsuaded him. The jury acquitted him, the Judge observing that he had a very fortunate escape. FRAUD B! A MILITARY OFFICER.—At the 0:d Bailey. OD Tuesday, John R. Vincent, late lieutenant in the Yorkshire Regiment, pleaded guilty to forging and uttering cheques. Mr. Poland prosecuted for the Treasury. The offence was proved to have been committed in November and Dacember last in the Army and Navy Club, where the prisoner asiurned the name of Captain Spottiswood ; and in the Guards' Club, where he represented himself as an officer named Drum- mond. He was sentenced to five years penal servitude. A WELsri PRIZEFIGHT.—EarIy on Monday merning, a large crowd assembled at an isoloted spot near Aberdare Junction to witness a prizefight between two noted pugilists from Mountain Ash, named Tnomas Morgan and John Bevan. The third round had been fought without either combatant obtaining any advantage, and the men were commencing the fourth round, when several constables in private clothes suddenly made a raid on the Ting. The two men were captured, and lodged in Mountain Ash police station.

A VICAR'S Ormicaa .ov DissErez.—The Rev. N. Y. Birk- myre, the new vicar of St. Simon's Bristol, having refused to allow the church bell to be tolled at the funeral of a Dis- senting parishioner, gives the following reasons :—First, it is his firm conviction that the tolling of the bell being a very solemn thing and an important part of the church service, no Dissenter has any claim to it; and secondly, as a Church of England clergyman he can have no sympathy with any Dissenters, and it is plainly his duty not to re- cognise them, as he believes they are morally wrong in the sight of God. PARLIAMENTARY PROCEDURE.—The Press Association states that although the Government are reluctant to re- open the Rules of Procedure, it is not in/probable that some provision may be proposed to prevent the persistent and in- discriminate blocking of bills by a single member. Several members contemplate introducing or supporting a motion calling attention to the fact that the member for Bridport (Mr Warton) has blocked no fewer than 29 of the measures now on the order book of the House of Commons, which they regard as a public scandal and as tending to bring parliamentary procedure into ridicule. THREAT TO " BLOW trl? THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mr. William St Aubyu, M.P., for Helston, has received an anonymous letter, in a woman's handwriting, cautioning him not to be in the House of Commons two weeks after Easter, as" the party had made up their minds to blow up that House." The reason assigned for giving the hon. gentleman this advice is that he defended the writer's hus- band at the Old Bailey three years ago, and was the only Ccnservative who voted against the expulsion from Par- liament of some Irish members. This information is given on the authority of a Portsmouth resident who has seen the sensational missive. THE LIBERATION SOCIETY AND THE PARLIAMENTARY Oant.—The Executive Committee of the Liberation Society, at a meeting on Monday last, adopted the following. resolution :—" That the compulsory impositien. of an oath upon members of the Legislature, by operating asa religious test, violates the principle that the possession and exercise of civil rights should not be dependent upon religious be- liefs. The committee, therefore, is of opinion that the bill introduced by the Government to amend the law relating to Parliamentary oaths, by allowing members of either House of Parliament, if they think fit, to make a solemn affirmation in lieu of the existing oath of allegiance, is one which the friends of religious equality are taound to support." The number of failures in England and Wales gazetted during the week ending Saturday, March 17, was 222. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 266, showing a decrease of 44, being a net decrease in 1883, to date' of .7. The number of bills of sale published in Eng- land and Wales for the week ending March 17 was 262. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 935, showing a decrease of 673, being a net decrease in 1883, to date, of 8,359. The number published in Ireland for the same week was 40. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 38, showing an increase of 2, being a net increase in 1883, to date, of 70.—Kenzp's Mercantile -Garette.

MYSTERIOUS DEATHS OF HUSBAND AND WIFE.—A mysterious circumstance has occurred in connection with the recent death of a commercial traveller named Thomas Dawson, of Dennetts-read, Peckham, as to which an inquest was opened on Saturday. Deceased was found on Cie 14th instant with his throat shockingly cut, and he expired shortly afterwards. It was stated at the inquest that the widow could not be found. The Coroner adjourned the in- quiry.and instructed his officer to spare neither trouble nor expense to bring her before the court. Early on Monday morning her body was washed ashore at Hastings. Some letters and £3O were found upon the remains.—At the in- quest on Tuesday a verdict of suicide under temporary insanity was returned. hum r WHIS3EY MAKING —At the Hanley Police Court on Tuesday, Dinah Parsons, butcher, alias Jones, was charged with having in her possession an illicit whiskey still, and Hannah Simpson, butcher and milk seller, and William Elkin, a small shopkeeper, were charged with aiding and abetting Parsons. A man named Platt, a potter, was also charged with being concerned in the offence, but being ac- cepted as a witness for the prosecution, he was discharged. It was shown that a few nights ago the excise officers, as- sisted by the police, made a raid upon Rag Hall, a building in the neighbourhood of Hanley, rented by Parsons, where they found a large copper still, containing 80 gallons of so- lution in full operation, there being a large fire under the stiil and spirits running from the worm at the time. There were also found on the premises 300 gallons of fermented 'wash," and 20 bladders, the latter being used for carrying whiskey away. So extensive had been the manufacture of whiskey at Rap... Hall that the revenue bad been defrauded of from £4O to £5O a week by the prisoners. Parsons was fined £260, and Simpson and Elkin £l6O each. ENGLISH PATENTS.—The following patents, amongst others, published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal, were sealed during the week ending March 17th, 1883 : Francis William Crossley, Manchester. engineer, improve- ments in gas motor engines; William Hamer and Cobden Willie Pright Hamer, Northwich, engineer, improvements in apparatus for measuring water and other fluids, and applic- able also as a motive power engine; John Horrocks and James Horrocks, Manchester, machine makers, improve- ments in machinery for doubling and winding fibrous yarns or threads; Henry Slack, Sheffield, improvements in appara- tus for grinding,trueing, surfacing,and polishing metal bars, &c. ; Wm. Whitworth Nightingale, Southport, improvements in means and apparatus for operating upon the atmosphere of apartments in which sheet ice obtained by artificial means is used.;. Thomas Coulthard, Preston, improvements in machinery or apparatus for spinning or doubling cotton ad Other fibreua substances; John Cresswell Brentnall, Timperley, improvements in furnaces and mechanical stockers, and inarrangements and parts connected therewith; Isatc Sowden, Bradford, improvements in pickers employed in weaving.—List . supplied by George I3avies,,C.E., Feb. Inst., P.A., patent solicitor, 4, St. And's-square, Man- chester.

THE NATEONAL •SHNDAY LEAGUE. The 27th annual public meeting et the members and supporters of this League was held on Monday night, in St. James's Hall, London, Mr. James Beal, the president, occupying the chair. The report showed that during the year the museums at Stolre-upon-Trent and the libraries at St. Helens and Dundalk had been cpened on Sundays, as had also the Dublin Exhibition. The Sunday attendances at the Man- chester Free Library had :risen from 151,247 in 1881 to 200,600 in 1582; while the Birmingham Free Library, after its rebuilding, bad also been re-opened on Sundays. Seventv-three petitions, with ,C 2,742 signatures (without counting petitions with 2,000 signatures lost by the officials of the House), had been presented to the House of Corn- mons. Debates on the question had been taken in that House, in which Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., had made a speech against the objects of the League. At a meeting organised by the Workmen's Sunday Committee, delegates represent- ing 46.000. working men condemned that speech, and refuefli to accept its author as a representative of labour on the Sunday question. The other worlcof the League had also been of a fairly satisfactory character. The chairman, in his opening address, referred with (leap regret to their lath friend and supporter, Mr. Ashton Dilke and expressed his sanguine cxpectations of the results Of the labours of the I,,agtre in he near future. The report was then re- ceived and adopthi. Resolutions were carried for present- ing a petition to the House of Lords, and pledging the Council to use their Lest efforts to support Lord Dunraven's motion for obtaining the opening of the national =aseurns and art galleries to the pe2ple on Sunday afternoons.
