div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 24, 1883.

IThe Glendale crofters have again driven proprietor's stock off the hill. There is great excitement. Lord Elcho' M.P., in addressing the Edinburgh Conserva- tive Working Men's Association, on Wednesday night, said he believed the time was coming when moderate Liberals would be found strengthening the Conservative party. "LOVING HUSBANDS."—The following entry was made in the diary of the Newcastle Infirmary on Monday : " Mar- garet Robson, Amen Corner, Bruised elbow, quart pet; Mary Davidson, Close, bruised shoulder, poker. Loving hus- bands again." A vacancy is created in the representation of Southamp- ton by the elevation of Mr. Bntt, Q.C., to the judical bench. At the general election Mr. Butt was second on the poll, with 3,023 votes, Mr. A. Giles, Conservatives, being third, with 2,972 votes. An inmate of the Albert Asylum at Lancaster, named Shaw, belonging to Manchester, has killed another patient in resenting a" practical joke." Lord Winmarleigh attended the inquest on Tuesday, and stated that the Managing Com- mittee had satisfied themselves that none of the officials were to blame, an opinion in which the jury fully concurred. ' For tying a dog to a stake, beating its head with a , hammer until its skull and jaw were broken, and then en- deavouring to bury it alive, the Bootle magistrates on Wednesday fined Robert Craig, a small farmer, 40s. and costs. Such a punishment for what the magistrates them- selves described as "a most gross case of cruelty" seems to fall far short of the requirements of the case. AN OVER ZEALOUS POLICEMAN.—At the County Police Court, Liverpool, on Wednesday, Arthor Wilkinson, Church- road, Stanley, was summoned for allowing a dog to be at large. The case was stated by a police officer, but for the defence it was shown that the constable himself had enticed the animal from the defendant's house and then laid an in- formation. The case was dismissed, with costs against the officer. • I

ROBBERIES ON THE MIDLAND RAILWAY. - George Rooks, a goods guard on the Midland Railway, and John Harris and James Revell, under-guards of goods trains, were charged on Wednesday, at the Central Criminal Com t, with stealing property from goods packets carried by the rail- way. The prisoners were all convicted, and it was stated that there was reason to believe that Rooks had been acting dishonestly since the year 1881, and the company had to pay over £2OO for claims for losses. Rooks and Harris were sentenced to five years' penal servitude, and Revell to 18 months' hard labour.

REWARDS FOR VALOUR.--A presentation of rewards for valour was made at the Swansea Guildhall -by the Lady Mayoress, on Wednesday afternoon. Police-constable Deo received the Albert medal from the Secretary of State, £5O from the Swansea Corporation, and other rewards for gallant efforts to save life at a fire. Jenkin Jenkins, coxswain of the Mumbles iifeboat, was presented with a silver medal and £5O for gallantry at the wreck of the German barque Admiral Prince Adelbert. Certificates and rewards were also given to the lifeboat crew' to Artillery Gunner Hut- chings, Police-constables Paine, Parry, and Williams. Sir John Jones Jenkins, M.P., delivered an eulogittic address.

AGRARIAN OUTRAGE IN MONTGOMERYSIIIREI—A farm near Cemmes, a Montgomery village, having been vacated for more than a year, got into a neglected condition, sheep and cattle belonging to neighbouring farmers trespassing freely on the land. A few days ago the agent of the estate made his appearance, and found 140 sheep trespassing, all of which he proceeded to impound; but a number of neigh- bours rescued them from him. Two nights afterwards the farm buildings were discovered to be on fire, and when the police arrived they found that some of the doors of dwell- inghouse, all the doors of the outbuildings, and several field-gates, had been piled in the stable, above which was a lot of dry deals, and the wh.ole set on fire. Before the flames could be subdued they had consumed the stable, barn, and outbuildings. ATTEMPT TO WRECK A MAIL Traim.—A correspondent at Alford telegraphs that a dastardly attempt was made on Wednesday to wreck the mail train which reached Alford, on the east coast line of the Great Northern Railway, at 4-20 a.m. Some platelayers proceeding along the line found a sleeper in the four-foot about half a mile north of Alford. Proceeding further along the line they found a second sleeper in a similar position. A mile further on there was a third sleeper, and 400 yards further another one,. The driver on his return journey was questioned, and upon ex- amination touted the guard irons of his engine much bent. The sleepers must have been placed on the line some time after nine o'clock on Tuesday night, as the London express passed over the line in safety at 8-50 p.m. The pence, under the direction of Mr. Superintendent Stewnett, are in- vestigating the affair. MR. LEITHAM AND MR. LABOECHERE AT EIPDDEDSFIF.LD. —Mr. E. A. Leatham, M.P., speaking at Huddersfield, on Saturday evening, referred to Mr. Cowen's statement that the Irish hatred of England was irradicable, and asked what symptoms there were in this hatred more startling than the evidence of hatred to the Union which was found through the Southern States of America before the I"Var of Seces- sion. But, he said, the enterprise of breaking up the Union had to be abandoned, and the people of this country, rather than the kingdom should be torn asunder, would bring to bear upon the rebellious people of Ireland so vastly prepon- derating a power that there would not be a rebel left in the country. Mr. Labouchere, M.P., spoke at the same meeting. On theluestion of affirmation in Parliament, he said that even Sir Stafford Northcote was in favour of it, but allowed himself to be so far wagged by the tail of the Tory party that he had given the Government measure and his (Mr. LaboucherO's) ball his opposition. RECENT WIELS.—The following have been proved :—Of the Rev. Sir Frederick Vincent, Bart, J.P , cancn of Chi- chester, of Grove Lodge, Bracknell, and Villa Flora, Cannes —the personalty was sworn under £230,000; of the Rev. Richard 'Thomas Lancaster, late of Stanmer House, Suffolk Lawn, Cheltenham, upwards of £137,000; of Mr. Charles James Barnett, J.P., DL., formerly of Bays Hill La.wit, Cheltenham, but late of No. 12, Chichester-terrace, Brighton, over £72,000; of Guy Henri Prosper Lionel Duval, Count de Bonneval, late of No. 41, Rue Cambon, Paris, over £04,000; of Miss Mary Ann Lancaster, late of Stanmer House, Suffolk Lawn, Cheltenham, exceeding £49,000; of Major-General Sir George Hall Macgrego-, K.C.8., late of Glencarnock, St. Michael's-road, Torquay, exceeding £17,000; of the Right Hon. Sir Andrew Buchanan, Bart., P.C., G.C.8., late of Craigend Castle, in the county of Stirling, the personal estate in England and Scotland amounting to over £l2,ooo.—lllustrated London News.

DISASTROUS RAILWAY COLLISION.—OR Monday evening, shortly after six o'clock, a collision occurred at the Eglin- ton-street Station, Glasgow, between a train from Edin- burgh and another for Busby and East Kilbride, which 'had shortly before been despatcha from the Central Station. The collision was of a most violent character, and it was followed by a " telescoping" of carriages, with the result that four persons were killed and between twenty and thirty injured. The information gathered as to the cause of the accident tends strongly in one direction. The Edin- burgh train was in charge of a man named Wood, a Welsh- man, and who is one of the drivers appointed during the recent strike on the Caledonian system, and he, it is said, took his train out of Eglinton-street Station while the signals were against him. This statement is supported by Matthew Sharpe, the driver of the East Kilbride train, who says that as be approached the station the signals were in his favour, and therefore against the incoming train from Edinburgh. He did not see the latter until it was within one length of his own train, when it was too late to pull up and avert the disaster. The engines, he further says, struck each other on the left cylinder. The line was blocked for several hours, but traffic was conducted by a loop line by y of Shields-road, and suffered little interruption. LORD BEACONSFIELD'S CONVERSION.—A local weekly publication, in a recent article, contending that Lord Bea- consfield, shortly before his death, was converted to Roman Catholicism, declared, as a corroborating incident, that dur- ing the late Government "his Eminence Cardinal Manning proceeded on a special mission to Rome. What was his chief business at the Vatican? To negotiate an informal treaty between Lord Beaconsfield and his Holiness'Pope Pius the Ninth. To the Tories, who regarded their Hebrew leader as one of the pillars of the Protestant Establishmeat ; to the Orangemen, who associated him with their 'no surrender' policy in Church and State, this may seem astounding; but there are strong grounds for believing that it is an absolute fact. What was the proposed treaty? That in the event of his Holiness obtaining, through the Catholic Bishops of Ire- land, the support of the Roman Catholic party there for the Tories, Lord Beaconsfield undertook to pass a Catholic Uni- versity Bill for Ireland." A Liverpool gentleman, believirg such statements should not pass unnoticed, forwarded a copy of the paper to Cardinal Manning. He has just received the following reply from his Eminence :—" There is not a sha- dow of truth in what is said about me in the enclosed. I never had any mission—special or otherwise. There was never any compact between me and Lord Beaconsfield. The whole is fabulous." THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—The iron market has decidedly quietened down se far as the demand for pig iron is concerned. Since Friday the business doing has been very limited, and the inquiries on 'Change on Tuesday were only small. Lancashire makers who last week put up their list rates to 47s 6d and 48s, less 4,, for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, have completely stopped buyers at these figures, but as they are well sold over the next three months they are not anxious to press sales. Finished iron shows very little change; there is a moderate inquiry for home consumption, with some of the makers fairly supplied with work, and if anything a tendency in prices to harden slightly on the lowest rates, but where orders are offered they can still be placed on the basis of £6 5s per ton for bars delivered into the Manchester district. Although there is not activity in the coal trade to enable colliery proprietors to realise any better prices, a good demand is being maintained for all descriptions of fuel, which keeps prices steady at full rates. The better classes of round coal for house fire purposes still move off freely, and some of the collieries have great diffi- culty in supplying the wants of their customers. Common round coals continue in fair demand for general trade pur- poses. Engine classes of fuel meet with a good inquiry. and although the activity in the house fire coal trade la.aS naturally caused an increased production of slack, supplies of this description of fuel are not at all abundant in the market, and, if anything, the better sorts show a tendency to harden in price. Prices are firm at late rates, and at the pit mouth awerage about as under: Best coal, Os 6d to lOs ; seconds, 7s 6cl to 8s; common house fire coals, 63 to 7e; steam and forge coals, 58 Od to 63 3d; burgy, 4s 9d to ss; good slack, 33 9d to 4s; with some of the best qualities fetching 4s 3d to 4s Gil per ton. There are very fair Ishipping orders in the market, but the scarcity of vessels still interferes seriously with the transaction of busi- ness. For delivery at the high level, Liverpool, or the Garston docks, steam coal is offeretl at aboct 7e Cd to 78 Pd per ton.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS, MONDAY.

Lord STRATHENDEN and CAMPBELL made a long discur- sive and almost inaudible speech upon the whole foreign policy of the Government, the pith of which, according to Earl Granville, was that the policy of the Government had been based on enmity of Turkey.—This the FOREIGN SECRE- TARY denied.—The Irish Sunday Closing Bill passed through Committee, and the National Gallery (Loan) Bill was read a third time. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.
NEW MEMBER —Mr. Alan Egerton, the new member for Mid-Cheshire, took the oath an his seat.

THE SKYE CnorrEns.—Tbe HOME SECRETARY announced that the Royal Commission to inquire into the Condition of the crofters in the Highlands had new received the sanction of Her Majesty, and that it would be presided over by Lord Napier of Ettrick. PROTECTION or YOUNG PERSONS.—Sir. W. HARCOURT stated that it was the intention of the Government to intro- duce in the House of Lords a bill to strengthen the law in preventing the corruption of youg persons and their intro- duction to an immoral course of life. PUBLIC BUSINESS.—Mr. JESSE COLLINGS asked the Go- vernment to give an assurance that the present session of Parliamert would be continued until the measures named in the speech from the throne had been considered and disposed of.—The PREMIER replied that it would be premature to make any declaration as to the prolongation of the ses-ion to pass bills until they had been able to judge of the pro- gress of business through the agency of the Grand Com- mittees.

THE BANKRUPTCY BILL.-Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, in moving the second reading of the Bankruptcy Bill, remarked that the main objects of a good bankruptcy bill were, first, the economical and honest administration of bankrupt estates with a view to the fair and speedy distribution of the assets among the creditors, and secondly, to do something to im- prove the general tone of commercial morality, to promote honest trading, and to lessen the number of bankruptcies. They could only gain these objects by securing in every case an independent and impartial examination, and that was the cardinal principle of the bill, by which it must stand or fall. He stated that the primary duties of the official receiver would be, first, to investigate the conduct of the bankrupt, and the circumstances which had led to the bankruptcy; next, to conduct tiro public exam- ination of the debtor before the Court; and in the third place to report to the Court when it was called upon to consider the question of discharge both as to any proposition for the settlement of the debtor's affairs and as to any misconduct on the part of the bankrupt which had been disclosed In the course of the proceedings. He had adopted the principle of collection and distribution of assets as primarily the duty of the creditors themselves, with limited official supervision. A preliminary stage was pro- vided for, which he called the receiving order, and which might or might not ripen into bankruptcy. At the first meeting the creditors might decide to make the debtor a bank- rupt or might entertain a proposition for a composition,and at the second meeting, which could not take place till after the examination of the debtor, the composition might, with the sanction of the Court, be accepted. When bankruptcy was declared the creditors would have to select a trustee, to whom, however, the Board of Trade might object, but then- objection would be subject to an appeal to the court. He proposed to make it a misdemeanour for any man being an undischarged bankrupt to obtain credit for any sum exceeding £2O without stating what his position was. He anticipated a great deal of discussion upon his proposal to do away with the preference given to rent and imperial taxes and local rates and to leave only a prefer- ence in favour of wages, and ne left the matter to the judg- ment of the House. As to small debts, he proposed that a debtor summoned to the County Court might furnish the judge with a schedule of his debts, and provided they did not exceed MCI, an order might be made for payment by instalments. Mr. STANHOPE moved an amendment, declaring that the House, while anxious to remedy the proved dOfects in the existing law and practice in bankruptcy, is not prepared to entrust the powers proposed in the Bill to any department of the Government. —Mr. Dixon-Hartland and Mr. Wills agreed in supporting the second reading.—Mr. A. O'CONNOR thought the clauses betrayed hasty preparation, and, in the public interest, suggested a further postponement.—Mr. COWEN took the same view as Mr. Stanhope in respect to the extension of the agency of officialism.—Mr. C. LEWIS thought the clauses of the Bill were unduly harsh, and therefore not it, favour of the creditors.—Mr. H. Fowler supported the Bill, Mr. Gregory also approving of it.—Mr. Serjeant Surma regarded the measure as a step forward in* the desirable direction of abolishing bankruptcy laws altogether.—Mr. Edward Clarke and Sir John Lubbock took exception to some clauses of the Bill, though the latter said there was so much good in it that he should vote for the second reading.—Sir HARDINGE G/FFARD criticised the working of the measure, more particularly with respect to the duties of the official receivers. Eventually the Bill was read a second time.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUESDAY
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUESDAY

The Royal Assent having been given by commission to some money bills, the Sale of Liquor on Sundays (Ireland) Bill was read a third time and passed. Their Lordships upon rising adjourned until the 3rd of April.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUFSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUFSDAY.

THE TRANSTAAL.—Mr. E. ASHLEY informed Mr. Cropper that the Government would wait the r2sult of the Transvaal debate before making arrangements to compensate the frieadly Bechuana chiefs. The negotiations were pro- ceeding. 11i ADAGASCAR.—In reply to Lord R. CHURCHILL, Lord E. FII ZNIAURICE stated that in the negotiations about Madagas- car Her Hajesty's Government had shown a desire to pro- mote a peaceful solution of the Iptestion, and would continue to do so, but beyond that they were not prepared to go.

THE ATTACK- ON LADY DIXIE.—Sir W. HARCOURT in- formed Mr. O'Shea that the attack on Lady Dixie was un- dergoing investigation by the police, and he was not in a position to make any statement upon it.—Mr. LABOUCHEEE inquired whether it would be desirable to offer a reward to any person who came forward with evidence as to who was the guilty party in the case ?—Sir W. HARcorwr asked the House to be satisfied with the reply already given. THE TENANTS' COMPENSATION BILL. The PRIME MINISTER informed Mr. A. Arnold that the Tenants' Com- pensation Bill was still under the careful consideration of the Government, and it was in a very advanced stage. As a rule, it was not wise to introduce important bills which were likely to excite differences of opinion until the pro- moters were prepared to go forward with them. THE HIGHLAND CROFTERS.—In the course of a conver- sation on the distress amongst the crofters in the Highlands, Mr. A. O'CONNOR, pointing to the .mace on the table, sug- gested that the Government should get rid of that "thing " and send money to the poor people.
THE BUDGET.—The Ortarrc.ELLort of the EXCHEQUER in- timated to the Leader of the Opposition that he hoped to make his financial statement on the sth April.

THE BANKRUPTCY BILL.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN moved that the Bankruptcy Bill be referred to the Standing Com- mittee on Trade, Shipping, and Manufactures.—Mr. 'EAMES moved as an amendment that it was inexpedient to transfer to the Standing Committees the jurisdiction hitherto exer- cised over public bills by Committees of the whole House.— After an animated debate upon the new scheme of Grand Committees, Mr. RASHES withdrew his amendment—The reference to the Committee was then agreed to, Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN intimating that the Standing Committee would meet on the 9Lh of April.—At seven o'clock the House ad- journed for the Easter recess.

div.head: EXPLOSION AT THE GOVEfIN-111ENT OFFICES.
div.p: THE EXPLOSION AT THE GOVEfIN- -111ENT OFFICES.

Nothing fresh has transpired with reference to the explo- sion ef Thursday night week, at the offices of the Local Government Board in London, so far as any clue to the per- petrator of the outrage is concerned. The police are actively pursuing inquiries, but the chief reliance is upon the fact that such a matter must be known to several persons, and that one of them, for the sake of the reward of £l,OOO that has been oflered by the Government, will give private information. On Saturday morning Col. Majendie, the Inspector of Explosives to the Government, and Professor Abel, of Woolwich, resumed their examination on the spot. By taking exact measure- ments to where various things have been thrown they have traced the identical spot where the canister was placed. This was inside the balustrade of the window, and about one foot from its right-hand side. That the dynamite, for dyna- mite it undoubtedly was, was contained in a canister is also plainly shown, as small pieces, almost microscopical, have been picked out, not only from the debris at the comers of the windows, but from the stonework above, where the first shock of the explosion took effect. No trace of anything in the way of a fuse has been found, nor is it expected that such a thing will come to light. Professor Abel calculates that the maximum quantity of dynamite used was 20pounds, which would be fully sufficient to cause all the damage that has accrued.

Professor Abel has analysed the contents of the box with which the attempt was made to blow up the Times office. He finds that the material is precisely the same as that used in the explosion some weeks ago at the gasworks at Glas- gow, on which occasion he analysed the fragments of the explosive discovered. Sheet-iron bandbox-like cases were used in both outrages, and are precisely similar in appear- ance and construction. The authorities have, therefore, come to the conclusion that the attempts at Glasgow and the Times office were the work of the same organisation. It has become manifest to the authorities that it was the Home Office which was intended to be blown up. Sir William Harcourt has been many times threatened, and so also has been the Home Office, but nothing has ever been ascertained to cause any danger to the Local Government Offices to be apprehended. Part of the Home Office runs over that spot where the explosion occurred, one room being occupied by Mr. Machonoehie, chief of the Criminal Inves- tigation Department of the Home Office. In consequence of the disquietude caused by the outrage, it has been determined to augment the metropolitan police force. Orders have been given to engage 500 more men as constables. The detective department will also be increased, as it has been decided to double the strength of the staff on duty during the night. It is stated that more than ordinary precautions will be taken by the Flintshire constabulary authorities for the pro- tection of Mr. Gladstone during his stay at Hawarden in the Easter recess.

A Dublin correspondent states that in consequence of the dynamite outrage it has been thought expedient to take additional precautions for the protection of the Lord-Lieu- tenant an the Irish Executive.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
ALTRINCHAM

ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD A RAILWAY COMPANY.—On Monday, at the Altrincharn Police Court, Joseph Roughley, a man of respectable appearance, was summoned for de- frauding the Manchester South Junction Railway on three occasions by riding from Manchester to Sale without paying his fare. Defendant took third returns from Bowdon to Sale, and returned from Manchester to Bowdon without pay- ing excess fare. Defendant denied any intention to:defraud, nd pleaded inadvertence, he having return half of ticket from Manchester in his posseBskin tIIQ time. Fined. 60s. and costs, or three months' ii.pprisonment.

div.head: ASHiON.
div.p: ASHiON.

AN UNGRATEFUL LODGER.—What appears to have been a most impudent robbery, was committed early on Monday morning last at Ashton. A man named Cannon had been lodging at the house of William Dowling, situate in Whit- ledge Green-road, or the old Wigan-road, for a considerable time past. At an early hour on Monday morning last Cannon disappeared, and the sum of Zl. 45., and an overcoat, the property of Dowling, were missed. The latter subsequently gave information to the police, but up to the present, P.S. Savage and his staff of police constables have not been able to ascertain the whereabouts of the wanted man. SPECIAL MEETING OF THE ASHTON LOCAL BOARD.—A special meeting of the members of the Ashton Local Board was held on Monday forenoon, at the Board Offices, Bryn- street, to examine the annual accounts of the Board. There were present :—Messrs. A. B. Moubert (in the chair), Gas- kell, Knowles, Burchall, Roberts, Latham, the Rev. H. Siddall, and Goldsworth (clerk).—The Clerk stated that that was a special meeting called to consider and examine the accounts of the Board which required to be paid pre- vious to the 25th of March.—The accounts amounted to 055 Gs. Pd., and they were examined and passed.—After some discussion the R9V. H. Siddall moved, and Mr. Roberts seconded, that the accounts of the Board should be presented immediately after the 25th March, and not delayed as for- merly until after the audit. The loss on the water account was also ordered to be transferred to the general drstrict rate, and the collector was instructed to take the usual steps necessary to obtain payment of outstanding accounts.—This was the only business.

THE Qt:TEN:;-..;;;SUSTICES OF LANCASHIRE.—This was a rule in the Queen's Bench Division calling upon the Jus- tices of Lancashire, sitting in quarter session, to show cause why a certiorari should not issue to bring up an order made by them for the purpose of its being quashed, the order being for the appointment of Mr. William Albridge, an accountant, to ascertain the amount of profit on the Ashton Gas Com- pany, and having been obtained at the instance of two gas consumers of the borough. The Solicitor-General and Mr. Michael, QC., appeared to support the rule; Mr. Wills, Q.C,, and Mr. Yates showing cause against it. Mr. Baron Pollock delivered the judgment of the court without calling upon the Solicitor-General to show cause. His Lordship said it had been argued on the part of the justices that a cer- tiorari would not lie, because their making the order was a ministerial and not a judicial act. True, the act was minis- terial in one sense, but in the real sense it was judicial, be- cause they made the order not as a matter of course, but in the exercise of the discretion vested in them by the Act of Parliament—they must see whether the matter came within the Act or not. Two other objections had been raised against the certiorari; but, although they were of a more substantial character than the last, they could not be allowed to pre- vail, and, on the whole, the court were of opinion that the rule for gnashing the order of the justices should be made absolute.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS.—Mr. Rowbottom, the deputy- coroner, held an inquest at the Victoria Inn, Golborne, on Monday last, on the body of Ann Waterworth, 87 years of age, residing at 45, High-street, who died from injuries received on the 9th February. It seems that the deceased had been in the habit of getting up during the might, and at four o'clock on the morning of the date named she was found lying badly injured at the foot of the stairs. She was conscious, however, and stated that she had fallen down- stairs. Dr. Worsley subsequently attended the deceased up to her death, which took place on Friday last.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." HA.YDOCK.

A Bow DROWNED AT HA.YDOCK.—On Monday afternoon, Mr. T. W. Barker, coroner, held an inquest at the Ship Inn, Blackbrook, on the body of William Hodgkinson, seven years of age, son of William Hodgkinson, a collier residing at Blackbrook, who was accidently drowned on the previous Saturday forenoon. It appeared that the deceased with two other children went to play near the basin, or end of the Sankey Brook Canal, leaving his home about half-past eight in the morning. At one side of the basin the end of a wooden 'fence comesto within a foot of the edge of the water, and while the deceased was attempting to pass he fell into the canal. Hearing his screams, a young man named Wilkinson, residing in Park-road, St. Helens, ran to the side, and after some considerable difficulty, succeeded in getting the body out, but not before the child had been drowned. —The jury returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned."..

WOMEN'S TREAT AT HATDOCK.—Mrs. EVaiiB entertained the members of several of the women's or mothers' classes of Earlestown. Newton, Haydock, and Ashton on Tuesday evening last. Mrs. Evans' generosity is well-known through- out the district, and, as might only be expected, the women who assembled—altogether to the number of nearly 200— were very kindly treated, and keenly felt Mrs. Evans' consi- deration for them. An excellent and substantial tea was pro- vided by Mrs. Jackson, of Earlestown, and the guests partook of it in the Meeting House, near the stables, Hay- dock. It was well served, and amongst other ladies pre- sidinr, at the tables were Mrs. Evans, Miss Lilly Evans, Mrs. Hayward, Mrs. Beilby and Mrs. Stelfox. Afterwards a pleasant, social, and " chatty " gathering was held, and oranges and cakes were distributed to those present. The Rev. J. Allatt, of Newton; the Rev. H. Wilson, of Ashton; Mr. E. J. Weaver, of Earlestown; and Mr. J. Barton, town missionary, Haydock, rendered assistance in making the meeting as enjoyable as possible, and gave appropriate addresses,

div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

UNLICENSED AND STRAY DOGS AT HIITTON.—At Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Robert Smith, Huyton, was fined ss. and costs for keeping a dog without a license.— Thomas Melling was similarly fined for a like offence.— Edward Hughes, Huyton (who was represented by his gar- dener); Robert S. Comberbach, Huyton; Henry Lawrenson, Huyton Quarry; Johnson Holland, Horn Smithy; and Thos. Riding, Huyton, were etch fined ss. and costs for allowing their dogs to be at large.

div.head: RAINHILL.
div.p: RAINHILL.

RAINHILL A On Friday the reports of the medical superintendents of the several county asylums for the past year were issued. The following is an abstract of the report of Mr. I'. L. Rogers, of the asylum at Rainhill : —lBl patients were admitted during the year, being 12 less than in 1881 • and of these 19 had been at some former time patients in this asylum. The daily average number through- out the year was 686. The number discharged as recovered was 76. Sixty-two patients died, being at the rate of 9 per cent. One was a female suicide, who hanged herself with the string of her petticoat. With refetence to certain im- provement,s, Mr. Rogers says it may be thought that well. dressed patients and tastefull-decorated wards have in reality no visible tendency to improve the mental condition of patients, and that therefore the money spent on such things is a needless expenditure. He thinks this is a mistaken view, and that they are positive adjuncts to recovery. _

div.head: TARBUCK.
div.p: TARBUCK.

A TARBUCK FARMER'S SHEEP Poo.—Margaret Garnett, farmer, Tarbuck, WAS charged before the Prescot magistrates, on Tuesday, with keeping a dog without a license.—Defen- dant said she had two dogs, a terrier and a sheep dog, and she had regularly taken out a license for the former but not for the latter, as she considered a sheep dog exempt from license. She had not, however, obtained a formal exemption from the excise, not having considered it neces- sary.—The case was adjourned for a fortnight, in order that Mrs. Garnett might obtain a formal exemption.

div.head: W H ISTON.
div.p: W H ISTON.

WIIISTON SCHOOL ATTENDANCE PROSECIITIONS.—Peter Houghton, Whiston, was fined ss. for neglecting to send his step-child, Jane Smith, to school.—Mr. Seddon, school attendance officer, stated that the child had only attended school 61 out of 05 times.—James Pickavance, Whiston, was also fined ss. for neglecting to send his child to school. —Mr. Hartley prosecuted on behalf of the Union School Attendance Committee.

AN FAST-GOING CARRIER AT WHISTON.—Thomas Taylor was charged at Prescot, on Tuesday, with leaving his horse and cart standing on the highway at Whiston Potteries.— P.C. Hall stated that he saw the horse and cart standing across the road opposite Mr. Plant's public-house, and on going into the house he found defendant playing at domi- noes. He told him that his horse and cart were obstruct- ing the roadway, but defendant continued his game, and did not leave the house till ten minutes afterwards. Defendant was fined 7s. 6d. and costs.

CONCERT AT WHISTON.—On Monday evening a concert was given in the National schools, Whiston, on behalf of the Wesleyan schoots in that township. Mr. J. Leather- barrow, the popular guardian for Whiston, presided, and, in introducing the singers, delivered a hearty address of wel- come to the audience, and expressed his good wishes for the welfare of the schools under whose asspices the concErt was given. The principal vocalists were Miss Gardner, Miss Parry, and Mr. George Barton, of St. Helens; and Mr. Wood, of Rainhill, who sang several of the most popular and admired songs in their reportoire to the manifest de- light of their hearers. The choir contributed a number of concerted pieces with much success. There was a large audience, and the concert was very agreeable throughout.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

WIGAN JuNcrnow RAlLWAY.—Considerable progress has been made of late in the construction of this railway. The main line from Glazebrook to Wigan is now all but com- plete, and the erection of the various intermediate stations is being rapidly pushed forward. A VIOLENT LovEn.—At Wigan, on Tuesday, a young man named Williams was charged with brutally assaulting his sweetheart, Sarah Jane Glazebrook. On Saturday night the prisoner met Glazebrook in Darlington-street, and ac- cused her of paying too much attention to another young man. She denied the imputAtion, whereupon Williams struck her a violent blow on the nose, gave her two black eyes, and knocked her to the ground, rendering her uncon- scious. He had no defence to offer, and was fined 40s and sosts.

--- ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. The Rev. J. B. Wheeler, who was rector of Coppenhall, Cheshire, from 1834 to 1869, has died in London, at the age of 67. The reverend gentleman left Coppenhall to take two years' duty in South Norwood and after that he officiated

for four years at Eastling, in Kent. Before bis appointment to the Cheshire rectory he held curacies at Crewe and Shrewsbury. In 1881 he was appointed a licensed preacher in the diocese of Canterbury.

AN UPROAR AT A SALTATION MEETING.—At the Crewe Police Court, on Tuesday, Joseph Jones, a mechanic, was charged with creating a disturbince at a service of the Sal- vation Army.—Defendant attended the barracks, on Sunday, and during the service he shon'ed and used bad language. On a remonstrance he threatened the officer with violence. Au uproar ensued, and the service had to be suspended until he was ejected from the building. The defendant pleaded that he only told the captain to speak up.—He was fined 308,, including costs. _ _

CATTLE DT SFASE ax CHESHlRE.—Lieutenant-Colon el Hammersley, chief constable for Cheshire, in a report for last week, states that 109 animals were attacked with foot and mouth disease. There were 378 animals under treat- ment from the previous week, and during last week eight died and 202 recovered, leaving at the end of the week 277 still affected. Fresh outbreaks had occurred on three farms, but there were no cases of pleuro-pneumonia. In the townships of Millington and Little Le seven pigs had been attacked with swine fever and slaughtered. Sheep scab existed on 15 farms, there being 56 sheep under treat- ment.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A PRISONER AT CHESTER CASTLE. —Dr. Churton, the coroner for West Cheshire, held an in- quest on Monday on the body of a woman named Charlotte Bundred, a native of Denbighshire, who was undergoing a term of nine months' imprisonment at Chester Castle for an offence committed in the county named, and who died on Saturday morning. It transpired that the woman gave birth on Wednesday to twins, and was attended by a medical gentleman, but she became very weak and exhausted, and was afterwards seized with convulsions, from which she died on Saturday as stated. A verdict in accordance with these facts was returned.

WEST EDDISBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.-A meeting of this Board was held at Chester on Saturday, Mr. H. Linaker presiding. A letter was received from Mr. H. P. Jones wi k reference to the fall of a portion of a wall at Barrow. The wall was a tetaining wall, built by the Board under an agreement with Mr. Jones in 1879. Portions of the wall had fallen several times, and the surveyor was now ordered to make an inspection of it and report to the Board.—Tl e surveyor was directed to include in his estimate for the en- I suing year the probaLle cost of repairing the Cliff-road, Alvanley, for a length of about 700 yards.—The surveyor announced that 19 miles of turnpike roads would fall within the jurisdiction of the Board next November ; and he also reported that the roads were mostly in a bad condition, and would require a large outlay upon them. He asked that the matter might be taken into consideration, and a committee appointed to inspect the roads with him.—After a discus- sion, he was ordered to inspect the roads and report thereon to the Board.

CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—A general meeting of the Cheshire Agricultural Society was held on Tuesday, at the Royal Hotel, Crewe, Sir Philip Grey Egerton, Bart, presiding. The chairman said that the first business was to fix a date for holding the annual show, so as not to clash with others held in the neighbouring counties. Mr. Cliffs proposed that the society have a two days' exhibition, and that it be held a week before the Manchester and Liverpool show. This was seconded by Mr. Coomer. Mr. Finchett moved, as an amendment, that the show be held a week later than the Manchester and Liverpool, urging that farmers would be busy with their harvest in August, and there was little prospect of having a good show of roots or ripe cheese so early. The amendment was carried by a majority of one, the date fixed being Friday and Saturday, Sep'ember-1.4 and 15, the place Crewe, the local committee offering £l5O and the free use of a site, stall accommodation, water, gas, Ac. Sir Philip Egerton said he would give for competition at the forthcoming show three £5 silver cups for the best shorthorn bull, best pair of dairy cows, and best pair of heifers under two years old. He would also give three extra prizes of equal value in the three cheese classes. (Applause.) A vote of thanks was accorded Sir Philip for his kind offer. The usual committees were then appointed.

div.head: ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION OF LADY F. DIXIE.
div.p: ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION OF LADY F. DIXIE.

A crime was committed in the neighbourhood of Windsor on Saturday afternoon, which will meet with universal re- probation, except among that section of Irish malcontents who favour assassination as a method of political warfare. The life of Lady Florence Dixie, who has made herself ob- noxious by her writings on certain phases of the Irish agita- tion, was attempted in a most dastardly manner, and, it is probably only owing to her being attended by a favourite dog that she escaped death. She was walking on the Wind- sor-road, near the riverside villa of her husband, Sir Beau- mont Dixie,when two persons dressed as women, but believed to be two men, asked her what time it was. Mer ladyship replied that she could net tell them, and turned into private grounds. Thither the two followed her, and the foremost seized her by the neck and pulled her violently to the ground, where she lay helpless and alone. Whether the dog attacked the miscreants at this particular juncture is not known, as Lady Florence was for some seconds insensible. It would appear, however, that one of the men bending down drew from the folds of the loose cloak which enveloped bins a knife or dagger, and aimed a blow at the lady's prostrate form, which was apparently in- tended to pierce the heart. The blade of the weapon pierced the lady's dress and struck the corset, but here encountered a steel, which caused it to glance cif. Deliber- ately, though hurriedly, withdrawing the murderous weapon, the wretch made another lunge at Lady Dixie. By this time her ladyship had to a certain extent recovered from the suddenness of the attack, and with sur- prising self-possession clutched the dagger by the blade, as it was descending, with her left hand. It would seem, how- ever, that after a brief struggle the instrument was wrenched from her grasp only to be seized again by the right hand of the courageous lady. Once more the weapon was torn from her, and on another blow being delivered, the point of it pierced her dress through. Again the corset afforded pro- tection. It would now seem that the dog came to the rescue, for, according to Lady Dixie, it was not until this time that the noble brute became aware of the danger to which his mistress was exposed. Bounding forward, the animal seised the would-be assassin, and dragged him off his pros- trate victim. At this moment, apparently, the wheels of some passing vehicle were heard proceeding along , the highway, and the villains, becoming alarmed, left the ' object of their brutal assault lying senseless on the ground, and took to flight. Whether or not they were followed by the dog, and how they effected their escape, must remain a mystery, but the only explanation of Lady Dixie's almost miraculous escape from death at the assassins' bands is that in some way or other her assailants were interrupted in their fiendish work, and sought safety in a speedy retreat. At all events, on recovering from the fit of unconscious- ness into which she had fallen, Lady Florence founl her- self lying quite alone on the ground. The men had disap- peared and so had the dog. On recovering sufficiently, she got over the fence and proceeded toward S home as fast as her exhausted condition would permit. A statement which has been supplied to the limes by Lady Dixie is substantially the same as the foregoing narrative.

I The startling news was, it is reported, at once conveyed to her Majesty the Queen. who expressed her sympathy with Lady Dixie. Her Majesty, it is said, was much con- cerned at the attempt upon ber ladyship's life, and subse- quently made anxious inquiries for full particulars. In Windsor itself, when once the details of the.outrage became known, the indignation of the inhabitants knew no bounds. The greatest possible excitement prevailed, and the latest information was eagerly sought after. Public feeling, how- ever, calmed down somewhat when it became known that I Lady Dixie had fortunately escaped without sustaining any positive injuries of a serious character. Lady Florence is well known as a lady of adventurous disposition, experienced as a traveller in distant semi-bar- barous regions, and never afraid to express boldly the de- cided opinions she is in the habit of forming upon public questions which excite her interest. It may be remembered that her ladyship was somewhat conspicuous as a champion of King Cetewayo, whom she visited during his captivity, previous to his recent visit to this country. In both the Zulu and Transvaal wars she acted, during at least a por- tion of the campaigns, as special correspondent of one of the London morning newspapers. One of the two assailants of her ladyship is said to have been attired in the green-coloured dress of a female, and rumours have since been current that during the afternoon, and previous to the attempted murder, a woman thus at- tired was seen walking through the streets of Windsor, and was particularly noticed in William-street. A Dublin correspondent says: The daring attempt upon the life of Lady Florence Dixie is in some measure ex- plained by the' fact that in August last she received an extraordinary threatening letter, which, in the light of recent events assumes an important character. The letter was dated Dublin, July 7th, and was signed with the word "Liberty." It was handed to Lady Florence Dixie in the grounds of her residence in Leicestershire by a man, who, as soon as she had taken the missive into her hand, quickly decamped. The writer de- dared that he had been deputed to warn her that the prin- ciples she was endeavouring to instil into the minds of the Irish people were not in conformity with and would subvert those held "by the party to which I belong. That party now rules Ireland in secret, but the time is fast approach- ing when the mask will be thrown off." The letter farther warned Lady Florence Dixie that if she returned to Ireland she would be assassinated, and stated, "The hand that writes this killed Lord Frederick Cavendish. It has £20,000 offered for its discovery, but we defy discovery." I Much doubt has been cast upon Lady Florence Dixie's account of the outrage, and it has been freely stated that the soft ground at the place where the assault took place showed no signs of a struggle. A Windsor correspondent, however, who was the first representative of the Press to visit the scene of the outrole, now repeats his statement that on his first arrival the marks of men's feet were distinctly visible, and that he could also trace the footprints of the dog, while the soft soil bore further evidence of a struggle having taken place. IC is stated, too, that on Saturday evening, at about half-past six, two suspicious looking persons called at a , public-house at Egham, the intervening distance of about 'seven miles corresponding somewhat closely to the distance that could have been walked between the time of the assault land their arrival at the house of call. These persons were supposed to be women and are said to correspond with the description given of her assailants by Lady Florence Dixie.

HIGHWAY RATE FOR WINDLE.—On Monday, at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, Mr. W. Swift, assistant over- seer for Windle (rural), applied for the magistrates sanction to the new highway rate of 10d. in the pound. The appli- cation was granted. TRANSFER OF LICENSES.—At Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, the magistrates (Messrs. A. R. Gladstone, H. Bright, and Willis) sanctioned the following transfers : Waterloo Hotel, Widnes, from John Barrow to Geo. Cook; Commercial Hotel, Widnes, from J. A. Greaves to Owen Tansey ; Tine Hotel, Widnes from P. Blessington to Wm. Ornisher ; beerhouse, at Appleton, from Owen Tansey to IJames Concannon ; beerheuse, in Kemble-street, Prescot, from William Houghton to Joseph Berry. I Pnascor PARISH CHURCH.--When it became known Ibnmetime ago that the Rev. H. S. Bolton the popular junior curate of Prescot Parish Church, was about to remove to Ravenhead, an influential committee was formed to concert measures for the presentation of a testimonial to the rev. gentleman. The committee have now decided that the testimonial shall take the form of a gold three-quarter plate watch, an illuminated address which will be embellished with a view of Prescot Church, and a purse. The presenta- tion will take place on the 2nd April, and it is expected that Mr. W. L. Evans will occupy the chair on the occasion. Mr. Bolton enters upon his duties at Ravenhead the first week in May. Tho new vicar, Rev. Mr. McNaughton, is expected to come into residence on April 6th. THE EARLY EASTER.—The spring quarter day falls this year on Easter Sunday, a very unusual coincidence. The Easter of 1883 has already caused sundry anomalies. Pancakes were eaten a week before St. alentine's Day, and the University boat race was decided dur- ing a snowstorm before the middle of Marck I [There were only two Sundays after Epiphany, while there are in some years six; and now the special lessons appointed for the Annunciation are merged in those for Easter Day. The coincidence of quarter day with Easter Sunday is of more general interest. The day following being Bank Holiday, all business regulated by statute stand over till the 27th. Those determined by usage and common law, such as payment of quarterly salaries, are made on tile 24th.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, MARCH 24, 1883.

The legislative work of the Session may be said to have commenced in earnest on Mon- day evening, when Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, the President of the Board of Trade, moved the second reading of the Bankruptcy Bill, which has since been transferred to one of the Grand Committees of the House for the con- sideration of details. Some measure such as that now submitted by the Government has for some time been demanded by the country, and from the general support which has been accorded to it on both sides of the House, we should say that it is likely to pass into law with its main provisions unaltered. It has evidently been well thought out by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and his colleagues in the Cabinet, and the fact that it receives the acquiescence of the judges of the land, the Contro:ler of Bankruptcy, the Incorporated Law Society, the Institute of Accountants, the Committee of the Associated Chainbers of Commerce, and also of the London bankers, is a guarantee that it is likely to abolish some of the evils which are unfor- tunately too much associated with the law affecting debtors. It has long been felt that it is by far too easy for a tradesman to relieve himself of the responsibility which he voluntarily incurs in his business relations; and also that receivers, trustees, and others, who live on bankruptcy estates, have too much power in their own hands and are not properly held: in check in dealing with the moneys of creditors and debtors alike, The honest trader is not sufficiently protected when he is overtaken by misfortune, and on the other hand the dishonest trader is not always punished according to his deserts, even though it may have been found that he has been criminally responsible for the condition in which he lands himself. The past history of legislation on this important question is not, as shown by Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN, very encouraging. Voluntaryism and officialism—that is, the administration of bankrupt estates voluntarily by the creditors, and by officials known as official assignees— have each played their part, and though the present bill provides for an extension of the official system, that extension is happily exceedingly limited in its operation. The two leading features in any bankruptcy bill ought to be, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN says, the economical and honest administration of bankrupt estates with a view to the fair and speedy distribution of the assets among the creditors; and next, following the idea that prevention is better than cure, the bill should do something to improve the general tone of commercial morality, to promote honest trad- ing, and to lessen the number of bankrupt- cies. In other words, says the President of the Board of Trade, the law has not only to protect the salvage, but to diminish the number of wrecks. These important objects, he contends, can only be secured by an independent and impartial examina- tion in every ease, and that independent and impartial examination is the cardinal prin- ciple of the bill now before the House. The honest trader certainly will not object to such an inquiry, he will rather court it in the hope of speedily getting his discharge ; nor on the other hand will the legitimate creditors offer any objection, for they will have the satisfac- tion of knowing that if the debtor has been overtaken by misfortune, at least what assets he possesses will be equally distributed amongstthem instead of finding their way into the pockets of one or two persons interested in retaining them. It is very certain that the fictitious creditors—creditors with colour- able claims, creditors who, with an obvious motive, would not scruple to double or treble their claims, tradesmen who have not been honest in their dealings, and trustees with an eye to peculation, will dislike inquiry, but it must be remembered that these are the very persons against whom this bill is aimed, and if it errs at all, we should say that it is on the side of leniency. If it be conceded that an inquiry is necessary, then the next step naturally follows that there must be a public official to conduct the inquiry, and in order to make him thoroughly responsible it is re- quisite he should be under the control of some department of the State, which in its turn is responsible to public opinion through the House of Commons. In the bill submitted the official is to be called the Official Receiver, and he is to be responsible to the Board of Trade. His primary duties are to investigate the conduct of a bankrupt and the circum- stances which led to the bankruptcy; to con- duct a public examination of the debtor be- fore the Court; and also to report to the Court, when it is called upon to consider the

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAllar. 24,188&
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAllar. 24,188&

question of discharge, both as to any propo- sition for the settlement of the debtor's affairs which may be before the court at the time, and also as to any misconduct on the part of the bankrupt which has been dis- closed in the course of the proceedings. This officer will be in fact, to some extent, a public investigator, and also to some extent a public prosecutor, and he will be bound to take notice of any special information submitted to him by any honest creditor desiring a full investigation. These are the primary duties of the Receivers, but there are others of less importance. It is estimated that 6o of these officials will be required, and that their cost will be j 50,000 per annum, a sum which will be provided for by the receipts from fees and the interests on moneys of estates de- posited in the Bank of England as provided by the bill, so that the cost of the working of the measure will be no burden on the tax- payers The only objection that has so far been urged to the bill is the introduction of the official system, but to us that seems its very strongest point, for if the inquiry is to be independent and impartial in something- more than name, it must be conducted by a res- ponsible officer; and those who contend that the Board of Trade is incompetent to conduct such inquiries satisfactorily would do i well to remember that this Department has I already charge of inquiries into accidents at sea, explosions in coal mines, accidents on railways, &c. The thoroughness of these inquiries, too, are rarely, if ever, called in question. The ease with which a person at the present time can resume business after bankruptcy is somewhat remarkable, and indeed, as Mr CHAMBERLAIN says, it seems a matter of indifference to a bankrupt whether he gets his discharge or not. For instance, according to the Controller's report for iBB r there were in that year 5,207 bankrupts, but of these only 606 applied for discharge, and only one-third of those who ' were entitled to take their discharge thought it worth while to go through the form Not- withstanding this scandal these bankrupts are able to continue trading without any , difficulty, but under the new Bill it will be a ' misdemeanour for any undischarged bank-' rupt to obtain credit to the extent of Rao without disclosing his position. At present there are preferential claims on bankrupt estates on account of wages, rents, taxes, and rates. The new Bill proposes to limit such claims to wages only, a very satisfactory arrangement; and another excellent feature in the Bill is this, that it puts the large and small debtor on an equality, which is not now the case. It has always been a defect in the present law that a large debtor can relieve himself of his liabilities, whilst a poor and often honest man is sent to prison because he cannot pay the full amount of what he owes, but this will. now be remedied, for under the provisions of the new Bill a County Court judge will be able to make an order for the payment of a debt of less than -..eso by instalments or otherwise. The Bill on the whole is one which deserves the support of the trading community generally, and the more it is studied the more equitable do its provisions appear. It is a conscientious and bold attempt to reform abuses which are far too common in dealing with bankrupt estates, and as such it ought to succeed. It will not, of course, make a .dishonest trader honest ; but it will at least make it much more diffi- cult for him to play a dishonest part, and it will at the same time abolish a class of irre- sponsible persons who, when the debtors' money finds its way into their hands, makes it quickly disappear without in many cases rendering any account whatever to the creditors.

In another page of to-day's issue we pub- lish a report of the proceedings at the fort- nightly meeting of the Board of Guardians on Wednesday. The details are again of the lively nature that seems to be inseparable from these gatherings, the conduct of the busi- ness of which is degenerating into a public scandal. It is not necessary for us to de- fend Mr. Mackey, but we may be permitted to say that he has filled the position of master of the Workhouse for a number of years, that we are not aware any complaint has been made against him, and that we do not believe it has been reserved for the present Board to discover any short-comings, real or imagin- ary, on his part. For the sake of argument, however, let it be conceded that he is incom- petent for the discharge of the duties de- volving upon him, and also that his children are maintained out of the ratepayers' money, we yet fail to discover, any justification for the Guardians parading every trifling matter affecting that gentleman before the public ; and although he is a servant of the rate- payers, that is no reason whatever why his domestic and private affairs should be periodically canvassed by the Board and sub- sequently by the public. If the Master and Matron are not suited to their position, let the Guardians, who are their masters, do their duty and dismiss them; if, on the other hand, fire fault-finding only arises from per- sonal animosity—as we believe it does—on the part of a section of the Board, we hope the ratepayers will perform their duty and refuse to elect gentlemen animated by personal, in- stead of public, considerations. The Chair- man is reported to have stated, on Wednesday, that the Board was becoming notorious by the constant squabbles, a statement which we do not dispute, and he added that they reflected upon the ratepayers and the mem- bers of the Board. We do not see how those squabbles reflect upon the ratepayers, except in so far as they are responsible for electing the malcontents; but we do see that these unseemly displays of feeling very seriously reflect upon the Board. We are disposed to think, too, that the Chairman, more than any other member, is to blame for those disturbances, for we are satisfied that the exercise of a little more firmness and dis- cretion on his part would have averted many an acrimonious discussion. We are not surprised to hear that certain members of the Board—the members, by the way, who have a sincere desire to see the business of the Board conducted peacefully, and who are anxious to act harmoniously with. the Master and all the other officials—do not propose to seek re-election. We should, on the other hand, be surprised if they continued to iden- tify themselves with the Board.

In consequence of the recent supposed Fenian outrages, the precaution has been taken to have a file of men on patrol at the Orford Barracks, Warrington, every hour during the night. PRESCOT SCROOT, BOARD BLEcriow.—The triennial elec- tion of members of Prescot School Board takes place on the 31st inst. The number of members required is seven, and the following gentlemen have been nominated by the Pres- cot Ratepayers' Association :—Messrs. W. L. Evans, C. Spencely, C. B. Johnson, T. P. Hewitt, J. B. Sanders, and William Goldsworth. Ail these gentlemen, except Mr. Johnson, were members of the Board whose term of office has just expired. Mr. J. Johnson Brown and Mr. Wycher- ley, also retiring members, having declared their intention not to serve again, they have not been nominated. In addi- ' to the candidates named, Mr. Henry Fogg and Mr. J. T. Hall have been proposed. Thus there are eight aspirants for the seven seats, and at present there seems every pros- pect of a contest.
RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.—The office of the Runcorn County Court was closed on Thursday evening last for the Easter holidays. Business will be resumed on Wednesday next.
CONFIRMATIONS IN THE DIOCESE OF CHESTER.—The Bishop of Chester, assisted 17 Bishop Kelly, Archdeacon of Macclesfield, will hold confirmations at Runcorn and Prod- __
sham on the 29th inst.

TEMPORARY AUTHORITY.—James Casson applied at Run- corn Police Court, on Monday, for temporary authority to sell intoxicating liquors at the Village Inn, Halton, lately occupied by Joseph Taylor —John Beresford applied for a similar licence to sell at the Elephant and Castle, Halton, lately occupied by John Clark.—Both applications were

granted. WIDNE3 SCHOOL BOARD AT WORE.—At Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for neglec t- ing to send their children regularly to school :—Thomas Roach, Mary Riley John Fenny, Mary A. Bowyer, John Hill (adjourned), John McCann, Miles Gaul, Michael Con- nor, Henry Fountain James Plunkett, John Keating, and Sarah Howard.—The usual fine of ss. including costs was imposed in each case, except where ctherwise specided. Titia PROJECTED CHURCH AT ANDERSON'S CORNER, WIDNES—We understand that the Widnes Church Exten- sion Committee, who are in charge of this matter, have decided to at once'erect a portion of the building. The sure of £3.500 has been raised towards the totat cost, which is estimated at £7,000, and so much of the building as the former sum will cirry out has to be erected. Tenders bad been invited, but only one lo•zal _contractor .had tendered.
That of Messrs. Morrison and Co., of Wavortree, was
accepted. The chancel and transepts will be built at a later period, when the funds requisite are forthcoming.

ALLEGED DYNAMITE OUTRAGE AT DITTON.—Much ex- eitcment was caused in the neighbourhood of Ditton towards the clese of last week by a supposed attempt on the life of the Rev. A. M. de Haza-Radlitz, S.J., priest at the Jesuit Seminary, Ditton Hall. On Wednesday, a package, at first supposed to contain -explosives, was delivered to Pather de Ifiza's address during his absence at St. Helens, but it sub- sequently turned cut that it was nothing more combustible than a sample of prepared charcoal forwarded by a Liver- pool tradesman, accompanied by a circular pointing out its
advantAges awl uses. RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.—OR WedneSaly

afternoon an adjourned meeting of the Runcorn Commis- inners, was held for the purpose of passing the accounts before the close of the financial year. Dr. Steele presided, and there were present: Messrs. R. Shaw, W. Fisher, P. Briscoe, P. Speakman, J. Meadnrfcroft, J. W. Lightburn, W. Broohs (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor.) The only business transacted of public interest was the adoption

of the rnommendation of the Finance Committee, that the residue of the p,,,nny rate for library purposes be not trans- ferred to the Free Library Committee. RurrcoßN SCHEOL BOARD AT WORK.—At Runcorn Petty

CI ucne, Felix McConn, Thomas Lawton (adjourned), Adam Peacock, and Charlotte Done. Except where otherwise specified a fine of 55., including costs, was imposed. Twe ACTION AGAINST A FRIENDLY SOCIETY AT WIDNES,. —At' Widnes Petty Session. on Wednesday, Mr. Massey, who defended in the case Mrs. Urquhart v. United Kingdom In- surance Company at the last sessions, which was an action brought to recover ten guineas on a life policy, asked the Bench to fix the sum he should deposit with their clerk as security for the costs of the appeal which he had made. He had, he remarked, been in comtnunication with Mr. Spencely on the subject, and that gentleman thought £4O would be quite sufficient. —The Bench made an order for that amount to be deposited. CRUELTY TO ANIMALS BY RUNCORN BOATMEN.—At the Al trincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, James Green, boat- man, Runcorn, was charged with cruelty to a mere at Altrin- cham.—lnspector Harper stated that on the 12th March he saw the defendant in charge of a brown mare. It was an old one, simply a skeleton, and actually staggered in walking. She was in a dreadful condition, and was compelled to draw 54 tons.—Defendant said the mere was taken ill at Winsford, and they had done their best with it.—He was fined 20s and costs. or one month.--Richard Draper, also a boatman from Runcorn, was summoned for cruelty at Sale. He pleaded guilty, and as the horse had since been destroyed he was only fined 5s and costs. VESTRY MEETING AT WIDNES.—The annual meeting of ratepayers for the purpose of nominating overseers for the township of Widnem for the ensuing year, was held in the assietant-overseees-office, Victoria-road, on Thursday after- noon. Mr. John Matthews occupied the chair, and there were prebent Mbaora 17 IT Pankhurst. W. martley, J. H. Lea, Wm. Gerard, Thomas Sadler. and John Goff (assistant- overseer). On the motion of Mr. T. Sadler, seconded by Mr. F. IL Pankhurst, it was resolved to submit the follow- ing list of householders to the magistrates as fit and proper persons to serve in the office of overseers : Messrs. John W. Wareing, John Matthews, Alcuin Cowley, James Ger- rard, John Phillips, James H. Lea, W. H. Kershaw, Samuel Stringer, Samuel Owen, Frederick Neill, Thomas Shuttle- worth, junior, J. B. unison, and F. H. Pankhuret. ROBBERY OE LEAD AT WIDNES. On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, James Keating and William Garrity, men of disreputable Appearance, were charged with stealing 177 ibs. of lead from the old Chemical Works, Ditton-road, formerly occupied by Taylor, Greenall, and Kidd.—P C. Lung deposed to seeing the prisoners place the lead in a barrow and wheel it away, and Mr. Buckley stated that the lead belonged to Hutchinson's trustees and was worth 14s. —Superintendent Barker remarked that Garrity had been previously convicted 20 times, and Keating 17. The pri- soners went prowling about the town pilfering everything they could lay their hands upon, and disposing of it for drink.—Each prisoner was sentenced to two months' im- prisonment with hard labour. FURIOUS DRIVING AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, John Antrobus and Thos. Clark, young men, were summoned to answer a charge of fueionsly driv- ing in High-street, to the danger of passengers therein.— From the evidence of Superintendent William- son, P.C. Cooper, and P.O Price it 'appeared that on the night of the 9th inst. each of the defendants was in charge of two boat horses, which they were gallop- ing up High-street. They were waving the'r caps and shouting in order to excite the horses and increase their speed. A Conservative meeting was being held in the Public Hall at the time, and a great number of people being unable to gain admittance, High-street and the end of Church- street were crowded, and Supt. Williamson remarked it was a miracle that no person was hurt.—Defendants stated that the horses had got beyond their control, and they stopped them as soon as they could.—Supt. remarked that he only took the ease as a warning to other persons, and would not press the charge against the defendants.—Eaeh defendant was fined is, and costs lie ad. FAMILY DESERTION AT WIDNES.--Before Messrs. Hol- brook Gasket!, jour., and George Pilkington, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas Feeney, was charged on remand, with neglecting to maintain his wife and family, who thereby had become chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union.—Mr. H. S. Hartley, clerk to the Prescot Board of Guardians, prosecuted, and stated that up to January bet the defendant was at work in Runcorn, and earning from 355. to £2 per week. At that time he was dis- charged from his employment on account of his drunken habits, and he had since then done nothing to support his family, whom ho deserted. His wife applied for relief to Mr. Scannell, the relieving officer, to whom she stated that she dare not go to her husband win) struck her when she last visited him. No relief was then granted her, but this month she again applied. Mr. Scannell then visited the house and found the wife and children in such a state of destitution that he at once ordered their remoyal to Prescot workhouse. The wife was now in the hospital.—The prisoner was sent to gaol for a month. How THE RATEPAYERS' MONEY GOES: A RUNCORIE " RoGun."—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Patrick Baxter, a dissolute-looking Irishman, was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and children who thereby became chargeable to the common fund children, the Runcorn Union, and were at present in the workhouse.— Mr. T. Houghton, the collector, said the family had been chargeable to the Union since April, 1881, and the prisoner bad served a month's imprisonment. The family had cost the Union something like £so.—The Rev. E. A. P. Camp- bell : He is an Irishman ; where is his settlement ?—Mr. Houghton: I don't know. He has been• in Runcorn a great many years. I must ask your worships to deal severely with him.—Mr. Campbell (to prisoner) : You are a rogue and a vagabond, and you look like one. You are committed to Knutsford gaol for three months.—The pri- soner said he had taken his wife and family three times, but she would not live with him.—Mr. Campbell: We won't listen to what you have to say. We have nothing to say to you- Tu. BOATMAN AND HIS BOOTS: AMONG THIEVES AT RUNCORN.—On Monday, at Runcorn Police Court, John Walsh, A young man, was brought up under a warrant charged with having, on the 28th June last, feloniously stolen a pair of boots and 3s. 61., the property of James Sharrock, a fletman. It appeared that on the day in question Sharrock, who was in charge of a small steam beet, was in Runcorn, and during the evening visited a number of public houses in company with the prisoner and another man. Becoming "dizzy in his head, and losing the use of his legs," Sharrock was put into " Haywood's hay loft," where he fell asleep. On awakening next morning, his shoes had been replaced by a pair of dilapidated clogs, which it was proved were the prisoners, and his pockets had been turned "inside out," the money they contained having been taken. Information was given to the police, but the prisoner succeeded in slipping on board a vessel. He arrived in town about a fortnight ago, and on Friday last was apprehended by P.C. Noden. He pleaded guilty to stealing the shoes, but alleged that a man named Tenables took the money. The:prisoner was sent to gaol for a month's hard labour.
