On 'Wednesday, at Wit,nes Police Court, Patrick ' McCreece, John Queeney, and . Tobn Reynolds, boys, were charged with breaking into the lock-up shop of Peter -ern to the value of .E 1 McKinley, and stealing goods therefr, living in Travis- 13s.—Mary Dogherty, a single woman in Anne-street street, said she managed a smallware shop' fSt Helens i West, Widnes, belonging to Peter McKinley, o. • On the 19th inst. she was in the shop until na.le o'clock p.m., when she locked it up. In consequence of a .-I.llMIlr which she heard she returned to the shoo at midnight, found that the door had been unlocked. The interior wae'' in disorder. A great many articles were lying on the floor. They had been trampled upon. The articles produced were the property of her master, and were worth XI 13s. The bunch of keys produced did not belong to herself or master. -The shop door was fastened by a padlock, which one of the keys produced would unlock.—P.C. Timperley stated that on Monday night, about ten o'clock, he was on duty in Anne-street, in company with P.C. McDonald. -He ex- amined the lock-up shop of the prosecutor. He climbed aver the back yard wall, and heard a noise in the shop, which was in darkness. The back door was open, and he entered the place,, and made a search. lie found Queeney and McCreece concealed in a box under the front window, and he took them into custody. In that box he discovered ihe keys produced, 18 pairs of earrings, pair of leather garters, a thimble, one brooch, and two balls of wool ; on the counter were six elastic belts, 19 pairs of earrings, pair of braces, four cords of elastic, and 66 pairs of leather laces; all of which the prisoners were charged with stealing. They made no reply.—PC. Mc- Donald deposed that whilst Timperley was entering the shop he found Reynolds in an entry leading to the doer of the shop. Reynolds dropped a purse, and he (witness) took him into custody. He searched Reynolds' pocket, in which he found two purses and a reel of thread. In the back yard witness found two patent leather belts.—The prisoners were committed to the sessions for trial.

div.head: GOOD TEHPLARY IN RUNCORN.
div.p: GOOD TEHPLARY IN RUNCORN.

Under the auspices of the Good Templar lodges of Run- corn and Widnes, a series of lectures entitled " Sketches from every day life," have been held in Runcorn Public Hall during the past week. The lectures, as will be sur- mised had special reference to the drink question, and they received the contenance of the maj4rity of the ministers of religion in the town. On Monday evening, Mr. Robert Shaw presided, and, after prayer had been offered bl p by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, the chairman addressed the Moderately large audience which had assembled. He remarked that the subject of temperance was occupying the thoughts and minds of all sorts and conditions of men. Although Eng- land had been considered the most enlightened and the most religious nation on the bee of the earth, up to a short period ago, and perhaps still were so, its people were ad- dicted to the vice of drunkenness more than any other country. It was encouraging to those who had laboured in the cause of temperance for years to find that their doc- trines were making greater headway than they had ever done in the history of this country. He believer.' this pro- gress would continue, because if they showed the working- men that by abstaining from intoxicating liquors they would be better workmen, have happier homes, increased comforts, they wculd try and be able to change their lives. (Applause.) He concluded by expressing a wish for the success of the lectures. Herr Cohen then delivered one of his characteristic lectures. On Tuesday, evening the meet- indwas presided over by the Rev. Evan Williams, who delivered a short address in advocacy of the cause ot total abstinence. Herr Cohen delivered a lecture. In con- sequence of the Madrigal Club concert, a meeting was held at the Drill Hall, Widnes. on Wednesday evening. There was a fair attendance. Herr Cohen gave a lecture on tem- perance topica.

div.head: OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATH AT
div.p: OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATH AT
WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, William Miller, draper, Waterloo-road, Widnes, was summoned on a charge of obstructing the footpath.—P.C. Thompson stated that on Saturday, the 10th inst., about ten minutes past one o'clock, he saw several rolls of oilcloth and other goods placed on the footpath outside the defendant's shop. Besides, there was a large step ladder, and together they occupied about three feet of the footpath. A number of people were com- pelled to walk in the horse road to pass the place. Witness watched the shop half-an-hour to discover if any one used the step - ladder, but during that time he did not see anyone do so. He then told the defendant of the obstruction, when the latter stated he did not know the ladder was there, and shouted to some one to remove it. When informed that he would be reportcd, defendant said "Don't make a fool of yourself. If Tau teport rn,L0V,..13. make a-- fool of you." Defendant followed wit- ness out of the shop repeating the words, when the latter remarked that if he did not enter his shop and cease his dis- turbance he should report him for cammitting a breach of the peace.—Defendant: Did you draw my attention to any- thing besides the step-ladder? Yes, I told you of the oil- cloth.—Defendant; It's a mott emphatic lie, your worships. —By Superintendent Barker: I have cautioned the defen- dant twice previously for obstructing the footpath.—P.C. Heaton confirmed Thompson's statement, while Inspector Barnett deposed that he had several times cautioned the de- , fendant for obstructing the footpath. On one 1 occasion the defendant was reported, but on promising that he would not offend again, a summons was not issued.—Defendant : Is it not done all over the town ?—lnspector Barnett: You do it outrageously. People cannot pass your shop.—The defendant said he was sorry to be antagonistic to the police, but he did not think they had any case in this matter.—lie called Joseph Hors- field, his shop boy, who stated the ladder was outside about ten minutes. His master did not see it.— Defendant stated that the evidence of the police- men was not strictly accurate, and allerd that the case had been brought in consequence of his wife having driven Thompson away from the back door, where he was in the habit of speaking to the servants. (Laughter.)— Superintendent Barker said the defendant since he had re- ceived the summons had threatened the policeman several times. If Mr. Mills had any report to make about the con- stable, let him make it to him (the superintendent), and the matter would be properly investigated.—Mr. Gaskell said the Bench were satisfied there had been an obstruc- tion, and the defendant would be fined ss. and costs.

div.head: NATIONAL FORESTERS OF WIDNES
div.p: NATIONAL FORESTERS OF WIDNES
AND RUNCORN.

On Saturday the Irish National Foresters of Widnes and Runcorn celebrated the national festival in a manner credit- able to the occasion from a patriotic as well as a religious point of view. In the afternoon a procession was formed in the square outside the Pride of Erin club-house, Widnes, in the following order :—First, Branch Pride of Erin brass b_nd, under the leadership of Bro. M. Ryan; the Runcorn R.C. fife and drum band, led by Bro. J. Coleman, P.C.R. ; and the beautiful banner manufactured by Mr. 0. Connell, costumier, Great Britain-street, Dublin, a masterpiece of Irish art and enterprise, carried by four stalwart types of the bone and sinew of Ireland. Then followed, walking two deep, the officers and members of both branches, mar- shalled by Bro. F. Harris, P.C.R., Pride of Erin, Widnes, and Bro. E. Hill, P.O R , Wolfe Tone, Runcorn, all wearing their picturesque regalia, replete with national emblems, amongst which the shamrock, received that morning from loving hearts at home, was not the least conspicuous. The long procession paraded the principal streets of the town, the bands playing the soul-inspiriting music of the Emerald Isle. A halt was made at the residence Dr. O'Keeffe, branch surgeon, who, in a brief speech, dwelt forcibly on the neces- sity of every Irishman wbo had the interest of his country at heart, joining the Order, whose first great principle was unity, the keystone to that place amongst the nations of the earth to which Ireland aspires. At the conclusioh of bis remarks the prncessionists re-formed line, and marching by way of Victoria-road and Waterloo-road, reached the club-house, where they dispersed in the same orderly man- ner that had characterised the day's proceedings.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.
THE NOMINATIONS.

Thursday was the last day on which candidates for the Local Board could be nominated, and when the offices were closed at five o'clock, the following were the nominations: F. H. Pankburst, woollen draper, Victoria-road, Widnes; David Foister, boiler maker, Mount Pleasant, Widnes ; Dr. O'Keeffe, Brendon House, Widnes; Barnett Dutton, auc- tioneer, flelsby ; John Houghton, agent, Albert-road, Apple- ton, Widnes; and W. J. Hargreaves, watchmaker and publican, Kent-street, Widnes. The first five are virtually the nominees of the Owners' and Occcupiers', and the Rate- payers' Associations, and will be supported by them, while Mr. Hargreaves is nominated by James Tilley, of Lugsdale- road, and may be described as an "independent candidate." It will be seen that, unless a candidate withdraws, a contest is inevitable, because although there are only five vacancies there are six candidates for them. The opinion has been freely expressed that the candidates receiving the support of the associations will most decidedly win, and that it would be unwise of any person to enter into a conflict with them. Mr. Pankhurst, Mr. Forster, and Dr. O'Keeffe are not new to the office they seek. All three gentlemen have renderei valuable assistance on the Board during the past three years; and would be warmly welcomed back by their collealues. Mr. Dutton and Mr. Houghton, are gentlemen of business capacity, whose presence mty be expected to have some influence on the deliberations of the Board, and, we think, are likely to meet with a large share of popular support. Seeing that there is no real organiscd opposition to these gentlemen, we think it would be a great pity to put the township to the expenses of a contest, and although Mr. Hargreaves may be a most estimable ,man, there cannot be a doubt that he would be consulting the feelings of the rate- payers if he withdrew from the contest. Should the elec- tion be necessary, the voting papers will be distributed on April 2nd, collected on April 6th, and counted on Saturday, April Ttli.

div.head: ST. PATRICK'S DAY AT WIDNES.
div.p: ST. PATRICK'S DAY AT WIDNES.

IThe anniversary Of Ireland's patron aat—Fatrick—WAS celebrated by the Irishmen of Widnes on SattZdaY last with : more than the usual display. Irishmen with tht.:ir families form a very large proportion of the population of the "chemical centre," and almost eery third person one in the street was adorned with a piece of blue ribbon, or sported a root of the glorious Shamrock. In the afternoon a procession was formed, and the anniversary occurring on the Saturday, when a great number of workmen are at liberty, gave hundreds an opportunity of taking part in the celebration, who would not otherwise have had that honour. The procession, which was of considerable length, 4t, was headed by the Catholic brass band of St. Maly's voung Mons' Society, the Irish National Foresters brass bsans. and the Runcorn fife and drum band. These were followe,l by the Irish National Foresters of Widnes and Runcorn' who wore their picturesque regalia, the rear being formed by i",-ishme.73 of all grades wishful to pay a tribute to the memory of St. Patrick. The weather though cold was bright and sOnny, and largo crowds lined the streets. It is pleasing to observe that there was an .absence of street ,flistr.rWnces, and a decrease in the drunkenness. Perhapg the plenary indulgence issued by the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Westminster— Cardinal Manning—to those persome who abstained from in- toxicating liquors on that day will to some extent explain the latter fact, which is nevertheless very commendable, and speaks well for the Irish Catholics of Widnes. On Satur- day evening the St. Patrick's Amateurs performed the drama, "Robert Emmett," in the Volunteer Hall, to a crowded audience. The stage accessories to the piece were admirable, and we must compliment Mr. S. Quinn, who acted as stage manager, for the taste and ingenuity he had displayed. Mr. Quinn also showed much ability as an actor in the role of the Irish patriot, Robert Emmett; while Mr. J. Gordon's Impersonation of Emmett's friend, Dowdall, was all that could be desired. As a traitor Kernan, Mr. J. Bird, was a great success; and the humorous character of Darby O'Gulf, "a sprig of the emerald isle," bad an able expo- nent in the person of Mr. T. Stoner. O'Leary, an old sol- dier, was played by T. Mulvaney; Sergeant Topfall, J. Quinn; Corporal Thomas, J. Tanen ; Lord Norbury and Baron Daly, judges, J. Carroll and M. Whelan; Connor, jailer, H. Gorman; Maria, Emmet's wife, Miss E. Reilly ; Judy O'Dougherty, Miss E. Farrell. We feel constrained to pay a tribute of praise to the ladies for the excellent manner in which they pourtrayed the characters they represented. Miss E. Reilly, as the patriot's wife, acted with dignity and pathos, whilst Miss Farrell made a capital "Judy O'Dougherty." During the interval the duet, "The faithful hearts of Ireland," was sung by Miss Hewitt and Miss Jameeon with unimpeachable taste, and their performance was loudly applauded. Then followed
;he farce "The Irish Doctor,' which was provoca-

tive of much merriment. The casto was as follows : Sir Ralph Credulous. J. Carroll; Walter tovewell, J. Bird; Dennis Murphy and Dr. Murphy, T. Mulvaney; Squire Robert, J. Gcrdon : Simon, J. Nolan; Doctor Frantic, J. Gordon; Laura Credulous, Miss M. Muldoon; Peggy, Miss M. Edwards ; Bridget (wife of Denis Murphy), Mr. T. Stoner. During the evening the new brass band played the following: March, " Dreams of other days," valse, Brien Borhoime's March, fantasia. The performance was repeated on Monday evening, when the Volunteer Hall was again well filled with an appreciative audience.

div.head: RUNCORN MADRIGAL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN MADRIGAL CLUB.
PERFORMANCE OF "JUDAS MACCABiEUS."

The members of Runcorn Madrigal Club gave their last concert of the season on Wednesday evening, when Handel's oratorio "Judas Maccibazus" was performed. During the winter the performances of the club have not met with that recognition from the public which they eminently deserved, and the members determined on this occasion to spare no effort to score a success in every way. The well-trained voices of their own chorus were augmented by the members of Widnes Choral Society and Frodsham Musical Society, forming together a highly efficient choir of about 250 voices. The principals were all artistes of acknowledged ability, being Madame Bellini Porter, Miss Annie Richardson, Mr. H. T. Bywater, and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint. But notwithstanding these attractions, the audience which assembled was of very moderate proportions. The subscribers seats were pretty well filled, and also the side galleries; but the other portions of the room were disappointingly bare. To succeed in attract- ing the "popular ear" the club must, it would seem, select some less magnificent and less ambitious theme than that which they rendered in so excellent and finished a manner on Wednesday evening. It is doubtful, however, whether the sole aim of the club ought to be to cater for the public. If its 'subscriptions are sufficient even to allow it to exist, and merely pay its way, we should be sorry to see its musical repertoire void of the oratorios of the great masters, and their places titled by more popular but less elevating strains in order to raise a surplus. Of the performance of the oratorio we have to speak in terms of unqualified praise. The descriptive choruses, so distinctive of the work, were rendered with an intelligence ciety, and reflected the greatest credit on both the members of the chorus and their and their painstaking conductor. Madame Bellini Porter (soprano), Miss Annie !Richardson (contralto), Mr: H. T. Bywater (tenor), and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint (bass),were ex- cellent principals, and rendered the whole of the numbers allotted to them with taste and judgment, Madame Porter being- especially suctesstul in the beautiful airs 'Pious or- gies," and 'From mighty kings." Several of the solos alloted to Miss A. Richardson being written for tenor or mezzo- soprano were very exacting to a contralto; but they were taieen with spirit and precision, and her rendering of "Father of heaven" was a rich musical treat. Mr. By- water's (the blind tenor) masterly interpretation was a marvellous exaeiple of musical memoty, and proves how an apparently insuperable barrier can be made to give way to iudoeiitable perseverance and true genius; not a word or note being displaced, nor the time and expression at fault; his rendering of "How evain is man" and "Sound an alarm" leaving nothing to be desired. Mr. Bantock Pierpoint was in excellent form, his deep, full, and sonorous bass telling with splendid declamatory power in the inertial air " Arm, arm ye brave," and the fugal "The Lord worketh wonders.'t The band added greatly to the success of the performance, and though composed of both local and professional talent seemed thoroughly at one in the manipulation of their in- struments. The audience, which included many local musicians and sing,ers, was roused to a high pitch of enthusiasm, and though discriminating, was frequently demonstrative in its expressions of applause. Mr. W. J. Argent has every reason to be proud of his chorus which reflected the greatest credit on himself as the conductor of the three societies. We hoe he may be as successful musically in the forthcoming concert of the Widnes Choral Society, on which occasion we have incidentally beard assistance will be given by members of the Runcorn and Frodsham societies. We trust the Widnesians will avail themselves in great numbers (judging from the performance of Wednes- day evening last) of the rich treat in store for them.
ELECTION OF RUNCORN GUARDIANS.

The interest which is being taken in this election on the present occasion contrasts strongly with the apathy shown in it by the ratepayers tvg.4 ve months ago. Then only two Guardians were nominated and elected, aud for four months, until the Local Government Board issued a special order, Runcorn was most inadequately represented at Dutton Work- house. It would seem that this time, however, the Clerk was to be besieged with nominations. At the annual town- ship meeting on Thursday evening, five gentlemen were chosen for nomination, while previously, it was stated, a ratepayer had nominated a like number. A contest is, therefore, inevitable, and as a considerable time has elapsed since one took place, it will have, perhaps, a beneficial effect. Runcorn is at present represented by Messrs. W. Handley, W. Whitaker, W. Fisher, T. Norman, and G. S. Hazlehurst. Mr. Hazlehurst has, we understand, expressed his unwillingness to serve again, but the Miter retiring members will accept office if elected. Nominftions can be sent in until the 27th inst., and the voting papers will be counted on the 11th proximo. In consequence of the alteration made by the Local Govern- ment Board, Weston is now entitled to two representatives. The Rev. Canon Barclay, who is chairman of the Board, and has held the seat for a great number of years, will no doubt, be re-elected, but a contest may take place for the extra seat. Mr. James Handley has been nominated.

An interview which took place on Thursday* te. ween a Chester correspondent and the-Rector of Hawaraen, ts. nds to confirm a rumour which will be received, if m 503. with universal surprise, certainly with widespread regret. Hsi 11/' ing to a question as to whether there was any truth ink the rumour that the Premier might ere long retire from oats ial public life, the Rev. Stephen Gladstone said, "The rum,' 1r is quite in accordance with al idea he has entertained fort considerable time. He is of opinion that the old- shonia make way for the young. lie has long felt a wish to•retiree, and it may be th,tt he now sees his way to retirement memo clearly." Referring to the oft-repeated statement that Mr.-4 Gladstone would probably accept a peerage, the Rector of Hawarden said, " That is all speculation. I cannot speak with any certainty or authority on the matter, but my opinion is that he will never take a scat in the 1-1011.2 e of Lords, having done all his work elsewhere!' MR. BRIGITP AT GLASGOW.

On Thursday Mr. John Bright was installed as Lord Rector of the University of Glasgow. St. Andrew's Hall,. where the ceremony took place, was crowded with a dis- tinguished company, including many peers and members of Parliament. Principal Caird presided. Areonget- the gentlemen presented for the honorary degree for LL.D. were Professor Adamson and Mr. H. Duneklev; of Man- chester; the Rev. W. N. Molesworth, of Rochdale ;- and the Rev. R. W. Dale, of Birmingham. The students re- ceived their Lord Rector with great enthusiasm. The right hon. gentleman, in his address, said he asked him- self what it was that had brought him there in range of their sympathy and favour. It must be, he thought,. be- cause of some sympathy with his political labours. He- had taken some part in politics, and had perhaps been of service in the administration of the Government of the- country. There could be nothing better, nothing greater, to interest students than to direct their earnest attention, to some of those great questions in the political field that immediately concerned them, and those with whom they were connected. The students of to-day would become the nation of to-morrow, and therefore, if there was any question on which great interest was felt, and on which the future of the nation depended, there could be nothing better than for the student to keep his eyes fixed upon it. History told us that amongst Christian nations changes were going on, and even peaceful revolutions had a great bearing on human events fer all future time. As several points of departure of those changes; he indicated the Declaration of Americad Independence, the Fiench Revolution, and the Reform Bill of 1832. These, con- tinued, Mr. Bright, removed the destiny of nationa from monarchs and statesmen to the people. With those changes new rights were gained, new Dowers were possessed, and new duties imposed. Referring incidentally to the condition of Ireland, the Lord Rector observed that if the Treaty of Limerick had been fulfilled, if there had been freedo:n to the religion of the people, and if, added to that, the Government of Ring William had known how to make the land more free, the people in the two centuries- that lied elapsed would have become more civilised, peace would have been assured, and the kingdom would have been united and tranquil. Speaking of the Crimean War, he asserted that the rivalry of Ministers at home and the passionete vindictiveness of Ministers abroad were the direct and immediate cause of that war. Yet Russia had not been weakened, and Turkey had not been rendered more secure, while the armies of Europe had been •o,lllri hontlont Ilmrsair tha harmony and brotherhood that existed between the Austra- lian colonies and the mother country, and pointed out that the great problem of the future was India. In the evening Mr. Bright was presented with an address by the Executive of the Glasgow Liberal Association, and in 'reply- delivered a speech upon political topics. The right hon. gentleman renewed his attack on the minority clause of the Disraeli Reform Act, and called upon all Liberals to agitate against its retention.

THE LANCASHIRE ENGINEERING AND IRON TRADES. The most important feature to notice as affecting the engineering trades of the Manchester district is the con- tinued, and if anything increasing activity in iron ship- building, which has contributed so largely towards giving full employment to the machine tool making trades of Lan- cashire. Extensions and the laying out of new shipbuilding yards are being carried out in the important centres of this branch of trade, and the local makers of special tools for marine engine work are kept well supplied with orders. Some of the local firms are also very busy on the construc- tion of exceptionally heavy engines both for works in Eng- land and abroad; the activity in locomotive building is fully maintained, and there are large orders in hand both for home railways and for the Continent, India, and the colonies. Owing to the holidays the usual Friday's iron market was held on Thursday, but the attendance was extremely small, and there was practically no business doing. Prices nominally were unchanged, and for pig iron delivered equal to Manchester remain about as under : Lancashire, 47s 6d to 48s; Lincolnshire, 45s 6d to 475; and Derby- shire, 48s to 50s, less 21, for forge and foundry qualities respectively. In the present condition of trade there is, however, nothing to really test the market. On the one hand makers are so well sold, and on the other consumers are so well covered, that there is neither any pressure to sell nor anxiety to buy, and as there lc nothing to indicate a proba- bility of any early material alteration in values it is not unlikely that in the absence of any inducement to come into the market buyers and sellers will for the present be content to work on with existing contracts. The finished iron trade generally continues in a depreseed condition, and except that a moderate business is reported in hoops the orders going out are very small. North Staffordshire makers are- in some cases asking more money, but for prompt orders local makers are still taking £6 5s for bars and £6 15s for hoops delivered into the Manchester district, and anything above those figures is difficult to realise. A few sales of hematite are reported, but comparatively low prices are taken, good foundry qualities being offered at 62s ed per ton,_ less 2 delivered isto this district.

THE RENEWED, OUTBREAK IN SKYE. Telegrams from Portree state that excitement is spread- ing throughout the island, and that tha lawless action of the Glendale crofters in again driving the landlords' sleek off the Wateretein grazings is causing much indignation and anxiety. The AS'eotsman calla upon the authorities to take immediate action, and says that the speedy( and deter- mined enforcement of the law is the truest mercy to the Skyemen. A correspondent at Portres telegraphs that a large meeting of crofters has been held at Glendale, but details are not to hand. It is stated that the shepherds be- longing to the proprietors were ordered to remove the crofters' stock from the hill, but were prevented so doing, Dissatisfaction is expressed at the constitution of the Royal commission, on the ground that all the commissioners are proprietors. One speaker said the troubles were only beginning.

CRUELTY TO A. HORSE AT ST. HELENS. - At the St. 1 Helens Police Court, on Friday, a carter named William Finn was chirzed with having cruelly treated his horse.— P.C. Bremner said that on the afternoon 'of the 9th inst. he was on duty in t.iandfield-crescent, near to the defendant's house. He heard a sound as if some one were striking a horse, and he went to the back of defendant's house, and there saw him beat his horse several times on•the head with the stick produced, besides hitting it on the body and legs. In consequence of this severe thrashing the horse i kept beat- ing its head up against a wall.—Defendant said t was his own horse, and it had knocked him down. It was ayoung one, and had to be checked, or it would do an injury to ,•ither him or somebody else. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed.

div.head: "NO. 1."
div.p: "Number One," we learn from a New York correspon- dent, has been traced to the United States, and the necessary papers sent out with a view to an application being nude for his extradition. There is, however, some doubt, after the proceedings in Sheridan's case, as to whether the ap- plication for the extradition of "Number One" well be per- sisted in. His identity seems to be no doubtful matter to the authorities, his portrait having been sent out with the papers, and it is said that he reached America by way of France.

MR. PARNELL AND M. HENRI ROCHEFORT. WAR WITH ENGLAND ADVOCATED. M. Henri Rochefort, one of the French newspaper editors whom Mr. Parnell came to Paris to see, has written a violent article against England. He says :—" Wherever. France goes she finds England in the way. Why not, then, have done with her once for all? The French Government ought to foment rebellion both in Ireland and in India. The latter only awaits a signal to hurl one hundred millions of men ' against the common foe. France wouldthus neighbour of the most insupportable and most troublesome that the bazerds of geography AeTvewr placed EsraEsra Nt hers T Eit. doors." THE EXPLOSION The Press Association is informed that the supposed cluA to the perpetrators of the Westminster explosion is only one of the many that have been received at Scotland Yard., and that it is no more reliable than those which have preceded it. The statement is that a young person engaged as a. forewoman in a paper manufactory was, on Thursday even- ing week, proceeding along Charles-street, when she ob- served a man stooping down near the stone balustrade out- side the Local Government Board Offices, She noticed him particularly, owing to his eccentric posture, and states that she could recognise him again. The, young woman in question has been closely cross-e,xamised, and although she may have seen a man in the neighbourhood of the scene of the explosion, there is nothing 1* klex itatement which is likely to assist the -authorities,

THE RARE IN FOLK LORE.

Sir, In the current number of the Folk-lore Jour= there is an interesting article on "The Hare in Folk-lore," contributed by Mr. William George Black, F.S.A., Scot. In addition to recording many of the particulars in connec- tion with the "timid animal" alluded to in my previous letters,Mr. Black has gathered together many more various eau from out-of-the-way sources. In the hope that they may interest some of your readers, I send a summary of the article. Mr. Biack starts with the admission that the hare b regarded as an " uncanny " animal. He then goes on to record how Sir Thomas Browne tells us that in his time there were few above threescore years that were not per- plexed when a hare crossed their path. Aubrey notes the .same prejudice. Napier says many a person meeting a hare while going to work would return home and not again venture out until the next meal had been eaten, "for beyond that the evil influence did not extend." From India we learn that it is as unlucky to meet a hare as it is to meet a one-eyed man, an empty water-pot, a carrier without a load, a fox, a jackal, a crow, a widow [the poor widow, again !], or a funeral. Dalyell couples the bare with the weasel as ominous. At the Wheal Vor mine it is linked in similar ill- fame with the white rabbit; the appearance of either in one of the engine-houses is believed to presage a fatal accident in the mine. When Falstaff complains that he is as melan- choly as a gib-cat, or a lugged bear, Prince Henry replies, "What sayest thou to a hare, or the melancholy of Moor- itch?" Dyce cites from Turberville (through Staunton), "The hare first taught us the use of the hearbe called Wyld Succory, which is very excellent for those who are disposed to be melancholicke: shee herselfe is one of the most melanchoticke beasts that is, and to heals her own in- fermitie she goeth commonly to sit under that hearbe." Mr. slack says Dr. White Kennett supplies us with the follow- ing excellent reason for the melancholy of some intelligent hares culminating in suicide :—" Memorand Jt is found by experience that when one keepes a hare alive, and feedeth him till he have occasion to eat him, if he telles before he killes him that he will do so, the hare will thereupon be found dead, having killed himself." Again, he says that Cogan tells us that*" bare-flesh beside that it is bard of di- gestion, maketh grosse and melancholy bloud, and is one of the foure kindes of flesh that breed melancholy. Wherefore it is not for the goodness of the fl-sh that this silly beast is so often chased with hounds and hunters, but for pastime. Yet thus much will 1 say to the commendation of the hare, and of the defence of hunters' toyle, that no one beast, be it never so great, is profitable to so many and to so diverse uses in physicke as the bare and parts thereof, as Matth. sheweth . . . The ankle-bone of the foote of an hare is good against the cramp." The bare appears to be like the cat,an ally of the witch. Fishers of Fifeshire "look on all mankens (hares) to be devils and witches, and if they but see a sight of a dead mauken it sets them a trembling.; Mr. Gregor notes tbat to say to a fisherwoman of the north-east of Scotland that there is a hare's foot in her creel, or to say to a fisherman that there is a bare in his boat, arouses great ire, and calls forth strong words ; the word " hare" is not pronounced at sea. In Cornwall a maiden who has been deceived and dies, haunts her deceiver in the guise of a white hare, sometimes saving his life, but in the end causing his death. So, too, in South Northamptonshire the running a a bare along the street of a village portends fire to some house in the immediate neighbourhood. In the Isle of Man they say women are turned into hares, and can only be shot with a silver sixpence. When a witch is in the shape of a hare, the Scotch continue, she can only be hit by a crooked sixpence. The spot which discovered witches to the world sometimes resembled a hare's foot in the ex- perience of continental experts, but it must be borne in taut& c'est l'image d'un lie vre, tantot uno patte de crapaud, tantet one orraignee, on petit chien on loir." The hare is the good genius of the Calmuck. One family of the Moguls believed that they were descended from a hare, and that after death their spirits entered into hares again. They ac- cordingly wershipped the hare. The hare wns regarded with superstitions reverence by the Indians of the North; the rabbit was the sign "of the divine years in the Mexi- can calendar. In China the people of Yo-yang would not hunt the bare because it was A telluric genius. " Albino bares," says Dr. Dennys, "are regarded as omens of good, and their appearance is a mark of heavenly ap- proval." Children in Swabia may not make shadows on the wall to represent the sacred Moon Hare. It did not at once acquire the repute of being either stupid or inspired by a witch. A blind hare it was, in the North German tale of "The Blue Ribband," which ran before the

princess, and by plunging in a brook, diving thrice under water, recovered its sight and scampered off, thus teaching her to lead Hans to the same water, with the satisfactory result that after he had plunged in it three times, he, like the hare, recovered his sight. The Chinese refuse to eat the flesh of the hare. We read in Notes and Queries that a Dorsetshire mother in the autumn of 1881 was somewhat troubled with the care of recently-born twins. On paying a visit to inquire after the .mother, Mr, Black's wife was _ . .

consulted as to the desirability of a dose of hare's brains (as a soporific). Mentioning the circumstance to his keeper in the hope of eliciting some information as to the preva- lence of the belief, the latter said that about a fortnight ago the wife of the keeper of the adjoining manor, who bad been recently confined, called at his house and told his wife that she had been down to the squire's house to beg a hare's bead from the cook in order to give the brains to her baby as a sedative. The hare also appears to be occasionally employed as an Easter emblem in Germany. In tbe same number of the journal quoted from there is an allusion to the refrain of a street song used in the following modified form by the children ,in Northamptonshire, Oxfordshire, and North Bucks :
"Some say the devil's dead And buried in Cold Harbour; Others say be's rose again And 'l3 enticed to a barber.

There may be Newtonians alive who, recollecting how jbey were woke up so uncere noniously early one fine Sun- day morning in 1831, will fervently hope and pray that Auld Clootie, when he has sorved his time, will still remain with the barber, and refrain from concocting. in conjunction with mischievous Caxtonians and pugnacious dogs, fcberces for disturbing in the future the quiet of the early Sabbath morning. The after-consequences of that tea-fight were ludicrous enough; and bearing in mind the axiom " Love me, love my dog," heaven only knows what might result from a de.scent. into the main street of Newton of some of its.a,lder int:tintants clad initheir night-dresses, and armed Trvirn broom-sticks or fire-irOns. A certain namesake of we Willie Winkie, resident not a hundred miles from the stocks (or it may be where the stocks used to be), will confirm my assertion that modern disciples of Oliver Ledain can bring about as much mischief by the turn of a gas tap, the inser- tion of an extra spoonful of tea in a teapot, or the unequal diTision of half a pound of beefsteak between a couple of hungry dogs, as was ever produced by the most clever manipulations and contrivances of the celebrated barber that was executed in 1484.-1 am, sir, kc., Newington, London, March 2. ANGLO-SCOTUS.

A COSTLY SNova3m..—Wm. Devouport was summoned by Wm. Haydon, beerhouse keeper. Hollins Green, for doing dam- age to one of his windows to the amount of 4s,—The com- plainant stated that defendant came to his house in company with another man, on the 17th inst., and after staving a short time they went out and commenced to throw snowballs at the window. The defendant threw one, which broke a pane, doing damage to the amount stated.—Lucy Rosebud, niece to the last witness, gave corroborative evidence.—The defendant, who denied the charge, called Wm. Rycroft, who said that be and several other men threw snowballs at each other after coming out of the complainant's house, but that defendant did not take part in the throwing.—Lucy Rosebud was re-called, and said that she positively saw the defendant throw the snow- ball, which broke the window. There were a number of men a short distance away- The defendant was not throwing at them, but at the window.—The defendant was ordered to pay Is and costs, and damages.

The CLERK read the following which appeared in the Master's journal :—" March 9. The return prepared by the Clerk and put before the Board at their last meeting is in- correct, and not a proper statement of the facts of the case, or even in accordance with the information he obtained. If the Guardians will permit me, I will clearly show where the Clerk is wrong in reference to this and other unions named. I would respectfully ask for an inspection of the former minutes regarding the maintenance of my children, and for a committee to examine into and report upon the matter, after the full details are submitted, so that our case may be fairly decided."—" March 20. There was a state. ment made by Mr. Sutton and Mr. Mines, at the Board meeting, on the 7th ult., and reported in the local papers on the 10th February, which in the interest of truth and justice I should like any opportunity of correcting."—Mr. LONG- mew said it appeared that whatever the Board did was wrong, and that the Master was right, and called them to account. He thought the Master ought to have a seat on the Board [Mr. BURN: So be ought to have.] and correct them as they went on; or else he ought to be the chairman, because there was nothing they could do right at the Board. Since he had been a member, whatever they had done or said was not correct. If the Master was the sole ruler of the Guar- dians they might as well stay at home, and leave every- thing to him, What was the use of the members spending their time in arranging matters if everything was to be up- set, and the Board called to account 2—Mr. Bum said he was not present at the last meeting, but he thought Mr. Longshaw was quite wrong. If the Master or any other officer thought himself unfairly dealt with it Ras his duty to make a report, and he thought the officer should have a proper opportunity of explaining matters.—The CHAIRMAN: He has no right to make long statements 2—The CLERK: He has no right at all. He has been told if he wants to make a representation he sheald make it in person at an interview with the Board or put it on paper. This book is intended for entirely different purposes to these comments; but if you move in any direction that does not suit the Master's feelings you are subjected to abuse in this manner.—Major CARTwRIGHT rose to a point of order. He thought it was not within the Clerk's province to make a speech or say anything until the members of the Beard had had their say.—The CLERK: , The Chairman asked me a question.—Major CARTWRIGHT : But I don't like your procedure at all.—The CLHRK : And I don't like yours.—Major CARTWRIOHT : Why? Because you are evidently very bitter againet this poor unfortunate Master on this point, when you and others will not even allow him to express himself at this Board, but deal with him in his absence. In regard to what Mr. Longshaw has said about his being the master of this Board, I venture to say he has never offered to dictate to this Board in any shape or way whatever. All he has asked is for an interview with the Board as to the reason why he has been dealt with. He has charged the clerk in reference to those returns, and the clerk was obliged to ad- mit to a certain extent this day fortnight that there were mistakes, and I say this, that the decision of the Board a fortnight ago was based upon those returns. Then, sir, if it was based upon those returns, and if those returns are not correct, I say at all events the man who is most interested ought to have an opportunity of explaining before the Board. rn me Course ot rurcuea ieieataehe, akcd; why did not the clerk report the master 2.—The CLERK: If you say that is the case, I will do that at once.—Major CIIRTWRIGHT : Re- port the whole of the transactions.—The CLERK: Well, now don't you find fault afterwards.—Major CarerevutGerr : Oh, I don't care about your charging me with finding fault. ' Don't hold out threats to me. I have heard enough The CLERK here rose to speak.—Major CARTWRIGHT: I am on my feet. You take upon yourself to get up immedi- ately—l efore you give anyone else an opportunity to say a single word. You have no right to do so as clerk. You won't find it the practise in any other union in the kingdom for a man to get up and dictate be- fore the members of the Boarl—The Clerk and the Major here spoke at the same time, and the latter urged the clerk to "act honourably and honestly."—Mr. DARBYSHIRB (warmly) : He does so; there is no doubt about it, and you cannot say he does not. It is abominable to go on in this way. He does act straightforwardly and honestly, and don't ask a question of that character. We don't believe you.—The CRaeramaie : Major Cartwright, I must call you to order. If you caluminate the members of this Board I must put a stop to it.—Major CalerwarGerr : What do you wish me to do ?—The Crummier: I wish you to confine yourself to the point, and don't brow-beat the clerk.—Major CARTWRIGHT : I ant not brow-beating the clerk.—The CHAIRMAN: Yes you are.—The CLERK: Between the Master and this man it is impossible for me to do my duty.—Major CARTWRIGHT : I cannot stay here and hear remarks made by the clerk against another officer. The CLERK asked what remarks did he make? All he said was that if the Master wished to make complaints he should make them in a separate report or have an interview.—Mr. DARBYSHIRH (warmly): That is correct. The master is wrong in making reports in that book. He has no right to do it.—Majer CARTWRIGHT (calmly) : Don't get alarmed! Mr. Danny- SHIRE: I am not alarmed.—Major CARTWRIGHT: Act gentle- manly, and don't be coarse.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE: If there is any coarseness it is on your side !—Major CARTWRIGHT : What I have said, and what I say still, is that you have a very strong feeling against the Master.—The CLERK: Where have I? Will you tell me where I am wrong ? Major CARTWRIGHT : You made a wrong statement.—The CLERK: Tell me where ?—Major CARTWRIGHT : I pointed it out— in the number of our own inmates. I ask you this question: Will you allow your officer an audience with this Board to explain himself in the matter? The CLERK: I was going to ask. Major CARTWRIGHT : Why did not you do so ? The CLERK : Because you would not allow me to speak.—At this point the Master entered the room.—The CLERK remarked that , the master might have sent him word he had made the en- try—it was written more than a week ago—and he could have had the report there, and they eould have seen what gaiea it wa! he complained Of.—'l Ctaithit that the, eiaestion °.f e maintenance of the master's children had ban decided, and he did not see why it should come up again that day.—The CLERK, at the request of Mr. Burn,' P..gain read the entries in the journal, after which—Mr. BROWN moved that the master's request be granted, so that if there was anything wrong it could be pat right.—Mr. BONNELL seconded the motion.—The Masmg then pointed out that the Master of the Bury Union had 6 children, whereas the clerk had only entered 4 in his return. There was also an error respecting Prestwich Union.—The CLERK said the return was compiled from information supplied to him by the clerks of the various unions in Lancashire and Cheshire, and he admitted at the last meeting he had made a mistake, which was a very alight one, respecting Prest- wich. He complained that after the last meeting the Mister stated that he (the clerk) prostituted his office, and that Mr. Bleck:y was a public shipwrecker.—Mr DARBYSIIIRE: That's abominable. The MASTER: I respeat it. —The CLERK: He repeats it; and that is the kind of language he makes use of when he comes in- to the room. And he addressed the chairman in abusive language.—The CHAIRMAN said these mistakes would not have altered the decision of the Board.—The CLERK said he had given written evidence, and be asked the master for his —Major CARTWRIGHT: That is all very well, if he tells you there are six children you prove to the contrary.—The CLERK: How can I prove a negative to a statement of that kind I.—Mr. LONGSHAW: It is impossible. —The CLERK: I will undertake to find out what the Bury master has said before he is a month older.—Major CART- WRIGHT: You will be able to do that, will you? You have said that before.—The CLERK: I have sufficient in- fluence to do that.—The MASTER: I will say some very unpleasant things indeed if you don't— ' very unpleasant things indeed —The CLERK: I ask you to prove that part.—The CHAIRMAN: A fortnight ago you decided upon a certain course in regard to Mr. Mackey's children. Are you going to pass a resolution to rescind that—[Mr. LONGSHAW (emphatically): No ]—or are you going to play ducks and drakes with it ?—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE: The Clerk, I presume, put in that printed form information he got from the unions he applied to. If it can be proved be has not done so, then Mr. Mackey's state- ment should be correct; but so long as he has put down particulars he has received Mr. Mackey's statement is in- correct. Mr. Chairman and gentleman. it seems to me the time has arrived when we must make a decided change. I cannot sit here and allow business to go on as it has been going on this morning, principally through Mr. Mackey writing in a book in which he has no right to write the remarks that he has done. Therefore, I beg to

.40V6 that we ask Mr. Mackey to send in his resignation as Master of this House, and let us have another whom we can work more amicably with. The time has come, I think, when, in justice to the ratepayers and for the credit of the whole Board, we should have a change.—Mr. LONGSHAW : I have great pleaeure ifllaeond- ing that proposition. Ido think; with MY colleague, it is quite time we had a change in thie House, for either Mr. Mackey must rule this Board or we must let him write. I think it is quite time we put an end to this squebbling. Major Cartwright Seems to be his advocate in this room, and as nothing can be done without Major Cartwright, who seems to me to be exactly in the hands of the master, I think it time we pert an end to this kind of business; or we had better stay at home and leave things to Major Cart- wright and the master himself, for I am quite sure we can- not go on as we are.—Mr. BURN: This is a motion that can- not be entertained without proper notice ; but supposing it could be entertained is it wise—[Mr. LONGSILAW : Yes]— within the last meeting of the Board to attempt to carry such a resolution ?—The CLERK: I hope Mr. Derbyshire will withdraw it. There is a proper course to take in connection with this matter. I produced the returns themselves for the inspection of the Board as well as for the master.—Major CARTWRIGHT rose to speak, but the CHAIRMAN objected.— Major CARTWRIGHT: I have a right to speak, because I have been attacked.—The CHAIRMAN: You are not going to speak a dozen times this morning on one subject. You have already occupied the time of the Board Major CART- WEIGHT: If you don't understand The CHAIRMAN: I understand very well.—Major CARTWRIGHT: I insist upon my rights.—The CHAIRMAN: I only caution you. You are not going to speak half a dozen times each day upon every 1 subject.—Major CARTWRIGHT: No, I don't.—The CHAIR- MAN: You ..oceupy more of the time of the Board than any other member, and the moment the businese is over, and we come to the relief cases, you go and leaC:e other people to attend to them.—Major CART- WRIGHT said when he had a right to speak be would speak. He had been attacked without cause, but he said he was neither in the bands of Mr. Mackey nor anyone else. He was an independent member, and so long as he was such he cared for no one. He maintained that an attack of that sort ought not to be allowed by the Chairman. In regard to Mr. Derbyshire's motion, he said he liked the manliness with which it had been proposed ared seconded, but it was manliness of a description that showed:there was sometieing sub rosa. He pointed out that the Board were dealing with a man against whom the Local Government Board had not a single black mark, and said he was not surprised that the clerk should advise the gentleman, who in the heat of passion moved the resolution, to withdraw it.—The CLERK said he wrote the master a courteous letter telling him that such entries as were in the book should be made in separate reports.—The CHAIRMAN thought the time had arrived when the Board should take some action, as their time was frittered away meeting after meeting by die- agreeable discussions like the present. Chere was a serious charge now made by one official against another, and he thought they really ought to ask for a Local Government Board enquiry. They should pass a resolution asking the Local Government Board to clear away all these charges and see if they could not have some better mode of doing business. They were becoming notorious thrghout the world by these constant squabbles, which reflected upon the ratepayers and the members of the Board.—Major CART- WRIGHT: What a splendid lecture! I beg to move that the master be requested to make his statement with regard to these charges in writing, and submit it to the Board this day fortnight.—Tbe CHAIRMAN: We have got his statement in writing.—Mr. DARBTSIIIRI: He has made a statement in writing, and he has not substantiated ary of the charges yet. The clerk was right on every count, and I think Mr. Mackey ought to apologise for the statements he has made.—Mr. HUNT seconded the motion.—The CLERK : If you will order these entries to be scored through I will be satisfied.—The CHAIRMAN : Is that your opinion ?—Cries of yes.—Major CARTWRIGHT : It is not the opinion of the Board.—The CHAIRMAN: Strike them out, and I hope Mr. Mackey will never use that book for such a purpose agaiß.—Major CARTWRIGHT: Am I to understand there has been an apology given to the clerk, and that there are instructions to strike out the entries ? The CHAIRMAN: There is an apology given to the clerk. —Mr. BURN: By whom ?—Major CARTWRIGHT: I have heard no apology ; neither am I going to ad- vise him in the matter.—The CHAIR-31AX : I put it to the meeting.—The motion that the master apologise to the clerk was then put, and 15 members voted for it.—The CHAIRMAN: Now are you satisfied ?—Mr. DARBYSHIRE The centrary ?—Against the motion there voted 3—Messrs. Cartwright, Bonnell, and Burn. Major CARTWRIGHT: I question whether you have any power to cross the entries out.—The CLERK: I put on record that it was 15 against 3. —Major CARTWRIGHT: I protest against them being crossed out. The Curiae : In regard to the apology you have directed, I will not ask for it.—Major Cederwmearr: Because you are not deserving of it.— Mr. BURN contended that they had no right to alter the entries, because it was the proper book the Master had to make complaints in to come before the Board.—Mr. GREENING thought if they had an inquiry it would be more satisfactory. He thought it was the proper course to take or they would never get to the end of the matter. Mr. Mackey had certainly made charges which had not been substantiated. It was time this matter was put an end to, for he was sick and weary of it.—Major CearrwracenT : So are others—Mr. COOPER also remarked that there were many of the opinion of Mr. Greening that they were completely weary of coming to the Board Wednesday after Wednesday and hearing these discussions.—Mr. GREENING had every confidence in Mr. Mackey as to the way the accounts were kept, and he did not think they would ao wrong if they tried to settle the matter without any change.—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE ; We shall never settle ie—Mr. RnereEee said that if the matter was referred to the Local Government Board they would think the Guardians were not really capable of doing their duty, and that their conduct wanted enquiring into. He should not like it to go to the Local Government Board; they were able to settle the matter there he was sure.—Mr. GREENING: You had better suggest a plan, Mr. Bonnell.—Mr. BONNELL : I am sure I have been consider- ing if I could not suggest a plan, hut I really cannot.— The CHAIRMAN: Nor can anyone else.—Major CART- WRIGHT said if the chairman had stopped the first gentleman who attempted to make that speech they would not have heard anything more about it.—The CHAIRMAN : The Chairman has a perfect right to ask the clerk whether it is a proper thing to write in the book. The clerk immediately au3wered my question, and you immediately jumped up and attacked the clerk.—Major CARTWRIGHT: Simply because no other member had had an opportunity of saying anything.— Mr. Loerasiesav said in reference to the previous entries the clerk said the master had no right to make them, and why should he continue to make them 7—The CHAIRMAN: What is the next business? We have wasted two hours as usual; and then three or four of us must stay to the end and finish the most important business.—Major CARTWRIGHT: I do not sea that you have any cause to complain, because you have nct attended as chairman for the distribution of reIief.Mr.DARBYSHIBE : It's atominable.—The CHAIR- MAN said he had been present.—Mt. DARBYSIIIRE supported the chairman. He bad attended, and the chairman had always been present with very few exceptions.—The CHAIR- MAN: At all events I have stayed 19 times during the year. —Major CARTWRIGHT: Through the business? The CHAIRMAN; Yes.—Major CARTWRIGHT : I am very glad to hear it, and I apologise.—The subject then dropped.

DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT LOWTON LOWTON MILL SERIOUSLY DAMAGED. About seven a.m. on Thursday a fire broke out in what is known as the " Lowton Factory," belonging to the Low- ton Spinning Company, and before the flames were extin- guished, damage amounting to many hundred of pounds was done. The mill is a very old and well-known one, having been erected no less than 54 years ago. It is devo- ted exclusively to cotton spinning, and is divided into two portions—the " new " and " old' or " attic " ends. The former was burned down about twelve years ago, and now the latter has almost suffered a similar fate. The " attic" eni is situated the nearest to the Lowton and Golborne-road, and is nine windows long, two broad, and three storeys in height. The two bottom storeys are used as the engine. house and the mixing-room, while in the top room is a pair of mules for spinning. While the hands were at work, at seven o'clock, it was noticed that a portion of the mule in charge of William Ashton was on fire. The flames spread with alarming rapidity, and almost in an instant the room was filled with dense smoke. Information of the outbreak was at once sent to the manager, Mr. Bromley, and the overlookers, 'end the " whistle " was sounded. The news of the fire rapidly became known throughout the , village, and thc Utra9St alarm anti excitement Were Otcasioned. The majority of the hands quickly left the mill, but a large number of the men displayed a re- markable coolness and determination in their efforts to copo with the flames. In each of the rooms were a large number of buckets filled with water, and these, with a number fire extincteurs," containing a patent far -supPr:,ssing 'liquid, were immediately brought into requisiti. Owing to the dense and overpowering smoke,. ho7ieVer, the diffi- culty of reaching the seat of the cf;ittagration was almost insurmountable. Hose pipes w.'are attached to the iron water pipes on each " landinT ana by this means a better effort to reach the fire 7,;,a3 made. In the meantime a young man, named MT: Ilarraclough, mounted his bicycle, and with all Vella proceeded to the printing works of Messrs. George ; valcCorquodale and Co., and sought the aid of the fire brigade belonging to that establishment. He was informed, however, that the firm had stopped sending their brigade out—the reason no doubt being the sad accident which occured a considerable time ago. A man named Wilcock was despatched to Leigh for the fire brigade belonging to the Local Board, the men appearing on the scene a few minutes before nine o'clock. At that time, however, the flames had been extinguished, and the building partially wrecked. The efforts of the mill hands were put forth with praiseworthy determination, and to them alone rests the credit of having saved the mill proper, or the " new " end from being destroyed. Their labours were devoted to that end, and they succeeded in confining the fire to the room in which it broke out. This was entirely burnt out, however, and the roof was also burnt off—the slates, Jec., falling in with a crash about an hour after the fire had been discovered. Whilst the fire was raging a number of men were engaged in clearing the mixing room, in which a large quantity of cotton was stored. The damage will amount to nearly £l,OOO, but it is a pleasure to learn that it is entirely M office. covered by insurance in a 'anchester oce. How the fire originated has not yet been ascertained, but it is supposed to have been caused by friction. The company employ about 150 hands, and with the exception of a few, they have resumed work again. It may be stated that as one of the men was at- tempting to extinguish the flames with a fire extincteur, the smoke overpowered him, but he succeeded in getting out with safety, though his extineteur had to be left behind. The man Wilcock who went to Leigh for the fire brigade stopped a horse and cart passing on the road and proceeded on his journey on the horse, leaving the cart on the road- side. The services of the brigade were not called into requisition, though the men put in an appearance with commendable punctualitr.

div.head: WEAK SPIRITS AT HUYTON.
div.p: WEAK SPIRITS AT HUYTON.
-A-I-TB LICAN HEAVILY FINED.

I At Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. A. R. Gladstone, H. Bright, and Willis, John Hi'den, landlord of the Eagle and Child Inn, Horn Smithy, Huyton, was charged on two informations with selling to Superintendent Barker, a pint of whiskey and a pint of gin which were not of the nature, quality, and substance required of him.—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the defendant. Superintendent Barker stated that, accompanied by P.S. Ball, he visited de- fendant's house on the 19th February, and found defendant in the bar. He asked him the price of whiskey and he told him it was 4s. a quart. He purchased a pint, for which he paid 25., and then told defendant he had bought it far analysis by the public analyst, Dr. Campbell Brown, and sealed it up, defendant declining to retain a part of it. Next day ho sent the sample to Dr. Brown,who had since cettified that it was a mixture of whiskey and water, 47 per cent. under proof, and 22 per cent. weaker than the lowest limit allowed by the Food and Drags Amendment Act, 1879, viz., 25 degrees under proof. At the same time and under similar circumstances he purchased from the defendant a pint of gin, which Dr. Brown had certified to be a mixture of gin and water 48 degrees under proof, or 13 degrees weaker than the limit (35 degrees) allowed by the Amendment Act.—Superinten- dent Barker remarked that he need scarcely point out the immense profit defendant had been making by selling spirits watered in such a way.—ln answer to Mr. Swift, Superin- tendent Barker said defendant had recently been fined for using a spirit measure which was not of any denomination recognised by the Board of Trade. That measure was what was called a "big twopennortb," and the "big two- ponnorth "was made up with water.—Mr. Swift submitted that defendant, having recently been fined rather heavily, had already been sufficiently punished. He bad carried out the business of a pul4lican for thirty years at Knotty Ash, Eccleston, and Huyton, and he and his wife had grown old in the business. His explanation was that before Christmas his wife was taken ill, and since then the mixing of the spirits had been left to his daughter, who through inexne- Hence bad made a mistake.—Superintendent Barker said that when he visited the house an old woman was knocking about in the bar and taking an active part in what was going on, and he was informed that she was defendant's wife.— Mr. Swift c died defendant's daughter, who sail her mother had only came downstairs a week before Mr. Barker's visit. —The Bench imposed a penalty of 40s. and costs in each case.
