div.head: WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE UNION.
div.p: WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE UNION.
INAUGURAL MEETING.

Under the name of the Warrington Temperance Union have bten amalgamated the Warrington Temperance Society and the Gospel Temperance Mission, and the inaugural meeting was held on Monday evening under circumstances that augur well for the success of the Union. The meeting took place in the Co-operative Hall, which was crowded with the supporters of the temperance cause, some of whom appeared in the regalia of the Good Templar Order, and others wore the "bit of blue," the badge of the Blue Ribbon Army. The president of the Union (Mr. R. Garnett) occu- pied the chair, and he was supported by Revs. J. Cullen, Oughtrington ; J. Buglass, Haslingden ; J. D. Warr;;;s, Yonge, T. Rippon, J. Moreton, and 'Moore . Messrs. E. Twiss, H. Thornton, J. W. Han, Dixon, and W. Roberts, W. B. Pickering, and C. George, hon. secs. Letters of apology for non-attendance had been received from the Rev. W. Pilling, Mr. H. L. Riley (St. Helens), and Mr. R. A. Saykr. _

the PRESIDENT, in addressing the audience, said since their last Meeting this question had to some extent changed its position with them in Warrington. He did not know that he needed to go into details. They all knew the valu- able efforts which had been put forth by the Warrington Temperance Society for some 40 years, and he was quite sure they were glad to recognise with him the valuable ser- vices which had been rendered by men who had really been pioneers of the temperance cause in times whew temperance advocacy was a matter of some difficulty and danger. He was thankful to know they had men amongst them still who were standing by the old land-marks. Men who had ren- dered services to God and in His Church in the temperance cause were still with them, and he was glad to have their names associated with them. Since their efforts in connection with the Gospel Temperance Mission it had been thought on the principle that "Union is strength,' that if a combination of tha old Temperance Society and the Blue Ribbon Army could be effected, they would be all the more likely to ren- der greater service to the temperance cause; and after meet- tings of both societies it was ultimately decided that the two societies should be united and form one brotherhood. (Hear, hear.) They were glad that night to see so many present at the inaugural meeting in connection with the Temperance Union, and he believed the intention.of all was to prosecute the work with, if possible, redoubled zeal. (Hear, hear.) There was no doubt that while they were-thankful, they needed to be thankful without resting. (Hear, hear.) They had gained great advantages during the last few years, and he thought if they would read the newspapers carefully they would be astonished at the rapid strides which the temperance question had made throughout the length and breadth of the land. A great impetus was given to the temperance movement a few years ago. when what he thought was the missing link, the Church of England, took up the question, and there was no doubt they were greatly indebted to the Church party for their efforts in con- nection with this movement. In addition to them they had had a large amount of work done by the Salvation Army .and the Blue Ribbon Army, and what they had to do was to go out and make still greater acquisitions. They wanted to make their influence still further felt in our Houses of Legislature. They wanted the members to feel as they felt, that the country could do without that which de- moralised and did so much to damage our common humanity. He thought, however, they were within measurable distance of seeing the Sabbath Day at least kept sacred from the sale of that drink which so polluted the land —(applause)—and he felt confident they would in a short time have such a measure as would largely diminish the sale of that which did so much mischief in the land. (Applause.) The PRESIDENT afterwards read the following letter "The members of the Catholic Total Abstinence League of the Cross are happy to hear the Warrington Temperance Union are having a public meeting for the benefit of total abstinence, and wish a hearty success to the ause.—Yours, on behalf of the League, J. MULLINS, secretary." Mr. W. ROBERTS read the following report :

The committee, in presenting their 48511 annual report, rejoice to acknowledge that during the past year an increasing interest has been awakened in the temperance movement throughout the country, and that after half a century of earnest, devoted labour, the princip'es of total abstinence have , become popular with the great mass of the people. The com- mittee are thankful that this society has done some little in this great enterprise, though we are willing to acknowledge that much more might have been accomplished. The annual public meeting of this society was fairly attended, and the speeches of Meesrs. Thomas Whittaker and Hardy were highly app • eciated. The week's services conducted by Mr. King. of Chester, were lseld in various parts of the town, and his valuable addresses were attentively listened to. With reference to the mis,ion conducted by Mr. T. E. Murplay, in the Public Hall, we find a diffieulty in speaking. That it was a glorious success was admitted by all. At the commencement of the arrangements your committee invited the clergy and laity interested in the temperance question to meet in con- ference for the formation of an united committee to carry out the work connected with the mission, thus spreading the work over a wider area, and bringing in a large number of temper- ance wo kers who had hitherto been unknown. Of the workers we cannot speak too highly ; all gave an earnest devotion to the work never before witnessed in this t own, We should do an injustice to many if any namea, were specisilly mentioned; therefore, we cordially thank all who assisted for their gratui- tous services. Mr. Murphy displayed great tact and command of the meetings, which will long be remembered for their enthusiasm, the hall being crowded on fourteen consecutive nights The mission conducted by Mr. Hardy, of Manchester, was also very successful. The annual meeting in support of the United Kingdom Alliance wes fairly attended. The Rev. Dawson Burns, o London. and Councillor Swan. of Sunder- land, represented the Alliance and delivered most able add- esses. The numter of pledges taken has been greater than in any vast year :—Mr. King's mission 47, Mr. Murphy's mis- sion 8,931, Mr. Hardy's mission 34, cocoa-houses and other f 44; total, 9,623. Doubtless many have again brokea the pledge, but we have abundant testimony to prove that the Christisn churches in the town have benefited by the work which has been accomplished. The success of the Gospel Tem- perance Mission induced the comm'ttee to cmsider the desirability of forming one united sec ety for Warrington, It has singe been unanimously resolved by the committees of both societies, that an amalgamation should take p ace, the society henceforth to be called the "Warrington Temperance Union" (lasing the union of the Warrington Total Abstinence Society and Gospel Temperance Mieeion). This is now an accomp'ishe.t fact. The principles of the new society are— " Total abstinence from all intoxicating 1 tquours as a beverftge." These principles which have bsenadvocsted since the formation of the parent sccietv in 1831, we stds adhere me, and we remember wt h atitude the labours of the veterans in the cause, who, amidst discouragement, derision, and scorn, proclaimed the principles of total abs 'llene° as the only remedy for the evil of :nternperance. Your committee would refer to the list of officers for the en- suing year as an evidence of the support which has already been secured, and would conclude by snaking an earnest appeal to the friends of the cause in Warrington to assist them by generously contributing to the funds of the society, in order to c:ear off a small deficiency and to provide for future work, in aid of which the Ladies' Committee wiil shortly make a per- sonal appeal. The friends who are already subscribers are re- spectfully requested as far es possible to increase their subscrip- tions and those ahe do not contribute are cordially invited to I enrol their names,

The Rev. J. CunnEN moved the adoption of the report, and expressed the hope that when the Ladies' Committee got to work they would have a better list of subscriptions, for he thought they ought to have something like four or five times as many subscriptions as they found down in the report. He congratulated them most heartily upon the marriage of the VW° societies. One was rather old and the other rather young he supposed, but perhaps the union would be none the less loving for that reason; and he hoped since the Union had taken place they would realise the truth of the I, old motto—" Union is strength." (Applause.) He urged I them to work in a right and true spirit, which was nothing less than pure love of God and love of man—(applause)— for of all movements in which they could ba engaged, he thought this was the one in which they ought to use words of love. It was said if they wanted to hear intemperate language they should go to a tornperance meeting; but he thought the boot was on the Other leg, and that it was the temperance people who had to submit to hard language. He maintained by quotations from Shakespeare, Tennyson, Dr. Andrew Clarke, and Thomas Carlyle, that it was not, as a rule, teetotallers who were guilty of using strong language, but those who were not teetotallers; and that while perhaps teetotallers agreed with this strong language, they were generally careful to quote their authority for it. Referring to another charge which was very often brought against the temperance movement that it was a very narrow movement, he con- tended that it was the broadest movement in existence —(hear, hear,)—because the evil of drunkenness was the fountain of evil—a sort of father evil in the country. He argued that in taking up temperance work they were taking up the whole question of the morality of the country in a philanthropic spirit, a righteous and proper manner—such a manner as they might expect, and would realise the bless- ing of God upon their work. (Applause.) The Rev. J. Buaniss seconded, and the report was adopted. • The Rev. J. Yonan thought the appearance of the meet- ing that evening was a splendid augury for the success of the Warrington Temperance Union. He would like them to realise that that was a marriage ceremony. (Hear, hear.) They had to look upon themselves—those of the old Temperance Society and those of the Temperance Mission in the happy posi- tion of husband and wife, but which was the husband and which was the wife he would not attempt to determine. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) He believed the popularity that was given to the temperance movement, the manifest respect that was given to the temperance movement had arisen through the Gospel Temperance Mission, for they found the" bit of blue ' worn by peers and peeress, and he was not sure by princes and princesses, by bishops and archbishops, by clergy and dissenting ministers, by gentle- men and ladies in all walks of society; and he contended that that manifestation of a widespread sympathy with teetotalistn would do more for the temperance cause than anything which had been done in the previous days cf its history. (Applause.) Referring to the report, he said it seemed to be unintentionally incomplete, and that to make the report grammatical they should add another prin- ciple, and that was the manifest recognition of the Gospel as a great agent for temperance work throughout the ; country. He held that if the temperance work was to be- come the greet success they wished it to be it should be fol- lowed up, and when persons took the pledge they should never lose sight of them. He hoped the movement would receive an impetus from the meeting which would carry it on to greater and wider success than ever it had yet seen. (Applause.) The Rev. J. A. BEET gave his reasons for being a teeto- taller. -

The Rev, E. 310DRR thought the outlook of temperance reform was hopeful. Ic had now come so prominently be- fore the national conscience that it bad become a plank in the platform of a strong Government, and he confidently hoped that before the present session of Parliament closed

they would see some good and satisfactory advance made in 1 the direction of a further restriction of the temptations to drink which were now before workingmen. (Applause.) ! Interspersed with the speeches were an instrumental WO by Messrs. Pearson, Bond, and Ford, song by Mrs. Pearson I and a flute solo by Bugle Master Burgess, all of which were much appreciated. The meeting closed with the singing of the Doxology. 1

NEWTON IMPROVEMENTS. IBY X.'-1 The casual Vier Or friend returning to spend a few days with. tin relatives at this season will find, in sauutering tilratl6 Newton, that we are being beautified both ia our highways and in our by-ways. First comes the Main-street with its new plantation of saplings, which, if they will only take good root, will in due time be a decided benefit to both man—and beast, we were going to say, but we hear, whether the rumour be true or not, that the beasts which are usually to be seen in this street at fair times ere to assemble at Earlestown in future. We hope they may, and then they will not look so very few as they have done for a dozen years or so when scattered through the length and breadth of the High-street. Moreover, it will promote cleanliness, and, let us hope, trade at the same time. The footpath lead- ing from this Main-street to the Mains has at last been di- verted, if such a word can be applied to a road that was for- merly crooked, but now runs in straight line by the end of the last-built cottages in Mercer-street to the west as for- merly it went to the east of them. And anyone of an anti- quarian turn of mind may see, both mentally and visually, how the last traces of the Vicinal Roman-road which ran from Wigan to the River Sankey, at least, and to the en- campment at Cuerdly, and the Mersey, we think, came to be obliterated and totally lost at the archway in the middle of the Mains, by taking note of the ease with which such a pathway as this we are speaking of can be filled up and done away with. We remember perfectly well having daily made our way some thirty-six years ago through the " Slutchey- lane," as the last vestige of this Vicinal Road was then called, a spur of perhaps a hundred yards between high hedges immediately opposite the barn doors of Mr. Clarke's farm in Crow-lane, and at present indicated quite uncon- sciously by the pole of the telephone passing by that way. As shown on the ordnance survey map of L incashire, this road comes out into the Ashton-road at Wiswell's, not very far from the entrance to the Haydock Park coursing ground, which many sportsmen ale visiting at this moment, and bowling along one of the most ancient roads in the kingdom, which ought to enhance the pleasure of such a visit. It is yet quite possible that in turning up the ground at the new cemetery some further trace of this most ancient Vicinal Road may be found, for the late farmer of this ground used to declare that when ploughing a certain field there near Wargrave Church, a well-defined roadway, in which were , stones innumerable, used even in his time to offer an im- ps diment to his plough on this or that side of the wood near by We direct attention to the matter, hoping that some , inquiring spirit may find in some of the plough lands be- tween this and the Mersey further traces of this important roadway.

div.head: SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT RAINHILL.
div.p: SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT RAINHILL.

Mr. John Mather, newsagent and bookseller, Rainhill, met his death on Monday under very shocking circumstances. Mr. Mather; was 45 years of age, and tad been for many years resident in Rainhill, where he was well known and esteemed for many good qualities. He was by trade a tool- maker, and as such worked for some time in Prescot, but for the last 15 or 20 years he devoted himself mainly to the business of a newsagent in a shop in Mar- ket-street, Rainhill. It was his custom to meet some of the trains passing through Rain- hill Station in order to supply passengers with newspapers, and he was engaged in this occupation on Monday morning last when a mishap occurred, which cost him his life. As a train was starting for Liverpool a gentleman called from a carriage window for a newspaper. Mr. Mather ran to sup- ply him, and as he was reaching up to the window with the paper he overbalanced himself and fell between two car- riages. Four carriages passed over him, and he was killed instantaneously, his head and body being dreadfully in- jured. On Wednesday afternoon Mr. Barklr held an inquest on the body at the Victoria Hotel, Rainhill. Mr. Ferrand re- presented the London and North-Western Railway Co. The body was identified by Mr. John Mather, deceased's eldest son.—Alfred Swift, porter at Rainhill Station, stated that on Monday morning he saw Mr. Mather on the platform when the S-16 train from Manchester arrived. He was foll&eating his usual occupation of selling newspapers. Two ladies alighted from the train, and Mr. Mather stood talking to them until the train started for Liverpool. As the train was moving away at a slow pace a gentleman called from a carriage for a newspaper, and Mr. Mather, who was standing at the head of the train, ran to him. While reaching up to the window with the paper he over- balanced himself, struck his shoulder against one of the carriages, and swinging round fell off the platform between two carriages. Two carriages, the guard's van, and two carriage trucks passed over him. Witness went to him, and he breathed once or twice, but died before he could be lifted on to the platform. The platform at the place where Mr. Mather fell was not slippery, being composed of rough gravel. The train was going at the rate of about ten miles an hour.—Mrs. Ann Cunliffe, Haydock-lane, St. Helens, and Miss Annie Gould, the two ladle s referred to by Swift, gave corroborative evidAnce.—The Corner, in summing up, said it was perfectly plain the occurrence was purely acci lental. Deceased, anxious to discharge his duties and oblige the public, was running to answer the call of a gentleman from a carriage, and, unfortunately, in reaching the newspaper, he overbalanced himself, struck his shoulder against a carriage, and :wheeled between two carriages. It seemed he was in the habit of running along trains with newspapers as newspaper sellers generally were, and he (the Canoner) was afraid the public were somewhat to blame for an ac- cident of that character, because they were very careless. They kept in conversation till the train was moving and then they celled out for a paper, and 'people had to run to them alongside the train at considerable risk. When people had ample time to get a newspaper before they got into a a carriage, they ought not ta stand in conversation until the last. moment, and then call for a paper ani CALM a man to run the whole length of a train after them. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death."

At the Dublin Police Court, on Wednesday, a man an d a woman were committed for trial for having robbed a Con- nemara land agent, named Brennan, of money and valuables worth £164, in a disorderly house. When giving informa- tion to the police, the prosecutor gave the name of Sir Geo. Beresford, which he now admitted, amidst much laughter in court, was an imaginary title. The prisoners stripped him even to his trousers.

At the Bolton County Court, on Wednesday inorning, Samuel Smithies, a pianoforte dealer, sued Benjamin Coupe for 31s 6.1, the balance of the hire of a piano. There was a flaw in the case, and a verdict was given for the defendant. Judge Hutton characterised the.system of letting out piano, sewing machines, or furniture as most pernicious and mis- chievous. He should in future require cases to be clearly proved before he allowed the claims. On Wednesday there was an exciting porpoise hunt in the Ribble at Preston. One got up the Ribble to the shal- lows, and was there seen after the tide had receded jumping about in three feet of water. Several fishermen and beat- men tried the harpoon, but failed. At last a young fellow, named Crook, twice speared the animal with a boat hook, and holding on to his game succeeded in landing it. 'The porpoise was four feet nine inches long. Sir George Jesse!, Master of the Rolls, died at his desi- *dence in London at six o'clock on Wednesday morning. The deceased judge, according to " Men of the Time," was of Jewish extraction, being the youngest son of the late Mr. Zacariah Nathaniel Jessel, a merchant of Putney, by Mary, daughter of the late Mr. Henry Harris. Ho was born in London in the year 1824, and educated at University College, London, where he graduated 8.A., in 1843, as University Scholar in Mathematics, and proceeded M.A. hi the following year, obtaining a gold medal in mathematics. He was called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn in May, 1847, and was made a Queen's Counsel and a Bencher of his Inn in 1865. He is a Senator of the University of London, and at the general election of 1868 he was returned in the Liberal interest as one of the representatives of the borough of Dover. He was appointed Solicitor-General in Mr. Gladstone's administration in Navember, 1871. and re- ceived the honour of knighthood February 21st, 1872. In August, 1873, he was, on the recommendation of Mr. Glad- stone appointed Master of the Rolls, in succelsion to Lord Romilly. On this occasion he was sworn of the Privy Council. Sir George Jessel was the first Jew who ever oc- cupied a seat on the judical bench in this country. He married, in 1856, a daughter of Mr. Joseph Moses, mercleant, of Leadenhall-street, City. _ _ _ _ _

The demand in the labour market for workpeople keeps ' increasing, although the unsettled weather has impeded progress in the building trade, as well as railway construc- tion. The "restriction of output " still keeps the mining districts unsettled. At Barnsley, the ironworks, as well as the Bessemer steel works, are well employed. At Barrow- in-Furness the works are just keeping regular hours; an increase of labour in the steel rail works is anticipated. At Birmingham, hardware industries are quiet, but in tools, railway materials, and electric light fittings, there is plenty of work, and the nailmakers are busy. At Darlington the ironworkers are unsettled as to restriction of work. At the Hartlepools„ ship builders and marine engineers are very busy and are increasing their workpeople. At Newcastle- on-Tyne the rough weather has reduced the demand for labour in the docks, but work at the furnaces and coke ovens is up to the average. At Leeds there is a good deal of machinery idle, through loss of continental trade. The wholesale ready-made houses have plenty of work on export orders, and in the home cloth trade there is no lack of em- ployment. At Manchester there is a moderate amount of employment. At Leicester workpeople and machinery are fully employed in the hosiery and elastic web departmente,and shoemakers have regular work. At Nottingham the lace and curtain trade is sufficient to keep the In ichinety and workpeople in regular work, and the same may be said of the hosiery branch. Emigration is steadily i DC( easing, and the Charity Organisation Society have taken the initiative in promoting its further extension, awl the various Colonial Government agents in London are working. with extra vigour to increase and maintain a large exodus of the unemployed in this country.—Labour News. The yearly7:ticreanfr,% demand for non-intoxicant beverages- has ccsnvellel'ilTessrs. J. Cammack and Co. to meet it by the infusion of new' blood and additional capital into the firm; hence the formation of the present oompsny. The directors enter on their °face with the determination to give every pos- sible satisfaction to their patrons \ and to make the company second to no firm in the kingdoms whether h the excellence of its beverages, the modera.tion of Is prices, t..r the careful/ atten- tion of its officers tothe wants of customers.

The consumption of Idinecal and Aerated Waters has grown so rapidly that a keen competition, in their supply has been excited, resulting in the introduction of some very unsound and even poisonous b3verages.

This degeneracy bar arisen partly tin•ongh the incapacity or the old rule-o'-thumb manufacturers, who still maintain Mier- antiquated apparatus, consisting of copper vessels, whose tin lining, if they ever had any, has long since been removed:and common lead piping—sure and fertils sources of poisonous metalic contamination—and partly through the greed and rapacity of the modern but not less ignorant speculators in the business, who, descending to the vilest, because cheapest means of production, nce defective seosnd,hand machinery; and employ impure and often poisonous- ingredients in the composition of the various drinks. Even, the bottle in which cupidity, for the small wooden stopper adopted in the c.hespeet type of patent bottle in common use, instead of being weighted with pure block tin is frequently found loaded with lead, the most dangerous metal for such, a purpose, sa it is well known to be a virulent and an accumulative poisos.

The proper choice and erection of machinery and apparatus, the adoption of suitable precautionary measures during the process of manufacture, the ability to seleet and the power to make or purify the various ingredients, absolutely require the experience and knowledge of a trained Chemist. His active and unremitting personal supervision Is also needed be avoid or destroy the various noxious ferments which are so apt to form, and the myriads of organised germs, cells, bacteria, Btc., which are now admitted to be a frequent source of disease, and even death.

The Directors are therefore pleased to have retained the pro- fessional services of Mr. John Cammack (Fellow of the Insti- tute of Chemistry and of the Society of Chemical Industry), as Managing Director, whose name is so well and honourably known in the district of St. Helens, and whose long and varied experience in Scientific and Technical Chemistry will be a sure guarantee of the purity and excellence of the various beverages.

Moreover, they have adopted machinery and apparatus of the latest and most improved type. Every portion of it which comes into actual contact with the Aerated Waters and the Syrups is constructed of glass, porcelain, pure block tin, or at real gun metal (not corrodable brass) thickly lined with pure block tin. Lead is entirely discarded, even the solder used in making the various connections being free from that noxious metal,

For the storage of the Solutions and Syrups, only elate, earthenware, or glass vessels are used, wood being entirely dis- pensed with as too absorbeitt and retentive of foal flavours and energetic ferments.
All the Waters and Syrups are earefully altered before being used.
A special apparatus.is employed to thoroughly rinse even the last trees of the wash water from the bottles.
The Bweet Drinks are composed of nen, but real fruit essences and extracts and harmless egetable compounds.

The Mineral Waters eontain the purest materials, and are guaranteed strength. The SODA WATER, which is Vita=DLL by any other manufaoturers, eontains the standard quantity earbonate of soda, and is not, like the rubbish to often im plied, plain water Indifferently carbonated.
All the Patent Bottles used are stoppered with glass, and the Corked Goods are of a Special and Superior Quality.

Having Mr. JAMES BizinGin proposed a hearty vote of thanks to asked for and obtained the essential ticket, which was freely the lecturer, which was seconded by Mr. GHO. Onmanon, given, he and his friends made their way to the Catacombs. and carried with acclamation. After passing the Capitol, the Main prison, the Forum, the The leinetTersaiss briefly !Mottled. Arch of Titus, the Coliiseum, and through the noblest Arch I The proceedings concluded with singing and prayer. whio liclpf ehe weeld could boast, that of Constantine, I -trey proceeded erne distance and came to two diverging roads, Where stood a small chapel or church called " Domine eta) Vadis." The faithful were taught that St. Peter, hav- ing fled from Rome through fear of martyrdom, was here met by our Lord, who reproved him for his cowardice. But it would be time enough to speak of -dt. Peter having fled from Rome, when it was proved that he really ever was at Rome. (Hear, hear.) Histoly went the otleee eeey and led them to infer that he never was in le Scripture was ailett on the subject, and they (*tad net believe it would be had he ever been there. It Was, however, certain that he was never Bishop of Rene, hence the pope could not be his suc- cessor. (Applause.) In entering the catacombs they must descend a flight of many steps, when a chamber of consider- able size Was entered. Thia special catacomb was called after Callixtus, who, in the year 200, took the cemetery under his contreleanditbecame the favourite burying place of the Roman bishops. This Collixtus was originally a slave, who, by fraud and deceit, worked his way into the episcopacy, thus showing that as early as the third century eorruption showed itself in the Roman Church. There was one matter of great interest in connection with the cata- combs, and that was the great number of inscriptions which a learned investigator of the mysteries of underground Rome had characterised as "the faithful echoes of history, and the infallible guides through the labyrinth of subterranean gal- leries." To themselves the great value of the Roman Cata- combs lay in the inscriptions, for therefrom they learned what was the faith of the early Christian Church, and it had been remarked that were all other records of primitive Christianity destroyed they could .almost gather from the Catacombs records, not perhaps its dogmas and doctrines,* but the principal observances of the early Christian and primitive church. Proceeding to speak ef the structure of the catacombs, the lecturer observed that the entrance was generally low and obscure, like a fox's barrow, to which was attached a stairway leading to the subterranean excavation. That stairway conducted to nar- row passages or corridors about 10 feet high and from five feet to six feet wide. The roof WAS scmewhat circular, but in some Cases it was somewhat horizontal. The corridors in- tersected, bi-sected and transected one another at every kind of conceivable angles, and merely formed a network of gal- leries. On either side, rising tier upon tier, were the graves, which took the form of ships' berths, and were as close to- gether as the nature of the soil would allow. The number of graves computed to exist was 7,000,000. Those wondrous cities of the mighty dead, with their intricacies and labyrinth of cunningly formed streets so full of interest, were full of danger to the uninitiated, for to lose one's wav there meant a horrible death. But what concerned them most in con- nection with that branch of the Church Association was the doctrinal teachings of the catacombs, and how far they sup- ported the rites and doctrines of the Church, which, as a church, was holy, catholic and apostolic; apostolic in that she had come down from apostolic days and had a ministry of apostolic order and design. The church was Catholic in that she held the true faith, and a summary of which was found in the three create she affirmed, and they had the most certain warrant of God's blessed word. She accepted nothing but what the apostles and the primitive church held and taught; she discarded nothing which they professed and maintained, and she was in happy harmony with the orthodoxy of all ages. She was holy in that her aim was to beget holiness, and that her every doctrine had the stamp of holiness upon it. She was protestant in that she was a witness for the truth. Protestantism was not a negation—it was an affirmation for the truth. (Applause.) They would appeal to the Catacombs, which contained the belief of the primitive church to conform the orthodoxy, apostolicity, authority, and scriptnralness of the rites, cere- monies, doctrines, and teachings of the Protestant Church of England. From the Catacombs they obtained information as to the organisation of the church and of the administration of the sacraments. Fatheis of "the Itieltlltihe -entirdeneell ithe44iovat s_f sight almost reconstruct the whole fabric of the ecclesias- tical polity from the Catacombs. As to the ministryethey found that the three orders of ministers—bishops, presby- ters, and deacons, were accepted. It was remarkable that no trace whatever existed of any one bishop having arro- gated to himself or to having assigned to him the office of universal bishop, which the Roman Pontiffs now claimed to be. So far was the Bishop of Rome in early days from being regarded as the head of all, or as hiving any special superiority, that they found the bishops of other churches violently opposing the Bishop of Rome, and the phrase "Apostolic See," now restricted to Rome, was applied to every bishop's seat in early times. As to the pet term " pope," it was not found in the Catacombs until the fifth century. In the past it was addressed to other bishops be- sides the Bishop of Rome, and as to the title of Universal Bishop, Pope Gregory the Great declared that whoever was " bold enough to arrogate it to himself was the forerunner of antichrist—a sharp malediction on his present holiness of the Vatican. (Appleuse.) As to presbyters, they had teeny epitaphs designative of their office. Let it be well noted that not once in the New Testament, not once in the inscriptions c !the Catacombs, not 011C3 in the writings of the primitive fathers was the "sacrificing priests" applied to desienate a Christian minister. A good reason existed why it should riot, because there was no sacrifice for sin to be offered up. Christian ministers were not and could not be sacrificing prieste. (Applause.) As to the third order of s niters—deacans—they found the Catacombs recoguising taem. They had abundant proof from the Catacombs that their threefold order of ministers was primitive, apostolic, and scriptural. The ministry of the hurch of England was an ordinance of God's appointment, and was therefore not to be despised. Proceeding to speak of celibacy of the, clergy which the Romish Church and the Ritualists of to- day enforced and declared to he a more sacred condition than the married state, was not so considered by the primi- tive Church as the Catacombs testified. The Sacrament of Baptism was not neglected, but highly valued, by the early Christians. Infant leaptiern rece.eed authority from the Catacombs, as well as from scripture. There were epitaphs that told the baptism was administered to all ages—to in- fants as well as to adults. The Sacrament of the Lord's Supper was not celebrated or administered exclusively in , the morning, or at mid-day, but also in the evening, which was apparent from the Catacombs. To cry down evening communion, and te require persons to come fasting to the Lord's Supper was, to ray the least, to act in direct opposi- tion to the practice of the primitive Church and to the in- stitution of our Lord. The sacrament was administered in both kinds—bread and wine. It remained for the corrupt Church of Rome to rob the petiole of half the sacrament, and it was manifest that neitber Remish prieets administered nor Roman e'atholic laity received the sacrament according to Christ's institution. As to the clectrine of Transubstanti- ation, the primitive Church, or the Church of the Cata- combs, knew nothing of it. Regarding altars in connection with the celebration of the Eucharints, the primitive Christians knew nothing, and the entire absence of any approach to a sacrificial altar was the subject of ridicule amongst the Pagans. They had tables of wood, and they were placed not altar wise against the waJI as at the present day, but at some distance from it, so that the celebrant could stand behind and face the people. That was the primitive custom, and perhaps it would not be amis if they returned to the primitive custom, so that the clergy could stand and look at the pesple like an honest man. —(applause)—and not turn his back upon them as if he was ashamed of himself or ashamed of them. (Loud ap- plause.) The Church of England was in harmony with the early Christi Ins in requiring that the Communion table should be of wood—of jeineraa work, not mason's work. The Catacombs also tore a faithful witness against doctrines which held a leading position in the creeds of Romanists and Ritualists. He alluded t 3 the doctrine of Purgatory, Observing that the inscriptions in the Catacombs clearly in- dicated that the belief of the early Christians as regarded the departed was not that they went to so called purgatorial fires, but to the abode of blessedness and joy. Closely allied with that doctrine WAS that of praying for the dead, but did the Catacombs eariction it in a Rornieh sense? No. The marked silence of the Catacombs on the subject was a distinct proof that tI!, eerty Church held no such doctrine. The Catacombs disc, eel telt the Church of England WAS . in harmony with the early Church in doctrine and cere- monies, acknowledgire.s 011.3 Lard, one faith, and one Bap- tism. (Applause) Their examination and study of the Catacombs had more and !no, e canfirmed them in their belief in the truth, omiol ivenes, holiness, catholicity, and apostolicity of the teechinue and doctrines of the ancient but reformed Church of England, and more and more con- vinced them of the antagonism of Romanistn to the teach- ing, the doctrines, and principles of Holy Scripture and the primitive Church, from roth of which she had apostatised. (Applause.) Whilst they bad an active fee without they had a most dangerous one to contend against—the enemy within. (Applause). Rim diem was that unscrupulous, dishonourable foe. The controversey with it was not about millinery, vestrires, postures, and the like. It was not a barmleita form of rites and ceremonies. There was clear testimony that in faith and forms it was Remanism. Ritualism aimed at the extirpation of troteetantism, which was the Synonymous with civil and religious liberty—which martyrs' blood dearly

div.head: T.RAHPS AND THEIR LOD6rINGS.
div.p: T.RAHPS AND THEIR LOD6rINGS.

The following letter was read from Inspector Hollings- worth, of Runcorn :—" As the assistant relieving-officer for the casual tramps at Runcorn, I am requested by the Chief Constable of Cheshire to bring to your notice the fact that a many of the above class of persons are new applying at a Late hour of the night for tickets for shelter, and have there- fore to be sent to a lodging house instead of the vagrant ward of the workhouse. It is also becoming generally known amongst these persons that the Casual Poor Act 1882 has not been adopted in this Union, and consequently he is afraid, unless you can suggest some remedy to prevent it, there will be a very great increase of these applicants in future in your district.—The CLERK remarked that the only plan to deal with this question that he could discern was to erect casual wards at Runcorn, but he did not think the Guardians would regard such a proposal with favour. He suggested that the Visiting Committee should consider the question,'and ask Inspector Hollingsworth to meet them and state his views. He would then be able to give them much more information than he did in his letter. (Hear, hear.) Or the Board might defer the matter until the new Guardians were appointed, which would be in a month.—The last-named suggestion was unanimously adopted.

div.head: SALLEY 08, THE CLEM TO THE ASSESSMENT
div.p: THE SALLEY 08, THE CLEM TO THE ASSESSMENT

Mr. C. REYNOLDS said the Assessment Committee recom- mended that Mr. H. Linaker, clerk to the Assessment Com- mittee, be paid £75 for his ordinary services, and £35 for his extra services, which had been very heavy this year. He moved that the sums suggested be paid.—Mr. CHALLONER seconded the motion. He had been a member of the Asse,ssment Committee for three or four years, and he knew how numerous and important were the extra services performed by the clerk. He had often thought that the clerk had not been paid as much as he ought to have been for them. The subject was thorougkly gone into at the last meeting of the Assessment Committee, and although many of the members thought Mr. Linaker was not sufficiently remunerated, they agreed to the sum named as very reasonable, The alterations in the assess- ments which Mr. Linaker had obtained during the past year would save the ratepayers, especially the farmers, a lot of money.—The motion was unanimously carried.

Tim MEDICAL OFFICERIS REPORT.

The MEDICAL OFFICER (Dr. J. G. Bride) presented his annual report, which was of a most elaborate character, and occupied 18 sheets of foolscap. It stated that during 1882 there were 327 deaths-178 males and 149 females of all ages, as against 301 in 1881, showing an increase of 26. These deaths represented the low rate of 16.9 per 1,000 of the population. Seventy-one, or 3.6 per 1,000 were of children under one year of age and upwards, and 99, or 5.1 per 1,000 of persons aged 60 years and upwards. The births recorded during the year were 626-321 males and 305 females' as against 606 in 1881; equal to an annual' birth-rate 0f32 9 per 1,000, showing an increase of 20. He had investigated 45 outbreaks of infectious disease, three of which were serious epidemics, and the others of a less serious nature. There were 8 deaths from scarlet fever, 6 from measles, 1 from diptheria, 14 from diarrhcea, 4 from whooping cough, and 1 from puerperal fever. It was most desirable that some form of notification of infectious disease should be decided upon. In his judgment the per- son having the custody of tho infected person ought to be made responsible for the performance of this important duty. The onus should be exclusively borne by such individuals. Were medical men compelled to share the responsibility of reporting such cases, the public would protect the sanctity of their homes by excluding them, in which case the death rate would be much increased. A large number of uncerti- fied deaths this year called for special remark. Ii most cases old women, midwives, or quacks were consulted and their remedies administered. This practice could no doubt be checked if registrars had discretionary power to refuse an order of burial. All such cases should be dealt with by the coroner, who would no doubt inquire into the circumstances which denied the person medical aid. As there were so few members of the Authority present, the report was taken as read, and the members unaninsously decided that it be printed and circulated.

MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday afternoon, at the Masonic Hotel, Devon- shire Square, the Coroner, Mr. Ridgway was engaged in unravelling the mystery which surrounded the death of a young man named George Saunders, who, besides his trade as picture framer, was employed by the Runcorn School Board as assistant visitor. Saunders, it seemed, was paying his addresses to Harriet Burchall, a servant at The Mount, the residence of Mr. G. L. Wigg, and on Tuesday night he met her in the street, and accompanied her home. After having supper with the ser- vants, Saunders remained chatting with them in the kitchen. About half-past eleven he suddenly rose from the chair on which he was sitting and " ran " outside, leaving his hat and stick on the ball stand. As he did not speak, the servants concluded that he v,-,?uld be returning in a few moments, but not having dOnti SO at the expira- tion of five minutes, they opetr_ 1 tii6 hall , door. Nothing, however, was to be seen or heard, and. locking the door the servants retired to rest. Next morning:, about half-past eight, Matthew Broughton, Mr. Wiges gardener, was horrified to find Saunder's lifeless body lyings i soil, whichon the hadfrontenteredgarden bed,hi 3 His Glee was buried int ohe medical testimony showed t:dat the and Mouth. The e,§ poor fellow had been suffocated whilst in a fIP . to attacks of which he was sub- CV ject. toms of tb, It WaS state`l.. thTat he could always recognise the mp planation 0, .442 tad attacks, and this fact suggests an ex- servant- .. his strange conduct in the presence of the .4 . Feeling the indications of a fit, he evidently th - ...ought it best to go into the cool night air, and falling on the ground, he strugglel until he got his face into the soil, and was suffocated. The news of his sad end caused quite a sensation in the town, as he was widely known. He was only 25 years of age.—The first witness called was John Saunders, who identified the body of the deceased as that of his brother.—Miss Harriett Burchall housemaid to Mr. G. L. Wigg, The Mount, Moughland- lane, stated that on Tuesday night, when with a girl named Elizabeth Wilson, she met the deceased at the bottom of Regent-street. After walking through the town together, the deceased accompanied them to the Mount, where they arrived about half-past nine. The deceased had a cup of coffee and some bread and butter, and then they all sat in ' the kitchen talking together. She knew the deceased was subject to fits, but on Tuesday night he seemed to be as well as usual. About half-past eleven the deceased sudddeoly sprang from his chair and ran outside, closing the door after him. He did not make any remark and for a short time they, in the kitchen felt startled. When the deceased had been gone about five minutes, witness and another servant went to the front door, but not being able to see anything of the deceased, they closad the door and locked it. By the foreman (Mr. J Coxhill): The deceased left his hat and stick behind him.—A jurrman: You did not go off the front door step to look for him? 110.—Mr. Bowyer: You did not make any great effort to see what had become of him? We had not the courage to go out at that time of night.—But you knew that he had left his bat and stick behind? yes, but we afterwards thought that he might have had a smoking cap in his pocket, and Would come to the house next morning. By the Coroner: Deceased left his hat and stick on the hall stand. He had done some work for Mrs. Wigg.—Miss 1 Ellen Hassan, cook at the Mount, confirmed Burchall's statement. Michael Broughton, gardener, Bold-street, stated that about half-past eight on Wednesday morning he found the deceased lying in front of lhe Mount. The face of the deceased was embedded in the soil, and life was ex- tinct. The body lay about four or five yards from the front door, and it would be quite impossible to see it from the hall step.—Dr. MacDougall stated that be had made an ex- ternal examination of the body. An epileptic fit, followed by suffocation through deceased's face being buried in the soil, had been the cause of death. Had the deceased been properly attended the spasm would have passed off, and the poor fellow would have recovered.—The Coroner, in sum- ming up, expressed his satisfaction at the way in which the female witnesses had given their evidence. There was not the slightest hesitation shown in answering questions put to them, and he believed their statements to be trustworthy and true.—A juryman observed that the girls seemed to have done all that might possibly have been expected under the peculiar circumstances in which they were placed. —A verdict to the effect that death was the result of natural causes was recorded.

A Rome correspondent contributes the following to a Man- chester contemporary :—"Mr. Warrington Wood has so many friends and admirers in Manchester that I venture to send you a la, ief account of his continued success here. His de- lightful studio, charmingly situated near the great square of St. John Lateran, has long been one of the favourite resorts of English tourists, and, since the death of Mr. Macdonald, few of our countrymen have secured so high a position in the world of art as the modest and kindly sculptor of whom Lancashire has such just cause to be proud. In Manchester you know Mr. Wood chieily as a sculptor of portrait busts, , but though he has good work in the Town Hall gallery I am 1 not sure that his finest creations can be found there. More- over. no one can visit hji; gi,;;;;;-.7 and study his works, as I have had the opportunity of doing very often this winter, without coining to the conclusion that his artistic instincts are only fully displayed where his imagination is lice and his fancy unfettered, I say this while freely recognising the finished work and excellent likennesses in his best I.leown and more recent busts, notably those of Mr. Childer7, ILord Winmarleigh, the Dean of Wells, &c.; but in his mythological and Scriptural groups we have a truer niesee„.e of his genius and a more accurate idea of the powers. The Villa Campana, which Mr_. 7Yood purchased a year or two ago, formerly contain 'l;,ent of his ther Marquis Campana's Etruscsn gallery, and I?.oine does not contain a studio so admirably adapted for the display of a fine collection of modern sculpture. One wonders some- times at the artist' e patience, at his readiness to conduct his numerous visitors through the gallery and workshops, and at his willingness to explain the method of his workmanship and the mystery of his craft. We see the clay plastic under the master's hand, the marble in various stages of preparation, and, not least interesting, a large collectian of casts, including all Mr. Wood's important works; nor is it surprising that those who are allowed to wander through the alleys of the lovely garden, where winter is so successfully defied, are willing to return often to this charming spot. The first work which attracts a visitor's notice is one of Mr. Wood's most succesful figures, a life-sized Eve, for which he has received several commis- , sions. Another beautiful and effective group is the "Oberon 1 and Titania ; " and assuredly not less artistic are the grace- ful and interesting figures of "Ruth and Naomi." This is, perhaps, Mr. Wood's masterpiece, and is in every respect a notable work; the face of Naomi was evidently suggested by the classic and noble features of a lady whose bust invariably strikes one in entering the studio. I cannot venture, however, to enumerate all the refined and beautiful works which adorn the gallery of our Lancashire sculptor, and must be content with referring to a piece of sculpture which I consider one of the most beautiful creations of modern art, I mean Mr. Wood's lovely group of "The Sisters of Bethany." The inscription on the plinth, " The Master is come and calleth for thee," is scarcely necessary to explain the subject, the pathos of which is wonderfully realised, and it would be difficult to imagine anything more tender and impressive. Those of Mr. Wood's friends who are unacquainted with the fact, will be interested to hear that he was some time ago elected a member of. the Academy of St. Luke, an honour which conveys the high consideration in which he 's held by the most distinguished art society-in Rome.

div.head: VESTRY MEETINGS.
div.p: VESTRY MEETINGS.
RUNCORN.

The annual vestry meeting for the township of Runcorn was held in Bethesda school-room, on Thursday evening. There was a large attendance, and Mr. W. Handley (overseer) presided. There were also present Messrs. H. Coleburn, Robert Shaw, J. J. Speakman, F. Fairhurst, Dr. MacDougall, George Moss, F. J. Adams, John Wilson, W. Rushton, W. Dobson, T. Stringfellow, James Whinyates, J. W. Baguley, J. Richardson, W. Sutton (assistant over- seer), &c.—The first business was the appointment of two ratepayers to audit the accounts of the Burial Board for the veer endine. the 25th instant. Messrs. C. Cook, J. J. Speak- man, W. H. Rogerson, and B. Kniveton were nominated, but on a vote being taken Mr. Speakman and Mr. Kniveton were elected. It was decided to adjourn the meeting until the 12th April to receive the auditor's report.—The nomination of overseers was the next on the agenda, but the CHAIRMAN said that before proceeding with this, it might be interesting to give a little information regarding finance. (Hear, hear.) During the first half of the year ending the 25th inst., the assistant-overseer had collected rates amounting to £1,766, 11 LAIL: 5et;01.13.1. Off, -. heek interest £ll, made total receipts £3,545. There had been paid to the Guardians £2,632; the Burial Board £320; and the School Board £400; making the total amount paid to public authorities £3,352. The cost of collection and office ex- penses WaB .070; eo that tho osponcHturo ceipts by £77, thus reducing the balance of £862 in the bank in March 1882 to £785 in March 1883. When the late Mr. Lyon occupied the chair at the overseer's office he gave the rateable value of Runcorn at £46 630, the number of the assessments being 3,505, but this half -year the rateable value was £49,742, or an increase of £3,112; and the assessments 3,712, increase 207. An alteration of the boundaries between Halton and Runcorn accounted for the increase in the rateable value to the extent of £493 15s Od, and of 42 of the assessments. The size of the township was exactly the same, for whilst Runcorn had received two acres from Halton, it had also lost that acreage to the latter township. This has been done by the orders of the Local Government Board. But the question of the boundaries of Runcorn and Halton was by no means settled, as the present alteration affected only a a small portion. There was only swallowed up in Rnncorn as yet the property in Bridge-street, facing Wilson's Hotel, and running up to the gas works, the property in Irwell- lane, Rowle's shop, Egerton Arms, and the shop at the other corner, with the field running down to Mr. Craig's and Joseph Jeff's shop. These places were now in Runcorn, but there were two pieces of Mill Brow that were yet in Halton although situated in the heart of Runcorn, and he believed the overseers of Halton were taking steps under the Divided Parishes Act to have them also included in Runcorn, not for any benefit of their own, but simply because they were con- tiguous to Runcorn, to which it naturally seemed to belong. Of course this would increase the duties of Mr. Sutton, who, he supposed, must take it as it came, but he hoped that with his increased work. he would not get any lighter than he had for the last two or three years—(laughter)— but would look quite as well. He had given these facts because he thought they might be of interest to the rate- payers. (Applause.) Mr. Handley referred to a surcharge of £5 7s 61 made by Mr. Dolby, the district auditor, being the amount spent in purchasing an ordnance survey with the sanction of the ratepayers. A long correspon- dence had taken place between the auditor, the Local Government Board, and the overseers, with the result that the Board had declared that Mr. Dolby was wrong and the overseers right. (Applause.)—lt was decided that the following names should be submitted to the magistrates : Messrs. W. Handley, W. Whitaker, F. Fairhurst, T. Norman, W. Fisher, and R. Forrester. Only two overseers are required. —On the motion of Dr. MACDOI7GALL, seconded by Mr. STRINGFELLOW, Mr. John Simpson was unanimously re-appointed assessor.—Mr. Sutton was reap- pointed acting assessor and collector of assessed taxes, on the motion of Mr. Moss, seconded by Mr. F. J. ADAMS.— The nomination of five duly qualified ratepayers to serve as guardians was now proceeded with.—lt was pointed out by the CHAIRMAN that whatever was done at the meeting in regard to this matter would not prevent any ratepayer nominating at the proper time and place any person he thoweht proper. The following is a list of the gentlemen nominated with the number of votes given for each :—W. Handley 50, F. Fairhurst 49, T. Norman 42, W. Whitaker 38, P. Speakman 35, W. Fisher 19, F. Rigby 16, John Williams (Top-locks) 9. It was resolved that the first five should be nominated from the meeting, the nomination paper to be signed by Mr. Robert Shaw as the largest rate- payer present.—A vote of thanks haying been passed to the Chairman, the meeting broke up.

div.head: WESiON.
div.p: WESiON.

The annual vestry meeting for the township of Weston was held on Thursday evening in the National schools. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were present : Messrs. T. Handley, Clandet, E. Aaron, T. Ford, Jno. Poole, Wesley Kirkham, Jas. Collier (assistant overseer), &c. It was resolved to submit the names of Mr. Jno. Poole, Mr. Edward Aaron, and Mr. Wesley Kirkham, to the magistrates as gentlemen fit to serve in the office of overseer. Mr. James Handley was unanimously re-elected waywarden. Mr. Edward Aaron was appointed assessor, and Mr. James Collier assessor and collector of assessed taxes.—The CHAIR- MAN read.a letter which had been received from the Local Government Board stating that in future Weston would have two representati*s on the Board of Guardians instead of one as hitherto.—A discussion took place as to whether the meeting should nominate the Guardians or not, the CHAIR- MAN remarking that any ratepayer could nominate a quali- fied person whatever action the meeting took.—The Chair- man and Mr. Clandet were nominated, but it was stated that Mr. James Handley had already been nominated, and the meeting therefore took no further action.—A vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding and for the use of the room concluded the proceedinps.

PRES:OT RATEPATFRS' I.:S;OCIATION.—The members of this association, besides bestirring themselves in connection with the school board election, are also moving in the matter of the forthcoming elections for the Prescot Local Board and the Board of Guardians. For the former board they hays put'in nomination Messrs. IL Fogg, P. G. Twist, and James Appleton; and for the latter Mr. W. Tyrer and Mr. J. T. Hall, the present Guardians for Prescot.

div.head: SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION.
div.p: SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION.

The District Edu.cation Committee reported that during the month of February (four weeks) the numbers of cases summoned before the committee were the following : Application for payment of fees, 78; for contravention of Education Act, 291; total 369. Fees were recommended to be paid in 66 cases. Fifty-three persons were prosecuted before the magistrates, and a like numbei 04 convictions re- corded.—Mr. H. W. DEACoN, k moving the passing of the =mutes, referred to the insufficient accommodation in ele- mentary schools in the South and West districts. In the South district there were, according to the last census, 1,000 children between the ages of three and six, whilst the Board had only accommodation for 559 children between those ages ; and it was Netty clear that they wanted extra accommodation for the infants in tnat district. With regard to Simm's Cross or the West district, the figures were esdall-.. clear. 4ccording to the last census the number of ch.l.l,dren- between three and seven years of age in that `l....istrlet was 1,411. The Board had accommodation. tor 683 infants, and it was therefore quite evicle.;rt that they had a large number of young claildren in excess of the accommodation. The District Education Committee had some hiifficulty in making up its mind as to the best method to suggest for removing this deficiency, and after a good deal of Consideration and con- templation, it was decided to recommend that only West , Bank Infant School should be increased, as there was no sign app irently that the ether departments at West Bank were over full. But at Simm's Cross the case was different. The infant department at Simm's Cross was too small, and he had been informed that if the schools were larger, there would be a much larger attendance. The senior buys' school at Simm's Cross had also grown very rapidly, and whilst there was only accommodation for 160 boys, there were 170 in attendance in 1882. There were 197 infants in average attendance. The committee recommended the immediate enlargement of the senior boys' and the infants' schools at Simms Cross.—The CHAIRMAN remarked as there was a very small Board meeting, not a majority of the members being present, the subject be deferred until the next meeting. In the meantime the members could make enquiries, and form an opinion on the subject.—Father FINNEGAN observed that it was the first time he knew that the accommodation was deficient. He thought it strange that th 3 managers had heard nothing about it.—Mr. HART- LAND said at one time Mr. Deacon asked: Could not some of the senior boys at Simms Cross go to Warrington-road school? There was accommodation there for 200, and surely the senior boys at Simms Cross could walk there. If they would do so the difficulty would be met. The distance was not more than a mile, and boys of 11 to 14 years of age could certainly walk that. [ fhe CHAIR- MAN : It would do them good.] This would be a solution of the difficulty which would save the ratepayers money, as they would not need to expend any money in building.—Mr. DEACON said he had been of that opinion at one time, but after seriously considering the matter he had come to the conclusion that it would not work. The Board would lose in average attendance what small amount they would save by not expending anything in enlarginv the schools. The Board was greatly dependent upon the aver- age attendance for the grant, and a reduction of 10 per cent. in the average attendance would make a great difference in the grant.—The CHAIRMAN coincided to some extent in the views of Mr. Hartland. He asked could they popularise Warrington-toad school by lowering the fee charged there. By charging a lower scale of fees boys might be attracted to that school, and the average attendance and the grant would not be affected.—The CLERK pointed out that in order to get to Warrington-road school a level cross- ing had to be passed, and parents consequently declined to send their children there. There had been two accidents at the crossing during the past month.—The minutes of the committee were passed, but the subject with reference to accommodation was deferred to next meeting. CHANGES IN THE STAFF. -

The School Management made the following recom- mendations, wt.ich were accepted on the motion of the Rev. Father Finnegan :—That the resignation of Mr. Henry Davies, Assistant Master in the Senior Bays' Department, Simmis-cross school, be accepted from March 31st, 1883; that Mr. E. Robinson he appuinted Assistant Master in the Senior Boys' Department, Simm's-cross school, at a salary of £GS per annum, rising according to the scale of the Board; that Phcebe Hinton be engaged as a Monitor at the Simm's-crose schools, at the rate of .E 5 per annum ; and that Margaret Pilling be engaged as a popil teacher, in the Simm's-Cross schools, at a salary according to the scale of the Board, and that the seal of the Board be affixed to her indentures.

The Finance Committes recommended accounts amount- ing to £372 8s 10d for payment. During the m:mth £l5O 173 8d bad been paid into bank. div.head: PRESCOT .SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: PRESCOT .SCHOOL BOARD.

Th. last meeting prior to the triennial election of the members of Prescot School Board was held on Monday evening. Mr. Evans presided, and there were also present Mr. J. Johnson Brown, Mr. W. Goldsworth, and Mr. 11. auemiaimo um.e., VA 1 Duke, Miss McGregor, and Mr. Bartley, teachers, also attended.

div.head: NEGLECTED CHILDREN.
div.p: NEGLECTED CHILDREN.

The Attendance Committee referred to the Board the case of a boy named Peter Johnson.—Mr. BAYLIS said the boys' father was a watchmaker, living in Highfield-place, and was an idle, drunken fellow. His wife appeared to b 3 a hard- working woman, but she was behind with the school fe,s, and had applied to him (Mr. Baylis) for a remission of the fee.—The CHAIRMAN: On account of her husband's worth- lessness? It is hardly a proper ground.—Mr. BROWN ex- pressed a similar opinion, adding that it was on that account the committee had referred the application to the Board.— The CHAIRMAN: I suppose the man can earn money enough if be ebooses to enable his wife to pay the fees ?—Mr. BAYLIS: His wife says he earns enough to pay the fees if he likes.—lt was determined that a summons be itsued against the man for neglecting to send his child to school.

div.head: PRIVATE ADVENTURE SCHOOLS.
div.p: PRIVATE ADVENTURE SCHOOLS.

Miss DUKE mentioned a case *here a woman had been ' allowed a remission of fees on account of her alleged in- , ability to pay them, and yet had recently taken her child from the Board school and sent it to Miss Riley's private school, where the fee was 6d. per week. Miss Duke added that the child had been taken away just before the exami- nation with a view to escaping the examination, and as an excuse for irregular attendance, as no register was kept at Miss Riley's school, and it was not inspected.—Mr. BROWN thought it was driving a regiment of cavalry through the Education Act if there was no record of attendance and so on kept, so that one could judge of the character of the school.—The-Cnaanmax said he should have thought Miss Riley's school would have been examined and certified by Mr. Coward, the Government inspector, as well as the ' church schools.—Mr. BAYLIS remarked that it was hard children should be taught at the Board schools until close ' upon the examinations, and then be taken away ostehsibly to another school to learn sewing and knitting and so on, but in reality to go to no school at all.—Mr. Cnoss said that if a child went to a private school it rested on the parent, in the event of his being summoned before the magistrates, to show that it was receiving an efficient education.—Mr. IlnowN said it was a matter that ought to be tested, because the Board and the ratepayers were suffering injury from the loss of the grant, and for all they knew the children were always suffering injury. —Mr. Cnoss : If that is so it is for the Board to issue a summons, and it will lie on the parent to prove tbat it is going to an efficient school.—Mr. BROWN said no officer of theirs nor any officer of the Government could arrive at the efficiency of the teaching without a record of attendances. —Miss DUKE: Strange to say it is always the best scholars that go; girls that would pass in everything.—Mr. BROWN: And they will be put forward as proof that they are getting good teaching at the private scheols.—lt was resolved to summon the parents of two children named Margaret Berry and Fowler who had ceased to attend school in the way des- cribed by Miss Duke.

div.head: PUPIL TEACHERS.
div.p: PUPIL TEACHERS.

A letter was road from a St. Helens young lady applying for the situation of pupil teacher.—Miss DUKE said several persons had applied, but they were not in want of a pupil teacher at present. Moreover, she did not approve of taking pupil teachers from other schools, preferring that they should come out of their own schools.—Mr. GOLDSWORTH said they had been told they bad no pupils in Present who were fit for pupil teachers.—Miss DUKE hoped they would have some this year. They had some in the fifth standard now.

div.head: INCORRIGIBLE ABSENTEES.
div.p: INCORRIGIBLE ABSENTEES.

Mr. Blum asked for instructions to apply for an atten- dance order in the case of the two children of a man named John Cunningham. The man was a patient in the Royal Infirmary, Liverpool, having been injured at Carr's colliery when the series of accidents occurred there a month or two ago, and his two boys aged, respectively ten and twelve years, were running wild about the streets, having no one to attend to them but their mother, who, he was told, was as often drunk as sober. The father had been already summoned twice, and had been frequently before the attendance committee, but without effect. It was determined to defer taking proceedings until the man came out of the Infirmary, which it was expected he would do shortly. Mr. Baylis also asked for instructions with respect to the children of a man named McGarry who was in gaol for assaulting a constable, and whose children were running about the streets. It was suggested that an attendance order should be applied for as a preliminary to the children being sent to an industrial school, but after some conversation, in the course of which it transpired that there were many similar cases in the district, it was resolved to take no action at present in this isolated case, but to recommend the near board to adopt some rule for dealing with such cases.
The Court of Cassation at Brussels bas rejected the ap- peal for a new trial of the brothers Pelzer, sentenced to death in December last, and the sentence is consequently upheld.

div.head: WESLEYAN METHODISM IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: WESLEYAN METHODISM IN WARRINGTON.

The Marcia quarterly meeting, which is an important one In Methodist circuits, was held for the Warrington circuit in the large vestry of Bold-street Chapel, on Monday after- noon and evening, and proved the most successful meeting that has been held for some time. There was a very large ! attendance of officials and trustees of the circuit, and•for the first time in Warrington the principle meeting was held in the evening. Tea was provided by the circuit stewards, and after tea a vote of thanks was passed to the ladies, on the motion of the Chairman (the Rev. J. Eglinton), supported by Mr. Robert Cook, Rev. J. A. Beet, Mr. E. Ford, and others, for the excellent manner in which they had enter- tained the company. At the formal business meeting the Chairman reported that the members of society had steadily increased during the year, which was an unusual circum- stance after having had to report at two previous March meetings a very large increase. The members of society in the Warrington circuit numbered 826, an increase of 20 upon the previous year, and they might fairly take the con- dition of things in the circuit as cheering and flourishing. —The Rev. J. A. Beet said the figures which had been given amounted to a deal more when they were fairly con- sidered, and he felt that as a circuit they could look forward to further progress. He quoted the figures for the previous three years, which were as follows: 1880, 664 members ; 1881, 724 ; 1882, 806 ; and this year, 826. —ln reply to the Chairman, the circuit stewards expressed their intention of being present at , the May district meeting, which is this year to be held at I Preston.—The society stewards then proposed that Mr. Egllnton be requeeteci to remain in the circuit another year, land the proposition was supported by many of the infiuen- tial brethren present.—The CHAIRMAN, in replying, stated that he had been very happy in the circuit, and he would ; stay if the doctor in whose hands he left the matter said it I would not he injurious to his health to stay in this atmos- phere another 12 months.—Mr. RIPPON was then formally I invited to stay a third year, and the invitation being warmly I supported by members from all parts of the circuit, he inti- mated his willingness to remain another year. The society ! stewards afterwards proposed that a bonus should be given Ito Mr. Rippon for his services during the coming 18 months. —The Rev. J. Agar Beet, whose name is familiar to all students of Gospel history, will have completed the third year of his ministry in Warrington in August next, and he then leaves to take the superintendence of the Wrexham circuit in Norih Waks. It was. Therefor., necessary Tor tne meeting to invite some other minister to succeed -him here, and the Rev. James McTurle, of 131ixtou Hill, who bad been recommended by Sir William McArthur, Mr. James McArthur. and Mr. Vickers was formally invited to fill the place of Mr. Beet. Mr. McTurk was a fellow- student with Mr. Beet, who, in recommending him to the meeting, said he was sure that they could not help but love him, and that he would be very acceptable to the Warring- ton circuit. The report on the state of the Sunday schools, , which showed that there were 229 officers and 1,902 scholars, was submitted, and the meeting concluded.

PADGATE WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEM.FNT SOCIETY. The last lecture of the session was delivered in the Wes- leyan schoolroom on Tuesday, by the Rev Joseph Agar Beet. There was a good attendance. The chair was taken by Mr. Edwin Richardson, who, after a few appropriate in- troductory remarks, called upon Mr. Beet to proceed with his lecture on "The historical grounds of the Christian hope." The reverend gentleman commenced by referring to the prevalence of scepticism in these days, and spoke of the duty of acquiring such a knowledge of the Christian evidences as should enable us to be at all times prepared to give a reason, for "the hope that is within us." Having re- marked upon the fact that in every race the human mind had a perception of the distinction between right and wrong and traced this distinction to its logical source, viz., the existence of God, who had endowed mankind with this faculty of telling good from evil, Mr. Beet went on to say that naturally there fore the pursuit of good ought to end in good, and vice versa; that this was not so always in the world, for many good men were called upon to undergo suffering whilst many bad men prospered. This was not a logical outcome of our power to distinguish between good and evil, and hence we took refuge in the belief in a future state of existence where this could be remedied. Thus we had a belief in a supreme being and in the immortality of the human soul. This much admitted, had we the means of knowing anything about God and the future? Yes; we had the Bible. Was that a reliable revelation? Speaking generally, it was. Mr. Beet then elaborately proved this by reference to the epistles of St. Paul, of which MSS existed over fifteen hundred years old. Before that period Eusebius, Origen, Tertullian, and others had written works that plainly proved that the epistles existed at that time, were admitted to have been written by Paul, and were re- garded as undoubtedly authentic. It was clear from abundant evidence that Paul lived, that Paul wrote the letters attributed to him, that he believed the truth of what he wrote, that, though himself a master mind and little likely to accept unfounded opinions, he firmly believed in Christ, and bowed down his own intellect before One whom he was well assured was infinitely above him. He firmly believed in the crucifixion and ite resurrection, and other evidence amply corrobcrated these events. This proved, it followed that Christ was divine, which granted, the general acceptance of the rest of the Bible followed as a matter of conrse, all other difficulties dwindling when the primary fact of the death and resurrection of Christ was admitted, and the numerous alleged discrepancies and imperfections in the sacred record being comparatively easy of explanation. The lecture was listened to with great interest, Mr. Beet starting with no premises which could not be allowed, and gradually building up his argument in the most logical and masterly manner, and leading to the irresistible conclusion that there were many very good grounds indeed for the Christian hope, in spite of numerous current assertions to the contrary.---On the motion of Mr. Arthur Bennett, seconded by Mr. Thos. Corbett, a warm vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, and a similar compliment having been paid to the chairman, the doxology was sung and the meeting separated.

MR. Limn FILDES.—Mr. Luke Fildes, A.R A., will send to the Royal Academy a single picture, but this a very large and important one. The artist has been engaged on this work, "The Village Wedding," for considerably more than a year, and there is still so much to be done to it that it will occupy him until sending-in day. The scene is the open street of a Berkshire village, under a mid-day light. The painter has carefully eschewed anything like an ideal treat- ment of the procession ; the bridal pair are dressed in brand-new garments, such as approve themselves on Sun- days to a rnral taste. Behind them walk the mother of the bride; the bride's brother, a magnificent Lifeguardsman, and the sweetheart of the latter; and then the bridegroom's father, with other friends. The villagers, in their far more appropriate and picturesque everyday clothes, stand by in groups to watch the procession. The whole composition is a realistic page out of the actual village life of Southern England in 1882, and will possess great value to the anti- quarians of a century hence. It is likely to be one of the most popular pictures of the year.—Pall M 1 Gazette. j

The rev, gentleman illustrated his lecture by a number of large portrait., and treated his sub- ject in a manner which made it highly interesting, and sheered that he mutt have made phrenology or mental science a favourite study. At the close of the lecture Mr. Trotter gave the ecience a practical turn, and explained correctly the leading characteristics of several of the au- dience, who submitted to a phrenological examination. ALLEGED 'I RIFT OF FOWLS BY A FRODSHAM MAX.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Wedneeday, William Gardner, a respectable-looking man, was brought up on remand charged with stealing, on Sunday, six fowls' the property of Mr. D. T. Baguley, farmer, of Stockharn. From the evidence, it seemed that early on Sunday morning Mr. Baguley missed a number of fowls from his hencote. Among the missing birds wag a pure-bred Brahma cockerel. P.S. Lowndes was informed of the circumstance, and accompanied by P.C. Egerton he proceeded to the spot. During the night there had been a fall of snow, and the ground was covered lo a depth of several inches. Leading from the door of the hen cote were the footprints of a man, and these the officers traced to Hilton station, across the railway, and along Frodsbam side of the river to the prisoner's house at Overton. A search was here made, and a quantity of feathers was found. The wing of the cockerel was drawn from a concealed place, while in the oven a very large fowl was being roasted. The prisoner stated he had purchased the fowl on the previous evening for 28. 6d., but he was arrested and conveyed to the cells at Runcorn. The other fowls had not been discovered.—The prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Knuts- ferd Sessions.
