div.head: NANTWICH.
div.p: NANTWICH.

A &WORM IMPOSTBR.—A somewhat remarkable case of supposed swindling was heard on Tuesday evening at Nantwich, before Mr. Wilbraham Tollernache. The prisoner Mary Jones, alias Jane Clarke, was charged with obtaining various sums of money by false pretences from Mrs. Captain Cotton, Reaseheath, Nantwich, wife of the Conservative candidate for West Cheshire; Baroness Schroeder, Mr. Frank Behrens, IP., Mrs. Captain Massie, and several other influential ladies and gentlemen. The prisoner, a respectably-dressed woman, called at the residences of the ladies and gentlemen in question, and represented that she required sums of money to take several orphan children to London, to place in asylums. She showed a bill-bead from the Clerk at Nantwich Railway Station, stating that a ticket and a half from Nantwich Station to London would be £1 Os. 4id. The presiding magistrate said he sent her 2s. through his butler for suite another purpose. Prisoner, who was stated to be a stranger, was remanded till Saturday.

A YOUNG MAN DROWNED.—On Wednesday evening the body of a young man named Peach was discovered in the river Weaver at Winsford. Peach was last seen alive on Tuesday evening, and nothing further was heard of him until he was found dead in the river. How he got into the water is a mystery.

SeLvaTioi Sunday last the section of the army, at Winsford, bad one of their special days when, as the handbills proclaimed, "Staff Captain Black" would be assisted by about" 200 of the King's sons and daughters." They paraded the streets preceded by the band, which greatly attracted a certain set, bnt were anything but at- tractive to the church and chapel goers, the streets looking more as if there was a club walk. Those who were going to places of worship found some difficulty in getting through the crowds of roughs attracted by the band, SUBSIDENCE AT WINSFORD.—The premises occupied by Mr. Williams, printer, and Mr. Blackburn, butcher, High- street, having become dangerous owing to subsidence, are under repair, and might have been the scene of a serious accident. The walls of Mr. Williams printing shop being in a leaning state, he was having them put right, and the men having finished one wall began with the other, when bylo old =Atte uumtpzuet. Iwo Eta were nnuer the bui!ding, but were fortunately uninjured owing to some beams holding the erection just over them. Those who were inside escaped with a few bruises, but the printing machine and type were greatly damaged.

GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MOTEMENT.—During last week, in addition to the Salvation Army and Blue Ribbon Army there kas been a pushing to the fore of the Free Methodist Tem- perance workers, led on by the Rev. J. W. Chishohn, of Liverpool, who night after night had the hearty co-opera- tion of the ministers and friends of other Christian churches in the town—The Revs. J. T. Maxwell, J. Wright, and W. T. Symons, while the chair was taken respectively by Mr. J. Slater, Mr. E. Leigh, Dr. H. Leak, Mr. J. Dodd, and other brethren of the various Methodist bodies. Darin, the week nearly 300 took the ribbon, and 160 signed the pledge. The friends purpose holding regular meetings to secure by train- ing those recently added. On Tuesday night a public meet- ing for the same purpose was held by the Primitives of Station-road, when addresses were delivered on the Gospel Temperance question by the Rev. T. Turner and Messrs. Jabez Hulse, W. G. Newall, and the chairman (dr. G. Rogerson), while the choir sang with great effect several melodies and songs and Mr. J. A. Dale sang a solo.

A ROUGH CUSTOMER —PMrick Donnellan was charged at Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with being drunk and disorderly and refusing to quit the ht. Patrick Inn, Ketnble- street, Prescet. He was further charged with assaulting Miss Kenny, the landlord's sister.—P.C. Middlebrook stated that on Saturday night, the 17th instant, be heard a distur- bance in the St. Patrick Inn, and saw several persons trying to eject defendant, who was drunk, from the premises. He refused to go, and struck Miss Kenny on the face and tore her clothes--Miss Kenny gave corroborative evidence.— For the assault defendant was fined 20s. and costs, and for the other offence 103. and costs; or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment in each case. A WARNING TO APPRENTICES. - An application was made by Mr. J. 0. Swift at the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, on behalf of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, for an order to send a lad named John Bishop to prison for neglect of work. It appeared that on the 2nd October last the de- fendant had been brought before the Bench on a charge of neglecting his work, and an order for more regular attend- ance was thenlmade upon him. Since that time, however, he had shown no improvement; and Mr. Swift said, asde- fendant set a very bad example to other apprentices, his em- ployers bad no option but to ask that he should be sent to gaol.—Defendant was ordered to gaol for fourteen days.

Well, Lewis's are as well known in Liver- pool as the Pank-of England Is known in London. Lewis's began business in Liverpool thirty years ago. and Lewis's have at this present time one of the very largest businesses in Eng- land. Lewis's have not always sold Tea, but having a very large number of employes to provide with an afternoon meal, Lewis's were struck with the difficulty of procuring a good drinkable and refreshing Tea for them at a moderate price. The ordinary Teas were perfectly abominable. Tired of the constant and not unreasonable complaints and of the perpetual changing of their [Tea Dealers, Lewis's at last resolved t buy their Tea for the use of their establishment direct from the shippers, and to en- gage a qualified person to make the purchase. Lewis's could hardly believe there could be such, a ehange for the better in the cost and quality of the ;ea so , bought, but "experience teaches." Lewis's thought what was good enough for the use of all their establishments, public and private, would sorely be good enough for the general public. Lewis's then began to sell Teas to their friends, and at last were induced to make thesale public in Lancashire where they sell 20 000 pounds of Tea per week. Lewis', now feel they have benefited only a small pro- portion of the population; they intend in future to make their Tea known all over the United Kingdom. Lewis's pure, splendid Tea, is one stated price, 2s a paund. Lewis s have no other price Tea, neither higher nor lower, and this Two Shilling Tea is fit for the Queen to drink. Two shil- lings is a favourite prise with I ewis's, they having been able to supply the public with many excellent things at the price. Not till after much hard work did Lewis's succeed in blending a splendid and most eellciously-flavoured Tea- which they are giving to the public for 2s a pound. Many tea dealers charge the public 3s and Es ad for a similar quatty. Lewis's desire to be the universal suppliers of Tea. Tea is drunk in every house- hold in the United Tithed ; it should therefore be sold at a less profit than any other article of consumption, except bread. Lewis's wish particularly to direct the attention of every family and every househm der to the great advantage there lain buying Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The flavour is so good and the strcraita F o very great. that one pound goes further than 18 ounces of most other Teas, providing always the water boils thoroughly. The proof that Lewis's do not exaggerate the appreciation in which their Two Shilling Tea is held lies in the fact that they receive thousands of orders every day from all parts of the United Kingdom. Lewis's would like members of the Press all over the United Kingdom to write for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Ti a; they are sure to be satisfied tied astonished with h the result. Every hotel-keeper, and every public and private institution throughout the country, should write to Lewis's in Liverpool for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tea.
